nodeData.note: How to account for renting or hiring an asset under IFRS 16. A lessee shows what it may use (a right-of-use asset) and what it owes (a lease liability) on its statement of financial position, instead of just booking rent as an expense.

children.topic: What a lease is and why
children.note: Start here: the words, the idea of control, and why the old rules were replaced.

children.topic: Lease = paying to use an asset
children.note: A lease is a contract that gives you the right to use someone else's identified asset for a period, in return for payment.

manas.q: What is a lease under IFRS 16?

children.note: The lessee is the one who uses the asset and pays (the tenant). The lessor is the owner who receives the payments (the landlord).

manas.q: Who is the lessee and who is the lessor?

children.note: A duka renting its shop, a clinic leasing an X-ray machine, a matatu owner leasing vehicles, a firm renting office floors in Westlands. All can fall under IFRS 16.
Before 2019, IAS 17 let lessees keep 'operating leases' off the balance sheet and just expense the rent. Big debts for rented shops, planes and offices stayed hidden from readers.
IFRS 16 Leases took effect for periods starting on or after 1 January 2019 and replaced IAS 17. Its aim is a faithful picture of lease deals in the accounts.

manas.q: When did IFRS 16 become effective and what did it replace?

children.note: Under IFRS 16 a lessee puts almost every lease on the balance sheet: a right-of-use asset plus a lease liability. Only short leases and low-value items may be left off.

manas.q: What is the single lessee model?

children.note: Ask: is there an identified asset? Does the customer get almost all the benefits from using it? Does the customer decide how and for what it is used? Yes to all means a lease.
A specific asset, named in the contract or clearly implied. If the supplier can freely swap it for another and gains from doing so, there is no identified asset.

manas.q: When is an asset not an identified asset?

children.note: The customer, not the supplier, decides how and for what purpose the asset is used during the period.

children.topic: Example: van with or without driver
children.note: A van you choose routes for, kept at your depot, is likely a lease. A courier who sends any van it likes to deliver your parcels is a service, not a lease.
The right-of-use asset is depreciated much like PPE under IAS 16 (topic 1). Service parts of a contract are kept apart, as in IFRS 15 (topic 3).
How a lessee measures the lease on day 1 and in later years.
The non-cancellable period, plus extension periods you are reasonably certain to use, plus periods after a break option you are reasonably certain not to use.

manas.q: How is the lease term worked out?

children.note: The present value of the lease payments not yet paid at the start date, discounted at the right rate.

manas.q: How is the lease liability measured at the start?

children.note: Fixed payments (less incentives), payments linked to an index or rate, expected residual value guarantees, a purchase option price if reasonably certain, and break penalties if expected.

manas.q: What goes into lease payments?

children.note: Use the rate implicit in the lease if you can work it out. If not, use the lessee's incremental borrowing rate: what it would pay to borrow for a similar asset and term.

manas.q: What discount rate does a lessee use?

children.note: Cost = lease liability + payments made on or before the start − incentives received + initial direct costs + estimated costs to remove or restore the asset.

manas.q: What makes up the cost of a right-of-use asset?

children.note: Each period add interest (opening balance × rate) and take off payments. Interest goes to profit or loss as a finance cost.
Depreciate the right-of-use asset, usually straight line. Use the shorter of lease term and useful life, unless ownership passes to you, then use useful life.

manas.q: Over what period is a right-of-use asset depreciated?

children.note: Leases of 12 months or less with no purchase option may be expensed straight line instead. Example: a 6-month site office rental.

manas.q: What is the short-term lease exemption?

children.note: Small items like laptops, phones or office chairs may be expensed. Judge the value when new, not second-hand. The IASB had about US$5,000 or less in mind.

manas.q: What is the low-value lease exemption?

children.topic: Where it shows in the accounts
children.note: Balance sheet: right-of-use asset and lease liability (split current and non-current). Profit or loss: depreciation and interest. Cash flow: capital repaid under financing.

manas.q: How are leases shown in the lessee's financial statements?

children.note: If the lease term or payments change, recalculate the liability and adjust the right-of-use asset by the same amount.
A full lessee example from day 1 to year 5. All figures computed and rounded to the nearest shilling. The 10% rate is illustrative only.

Afya Clinic, Nairobi, leases an X-ray machine from 1 Jan Year 1 for 5 years. It pays KES 1,000,000 at the end of each year. Rate: 10% (illustrative). Legal fees to arrange it: KES 50,000. Useful life 8 years; no ownership transfer.
5-year annuity factor at 10% = 3.7908. PV = KES 1,000,000 × 3.790787 (unrounded factor) = KES 3,790,787, rounded to the shilling. This is the opening lease liability.
Liability KES 3,790,787 + initial direct costs KES 50,000 = right-of-use asset KES 3,840,787.
Dr Right-of-use asset KES 3,790,787 / Cr Lease liability KES 3,790,787. Then Dr Right-of-use asset KES 50,000 / Cr Cash KES 50,000.
Opening + interest at 10% − payment = closing. Total interest over 5 years is KES 1,209,213, which equals total payments KES 5,000,000 less the PV KES 3,790,787.
Opening KES 3,790,787 + interest KES 379,079 − payment KES 1,000,000 = closing KES 3,169,866.
Opening KES 3,169,866 + interest KES 316,987 − payment KES 1,000,000 = closing KES 2,486,853.
Opening KES 2,486,853 + interest KES 248,685 − payment KES 1,000,000 = closing KES 1,735,538.
Opening KES 1,735,538 + interest KES 173,554 − payment KES 1,000,000 = closing KES 909,092.
Opening KES 909,092 + interest KES 90,908 − payment KES 1,000,000 = closing KES 0. Interest is cut by KES 1 to clear rounding and close at exactly zero.
31 Dec: Dr Finance cost KES 379,079 / Cr Lease liability KES 379,079. Dr Lease liability KES 1,000,000 / Cr Cash KES 1,000,000.

Lease term 5 years is shorter than useful life 8, so use 5. KES 3,840,787 ÷ 5 = KES 768,157 a year (year 5 is KES 768,159 to absorb rounding). Dr Depreciation KES 768,157 / Cr Right-of-use asset KES 768,157.
Right-of-use asset KES 3,072,630. Lease liability KES 3,169,866: non-current KES 2,486,853 (end year 2 balance) and current KES 683,013.
Depreciation KES 768,157 + interest KES 379,079 = KES 1,147,236, more than the KES 1,000,000 cash paid. Costs are higher early on and fall as interest shrinks.
Lessors still use two types, much like the old IAS 17: finance leases and operating leases.
A finance lease passes almost all the risks and rewards of owning the asset to the lessee. Every other lease is an operating lease.

manas.q: How does a lessor classify a lease?

children.note: Ownership passes at the end, a cheap purchase option, the term covers most of the asset's life, PV of payments is close to its fair value, or the asset is specialised.
Remove the asset and show a receivable equal to the net investment in the lease. Earn interest income on it over the term.

manas.q: How does a lessor account for a finance lease?

children.note: Keep the asset and depreciate it under IAS 16. Recognise lease income straight line over the term.

manas.q: How does a lessor account for an operating lease?

children.note: A landlord lets a shop for 3 years: year 1 free, years 2 and 3 at KES 900,000. Total KES 1,800,000 ÷ 3 = KES 600,000 income a year. Year 1: Dr Accrued rent receivable 600,000 / Cr Rental income 600,000.
A business sells its building and rents it back. If it is a true sale under IFRS 15, the seller keeps a right-of-use asset and recognises only the gain on the rights passed over.
Places where students lose easy marks.
Old IAS 17 habit. Under IFRS 16 a lessee capitalises the lease unless it is short-term or low-value.
If payments are made at the start of each year, the first payment is not discounted and is removed before you charge interest.
Initial direct costs, payments before the start and restoration costs go into the right-of-use asset, not the liability.
Use the shorter of lease term and useful life, unless ownership transfers or a purchase option is reasonably certain.
Current part = this year's closing balance minus next year's closing balance. Do not just take the next payment, which includes interest (arrears case).
Many small Kenyan firms use IFRS for SMEs, which still uses the older finance/operating split for lessees. Check which framework the question says.
Try each one before opening the answer steps. Rates are illustrative.
Matatu SACCO leases a bus for 4 years, paying KES 500,000 on 1 Jan each year, first payment on day 1. Rate 8%. Find the liability at end of year 1 and its split.
KES 500,000 paid now + KES 500,000 × 3-year annuity factor at 8% = KES 1,788,548. Dr Right-of-use asset / Cr Lease liability KES 1,788,548.
After the day-1 payment the balance is KES 1,288,548. Interest 8% = KES 103,084. Closing year 1 = KES 1,391,632.
The 1 Jan year 2 payment of KES 500,000 reduces the debt within 12 months, so current KES 500,000; non-current KES 891,632. Total KES 1,391,632.
A small firm rents a printer for KES 4,000 a month for 3 years. How should it account?
A new printer of this kind is low value, so the exemption can be used.
Expense KES 48,000 a year (4,000 × 12). Dr Printer rental expense 48,000 / Cr Cash 48,000. No asset or liability is recognised.
A lessor leases a machine for 9 years. Its useful life is 10 years and PV of payments is 96% of fair value. Finance or operating?
The term covers most of the asset's life, and PV of payments is close to fair value.
Finance lease. The lessor removes the machine and shows a net investment receivable.

nodeData.note: How a company shows the tax on its profits: the tax owed for this year (current tax) and the tax effect of timing gaps that reverse later (deferred tax).

children.note: A company pays tax on its profits. IAS 12 tells you how to show that tax in the accounts: the tax owed for this year and the tax effects that will come back in later years.
A limited company is taxed on its own profits, separate from its owners. In Kenya this is called corporation tax and it is collected by KRA.
KRA's page (read 3 Nov 2026) shows resident companies at 30% and non-resident companies at 37.5%. Check the current KRA rate before you use it.

manas.q: What corporation tax rate does a Kenyan resident company pay?

children.topic: Two kinds of tax in accounts
children.note: Current tax is the tax for this year's taxable profit. Deferred tax is tax that belongs to this year's profit but will be paid or saved in a later year.

manas.q: What are the two parts of the income tax charge under IAS 12?

children.note: The accounts follow IFRS; the tax return follows the tax law. Some items are counted at different times, and some are never allowed for tax, so the two profits differ.
Tax is often one of the biggest costs in the income statement. Getting it wrong misstates profit, liabilities and the cash the business must set aside.
Depreciation (IAS 16), amortisation (IAS 38), revenue timing (IFRS 15) and leases (IFRS 16) all create gaps between accounts and tax. IAS 12 deals with the tax effect of those gaps.

children.topic: Current tax: tax for this year
children.note: Current tax is what the company expects to pay KRA on this year's taxable profit. It is an estimate at year end and is settled later.
Start with accounting profit, add back things tax does not allow (like depreciation and fines), then take off what tax does allow (like tax depreciation). The result is taxable profit.

manas.q: How do you get from accounting profit to taxable profit?

children.note: If the company has not yet paid all of this year's tax, the unpaid part is shown as current tax payable, a current liability.

manas.q: How is unpaid current tax shown?

children.note: If the company paid more during the year than it finally owes, the extra is shown as a current tax asset (a refund or credit due).

manas.q: How is overpaid current tax shown?

children.note: Use the tax rates that are law, or as good as law (enacted or substantively enacted), at the reporting date. Do not use a rate that is only proposed.

manas.q: Which tax rate does IAS 12 use to measure current tax?

children.note: Last year's estimate was too low and KRA's final figure was higher. The extra is added to this year's tax charge. It is not a prior-year restatement.

manas.q: What is an under-provision and how is it treated?

children.note: Last year's estimate was too high. The difference reduces this year's tax charge.

manas.q: What is an over-provision and how is it treated?

children.note: Kenyan companies usually pay tax in instalments during the year (check KRA guidance on dates). These payments reduce the liability at year end.
Deferred tax records the future tax effect of gaps that will reverse. It makes the tax charge match the profit shown in the accounts.
The figure for an asset or liability in the statement of financial position, for example a machine at cost less accounting depreciation.
The value the tax authority gives an asset or liability. For a machine, it is cost less tax depreciation already claimed.

manas.q: What is the tax base of an asset?

children.note: The gap between carrying amount and tax base. It will reverse as the asset is used up or sold.

manas.q: What is a temporary difference?

children.note: When an asset's carrying amount is above its tax base, more tax will be paid later. This creates a deferred tax liability (DTL).

manas.q: When does an asset give a deferred tax liability?

children.note: When an asset's carrying amount is below its tax base (or a liability's carrying amount is above its tax base), less tax will be paid later. This can create a deferred tax asset (DTA).

manas.q: When does a deductible temporary difference arise?

children.note: Deferred tax = temporary difference × tax rate expected when it reverses (using enacted or substantively enacted rates). Compare with last year's balance to get the movement.

manas.q: What is the formula for deferred tax?

children.note: Items never allowed or never taxed, such as fines and penalties. They change current tax only. No deferred tax arises on them.

manas.q: Does a permanent difference create deferred tax?

children.note: Usually to profit or loss. If the item went to other comprehensive income (like a revaluation), its deferred tax goes there too.

manas.q: Where is the deferred tax movement recognised?

children.note: These are the everyday items that create deferred tax in Kenyan company accounts.
Tax allowances often write assets off faster than accounting depreciation. Carrying amount stays above tax base, so a DTL builds up and later reverses.
A revaluation lifts the carrying amount but not the tax base. The deferred tax on the surplus is charged to other comprehensive income, not profit or loss.
A warranty provision is expensed now but allowed for tax only when paid. Example: provision KES 400,000 × 30% = DTA KES 120,000.
A loss carried forward can cut future tax. Recognise a DTA only if future taxable profits are probable. Example: KES 1,000,000 × 30% = KES 300,000.
The right-of-use asset and lease liability usually have different tax bases from their carrying amounts, so deferred tax arises on both sides.

children.topic: DTA needs proof of future profit
children.note: Only recognise a deferred tax asset to the extent it is probable the business will earn enough taxable profit to use it. Review this every year.

manas.q: When can a deferred tax asset be recognised?

children.note: Jambo Ltd, a Nairobi furniture maker, year 1. Tax rate 30% (check the current KRA rate). All figures in KES and checked.
Profit before tax 10,000,000 + fines (not allowed) 500,000 + accounting depreciation 2,000,000 − tax depreciation 3,600,000 = taxable profit 8,900,000.
Taxable profit 8,900,000 × 30% = current tax 2,670,000.
Last year Jambo provided 1,800,000 but KRA agreed 1,950,000. Under-provision = 150,000, added to this year's charge.
2,670,000 + 150,000 = 2,820,000 in profit or loss. Year-end liability for this year = 2,670,000.
Had KRA agreed only 1,700,000, the over-provision of 100,000 would cut the charge to 2,670,000 − 100,000 = 2,570,000.

children.topic: Example 2: deferred tax on a machine
children.note: Machine cost 6,000,000, accounting depreciation 2,000,000 a year for 3 years. Illustrative tax depreciation: 3,600,000, 1,800,000, 600,000 (not real KRA rates).
Carrying amount 4,000,000; tax base 2,400,000; difference 1,600,000 × 30% = DTL 480,000. Movement +480,000 (charge).
Carrying amount 2,000,000; tax base 600,000; difference 1,400,000 × 30% = DTL 420,000. Movement −60,000 (credit to tax expense).
Carrying amount 0; tax base 0; difference 0, so DTL 0. Movement −420,000 (credit). Over 3 years the movements add to zero.
Both methods write off the full 6,000,000 in the end. Deferred tax only smooths the timing so the tax charge follows accounting profit.
Jambo's entries for tax in year 1, using Examples 1 and 2.
Dr Income tax expense 2,670,000 / Cr Current tax payable 2,670,000.
Dr Income tax expense 150,000 / Cr Current tax payable 150,000. Then on settling: Dr Current tax payable 1,950,000 / Cr Bank 1,950,000.
Dr Income tax expense 480,000 / Cr Deferred tax liability 480,000.
DTL falls from 480,000 to 420,000: Dr Deferred tax liability 60,000 / Cr Income tax expense 60,000.
Profit before tax 10,000,000; tax expense 3,300,000 (2,670,000 + 150,000 + 480,000); profit after tax 6,700,000.
Explains why tax is 33% of profit, not 30%. Profit 10,000,000 × 30% = 3,000,000.
150,000 relating to last year.

children.topic: What to show in the accounts
children.note: How tax appears in the statements and notes.
One line, income tax expense, made of current tax, prior-year adjustments and the deferred tax movement.

manas.q: What makes up the income tax expense line?

children.note: Current tax payable (or asset) goes in current liabilities (or current assets).
Deferred tax goes in non-current items, never current. DTA and DTL can be offset only when they relate to the same tax authority and there is a legal right to offset.

manas.q: Is deferred tax current or non-current?

children.note: Show the split of the tax charge, the tax rate reconciliation and the deferred tax movement by type of difference.
Smaller Kenyan companies using IFRS for SMEs follow a similar idea in its income tax section, with simpler disclosure.
Where students lose easy marks.
An under- or over-provision goes through this year's tax charge. Do not reopen last year's accounts.

children.topic: Charging the full DTL each year
children.note: Only the movement (closing minus opening DTL) goes to profit or loss, not the whole balance.
Fines and other permanent differences never create deferred tax.
Asset carrying amount above tax base gives a liability, not an asset. Draw the table to check.
Use the rate enacted or substantively enacted at year end, not a hoped-for future cut.
Deferred tax on a revaluation surplus goes to OCI with the surplus.

children.topic: Tax payable is not the tax charge
children.note: Year-end tax payable is the unpaid tax for this year. The charge also holds prior-year adjustments and deferred tax, so the two figures differ.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Last year provision 800,000, KRA agreed 760,000. This year's estimate 1,200,000. Find the charge and liability.
Year-end liability = 1,200,000 (this year's estimate).
Asset carrying amount 900,000, tax base 600,000, rate 30%. Opening DTL 60,000. Find the charge.
Difference = 900,000 − 600,000 = 300,000 taxable.
Movement = 90,000 − 60,000 = 30,000. Dr Tax expense 30,000 / Cr DTL 30,000.
Profit before tax 5,000,000, non-deductible costs 200,000, rate 30%, no other items. Find tax expense and effective rate.
Extra on disallowed costs 200,000 × 30% = 60,000. Tax expense = 1,560,000.

maps.title: CA23 · 6. Provisions and events after the year end

nodeData.topic: Provisions and events after the year end
nodeData.note: How to treat uncertain bills (provisions), possible bills and claims (contingencies), and news that arrives after the year end. Covers IAS 37 and IAS 10 for CPA Intermediate.

children.note: Some bills are certain, some are only likely, and some are just possible. IAS 37 tells you which ones go into the accounts. IAS 10 tells you what to do with news that arrives after the year end but before the accounts are signed.
If a business hides a likely bill, profit looks better than it really is. These two standards stop that and make sure readers hear about big risks and big news.

IAS 37 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets covers uncertain bills and claims. IAS 10 Events after the Reporting Period covers what happens between the year end and the signing date.

children.topic: Small Kenyan companies: IFRS for SMEs
children.note: Many smaller Kenyan entities use IFRS for SMEs. Section 21 covers provisions and contingencies and Section 32 covers events after the end of the reporting period. The ideas are almost the same.

Site restoration cost is added to the asset under IAS 16 (topic 1). Assurance warranties sit in IAS 37, while extra service warranties are a separate performance obligation under IFRS 15 (topic 3). Many provisions are tax deductible only when paid, giving deferred tax under IAS 12 (topic 5).
A provision is a bill you are fairly sure you owe, but you do not know exactly how much or exactly when you will pay it.
A liability where the timing or the amount is uncertain. Example: a duka owner who sold phones with a 1-year guarantee knows some will come back but not how many.

manas.q: What is a provision under IAS 37?

children.note: A trade payable has an invoice with a known amount and date. An accrual is a close estimate with little doubt. A provision has much more uncertainty, so it is shown separately.
Recognise a provision only when all three are met: (1) a present obligation from a past event, (2) paying out is probable, (3) the amount can be estimated reliably.

manas.q: What are the three tests for recognising a provision?

children.topic: Present obligation from a past event
children.note: Something has already happened that ties you in, and you have no realistic way out. Plans for the future alone never create an obligation.
An obligation that comes from a contract, a law or a regulation. Example: NEMA licence terms that require a quarry to be restored.

manas.q: What is a legal obligation?

children.note: An obligation that comes from the business’s own behaviour: a published policy or a long habit that makes customers rightly expect it to pay. Example: a supermarket that always refunds unhappy customers even with no legal duty.

manas.q: What is a constructive obligation?

children.topic: Probable means more likely than not
children.note: In IAS 37, probable means a chance of more than 50%. If the chance is lower, you do not recognise a provision.

manas.q: What does "probable" mean in IAS 37?

children.note: Only in very rare cases can no reliable estimate be made. If so, you disclose a contingent liability instead.
Once a provision passes the tests, you must put a number on it. The goal is the amount the business would sensibly pay to settle or pass on the obligation at the year end.
Measure at the amount the entity would rationally pay to settle the obligation, or transfer it to someone else, at the year end, allowing for risks and uncertainties.

manas.q: How is a provision measured?

children.note: For a large group of similar items, like warranties on 5,000 fridges, weight each possible cost by its probability and add them up.

manas.q: When do you use expected value for a provision?

children.note: For a single obligation, like one court case, the most likely outcome is usually the best estimate. Look at other outcomes too: if most are higher, lean higher.

manas.q: How do you measure a single obligation, like one court case?

children.note: If the payment is far in the future and the time value of money is material, use the present value. Use a pre-tax rate that reflects current market conditions.

manas.q: When is a provision discounted?

children.note: Each year the present value grows towards the full amount. The increase is a finance cost: Dr Finance cost / Cr Provision.

manas.q: What is the unwinding of the discount and where does it go?

children.note: If an insurer will pay part of the bill, show a separate asset only when the money is virtually certain. Never net it off the provision on the balance sheet (it may be netted in profit or loss).

manas.q: How are reimbursements, like insurance, treated?

children.note: Check each provision at every year end and adjust it to the current best estimate. Release it if payment is no longer probable.

children.topic: Use only for its own purpose
children.note: A warranty provision may only absorb warranty costs. You cannot use it to soak up other expenses.
Some situations come up again and again in exams. Learn these rules by heart.
Expected losses next year are not a present obligation, so no provision. They are a sign the assets may be impaired.

manas.q: Can you provide for future operating losses?

children.note: A contract where the unavoidable costs of meeting it are higher than the benefits you will get. Provide for the lower of the cost of fulfilling it and the penalty for leaving it.

manas.q: What is an onerous contract and how is it measured?

children.note: Provide only when there is a detailed formal plan AND those affected have been told or work has started. A board decision kept secret is not enough.

manas.q: When can a restructuring provision be made?

children.note: Only direct costs that the restructuring must cause, such as redundancy pay. Exclude retraining, relocating staff, marketing and new systems.
If putting up an asset creates a duty to clean up later, provide for the present value now and add the same amount to the asset cost under IAS 16.
A future service of a matatu or plant overhaul is not a present obligation. The business could sell the asset and avoid it. Use IAS 16 component depreciation instead.
A fine for a breach that has already happened, or damage already caused where law or public promise requires clean-up, is a present obligation.
These are possible items, not certain enough to put in the main figures. Usually you only write about them in the notes.
Either a possible obligation that depends on an uncertain future event, or a present obligation where payment is not probable or cannot be measured reliably.

manas.q: What is a contingent liability?

children.note: Never recognised. Disclose in the notes unless the chance of payment is remote.

manas.q: How is a contingent liability treated?

children.note: A possible asset from past events that depends on an uncertain future event, such as a claim you are suing for.

manas.q: What is a contingent asset?

children.note: Disclose only when an inflow is probable. Recognise as a real asset only when it is virtually certain.

manas.q: When is a contingent asset recognised or disclosed?

children.note: Liability: probable = provision; possible = disclose; remote = nothing. Asset: virtually certain = recognise; probable = disclose; possible or remote = nothing.

manas.q: Summarise the probability ladder for liabilities and assets.

children.note: If a company guarantees a SACCO loan for a related company and that company is healthy, it is a contingent liability to disclose. If the borrower is failing, it may become a provision.
For each class: a short description, an estimate of the money effect, the uncertainties, and any possible reimbursement.
News that arrives after the year end but before the directors approve the accounts. Some of it changes the figures; some only goes in the notes.
From the end of the reporting period up to the date the accounts are authorised for issue. Events after signing are outside IAS 10.

manas.q: What period does IAS 10 cover?

children.note: The date the board approves the accounts for issue. The accounts must state this date and who gave the approval.
Events that give more evidence about conditions that already existed at the year end. You change the figures.

manas.q: What is an adjusting event?

children.note: Events about conditions that started after the year end. Do not change the figures; disclose them if material.

manas.q: What is a non-adjusting event?

children.note: For each material one, give its nature and an estimate of the money effect, or say an estimate cannot be made.
A customer at year end goes bankrupt; stock sold below cost after year end; a court case settled; discovery of fraud or errors; final price of an asset bought before the year end.
A fire or flood after year end; a big share issue; buying a business; a large fall in market values after year end; announcing a plan to close a branch.
Not a liability at the year end because there was no obligation then. Disclose in the notes.

manas.q: How are dividends declared after the year end treated?

children.note: If after year end management decides to close or has no realistic choice but to, do not use the going concern basis. This changes the whole basis of the accounts.

manas.q: What happens if going concern fails after the year end?

children.note: Each example uses KES and shows the journal. Year end is 31 December 2025 unless stated.
Sabuni Appliances sold fridges worth KES 10,000,000 with a 1-year guarantee. Expected: 75% no faults, 20% minor faults costing KES 400,000, 5% major faults costing KES 2,000,000.
Expected value = 20% × 400,000 + 5% × 2,000,000 = 80,000 + 100,000 = KES 180,000. The 75% with no faults costs nil.
Dr Warranty expense KES 180,000 / Cr Warranty provision KES 180,000. When repairs are paid next year: Dr Provision / Cr Cash.

children.topic: Court cases: one provision, one disclosure
children.note: Case A: a customer sues Sabuni for KES 5,000,000; lawyers say losing is likely (70%) and KES 3,200,000 is the most likely payout. Case B: a supplier sues for KES 1,500,000; lawyers say Sabuni will probably win.
Single obligation, outflow probable, most likely outcome KES 3,200,000. Dr Legal claims expense KES 3,200,000 / Cr Provision KES 3,200,000.
Payment is possible but not probable. No journal. Disclose the claim and the KES 1,500,000 amount in the notes.
If Sabuni claims KES 900,000 from a transporter and winning is probable, disclose a contingent asset. Record it only when virtually certain.
Mawe Quarry Ltd opens a quarry on 1 January 2025. Its licence requires restoration after 3 years, costing KES 6,000,000. Discount rate 10%.
6,000,000 ÷ 1.10³ = 6,000,000 ÷ 1.331 = KES 4,507,889. Dr Quarry asset (PPE) KES 4,507,889 / Cr Restoration provision KES 4,507,889.
10% × 4,507,889 = KES 450,789. Dr Finance cost 450,789 / Cr Provision 450,789. Closing provision KES 4,958,678.
Year 2: 10% × 4,958,678 = 495,868, provision 5,454,546. Year 3: 545,454 (rounded), provision 6,000,000, ready to pay. The asset is depreciated over the 3 years too.
Unga Millers must supply 10,000 bags at KES 900 each. Costs rose and each bag now costs KES 1,050 to make. Cancelling the contract costs a penalty of KES 1,000,000.
Loss if fulfilled = (1,050 − 900) × 10,000 = KES 1,500,000. Penalty to exit = KES 1,000,000. Provide the lower: KES 1,000,000.
Dr Onerous contract expense KES 1,000,000 / Cr Provision for onerous contract KES 1,000,000.

children.topic: Classify the events: adjusting or not?
children.note: Kilima Traders, year end 31 Dec 2025, accounts approved 20 March 2026. Decide each event and post any journal.
Adjusting: the customer was already in trouble at year end. Dr Bad debts (impairment) KES 800,000 / Cr Trade receivables KES 800,000.

children.topic: Stock sold below cost in January
children.note: Stock costing KES 1,200,000 sold for KES 950,000. Adjusting: shows the year-end net realisable value. Dr Cost of sales KES 250,000 / Cr Inventory KES 250,000.
KES 3,000,000 of stock lost. Non-adjusting: the fire happened after year end. No journal; disclose the nature and the estimated loss.
Year-end provision was KES 3,200,000; settled for KES 2,800,000. Adjusting. Dr Provision KES 400,000 / Cr Legal claims expense KES 400,000.
KES 5,000,000 dividend. Non-adjusting: no liability at year end. Disclose in the notes only.
These are the places where candidates lose easy marks.

children.topic: Providing for future losses or repairs
children.note: No present obligation means no provision, even if the cost is certain to come.

children.topic: Recognising a contingent asset too early
children.note: Probable is not enough for an asset. It must be virtually certain before you record it.
Show the reimbursement as a separate asset, not as a reduction of the provision.

children.topic: Forgetting the unwinding goes to finance cost
children.note: The yearly increase in a discounted provision is a finance cost, not an operating expense.
A restructuring needs a detailed plan that has been announced or started. A private board minute alone does not count.

children.topic: Accruing dividends declared after year end
children.note: Dividends declared after the year end are only disclosed. Do not accrue them.
Events after the accounts are signed are not covered. Check the approval date given in the question.
Try each question, then open the bubble to see the steps.
On 15 December 2025 the board of Duka Bora decided to close a branch, with redundancy costs of KES 2,400,000. Staff were told on 10 January 2026. Provision at 31 Dec 2025?
No. The plan was not announced and work had not started, so there was no constructive obligation at 31 December.
No provision at 31 December 2025. The January announcement is a non-adjusting event; disclose it if material.
A clean-up must be paid in 2 years: KES 2,000,000. Discount rate 8%. Find the provision now and the finance cost for each year.
Year 1: 8% × 1,714,678 = 137,174, balance 1,851,852. Year 2: 8% × 1,851,852 = 148,148, balance 2,000,000. Each year: Dr Finance cost / Cr Provision.
A hospital pharmacy faces two claims: one lawyers rate 60% likely to lose (KES 700,000), one rated 20% (KES 1,100,000). Treatment?
First claim: probable, recognise a KES 700,000 provision (Dr Expense / Cr Provision). Second claim: possible, not remote, so disclose a contingent liability of KES 1,100,000.

nodeData.note: A financial instrument is a contract that gives one side money it can claim and the other side a duty to pay, or a share in a business. IFRS 9 says how to classify, measure and impair them; IAS 32 says whether they are debt or equity; IFRS 7 says what to disclose.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Almost every business holds financial instruments: cash, money customers owe, loans, shares in other companies. Getting them right changes profit, assets and debt.
A contract that creates a financial asset for one party and, for the other party, a financial liability or an equity instrument.

manas.q: What is a financial instrument?

children.note: Cash, a right to receive cash (a trade receivable, a loan you gave, a bond you hold), or shares you own in another entity.
A duty to hand over cash or another financial asset, e.g. a bank loan, a trade payable, or a loan note your company issued.
A contract that gives a leftover interest in the assets after all liabilities are paid, e.g. ordinary shares. No duty to pay cash.

manas.q: What is an equity instrument?

children.note: A duka owner's M-Pesa float and bank balance, a SACCO loan, money a hospital pharmacy is owed by an insurer, Treasury bonds a company buys.
Inventory, PPE, prepayments and tax balances are not, because they do not give a contractual right to cash. Earlier topics (IAS 16, IAS 12) cover them.
Three standards work together. Learn which does what before the detail.
Covers recognising, classifying and measuring financial assets and liabilities, impairment (expected credit losses) and hedge accounting. Effective from 1 January 2018, replacing IAS 39.

manas.q: What does IFRS 9 cover and when did it take effect?

children.note: IAS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation decides if something you issued is a liability or equity, and when assets and liabilities may be offset.

manas.q: What is IAS 32 mainly used for?

children.note: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures asks for notes on the instruments held and their risks: credit, liquidity and market risk.

manas.q: Which standard sets disclosures for financial instruments?

children.note: Many small Kenyan companies use IFRS for SMEs, which has simpler sections on basic financial instruments. CA23 exam questions use full IFRS.
When to record the item and at what first amount.
Record the asset or liability when the entity becomes a party to the contract, not when cash moves.

manas.q: When is a financial instrument first recognised under IFRS 9?

children.note: At the start, measure at fair value, usually the price paid or received.

manas.q: How is a financial instrument measured on initial recognition?

children.note: Costs directly caused by the deal (broker, legal, arrangement fees) are added to an asset or deducted from a liability. If the item is at FVTPL, they are expensed at once.

manas.q: How are transaction costs treated on initial recognition?

children.note: Remove an asset when the rights to cash expire or are transferred; remove a liability when it is paid, cancelled or expires.
IFRS 9 asks two questions about each financial asset, then puts it in one of three groups.
Why do you hold it? Only to collect the cash, to collect and also sell, or for something else such as trading.

manas.q: What is the business model test?

children.note: Are the contract cash flows solely payments of principal and interest? A plain loan or bond passes; shares and derivatives fail.

manas.q: What does SPPI stand for and what does it test?

children.note: Hold to collect + SPPI passes. Carried at cost adjusted using the effective interest rate. E.g. trade receivables, loans, bonds held to maturity.

manas.q: When is a financial asset measured at amortised cost?

children.note: Hold to collect and sell + SPPI passes. Fair value in the balance sheet; interest in profit; other value changes in OCI, moved to profit on sale.

manas.q: When is a debt asset measured at FVOCI?

children.note: For shares not held for trading you may choose, at the start and for good, to show value changes in OCI. They are never recycled to profit; dividends go to profit.

manas.q: What is the FVOCI election for equity investments?

children.note: Everything else, e.g. shares held for trading and derivatives. Fair value at each year end; all changes go straight to profit or loss.

manas.q: What is the default category for financial assets?

children.note: Most liabilities are simple: amortised cost.
Loans, loan notes and payables are carried at amortised cost: cash received less costs, plus interest at the EIR, less payments.
Liabilities held for trading and derivatives (and some designated ones) are at fair value through profit or loss.

children.topic: Debt or equity: the key question
children.note: Under IAS 32, if the issuer cannot avoid paying cash, it is a liability, whatever the legal name of the instrument.

manas.q: What is the key test for debt versus equity under IAS 32?

children.note: If redemption is compulsory or the holder can demand it, they are a liability and their dividends are a finance cost.

manas.q: How are mandatorily redeemable preference shares classified?

children.note: Ordinary shares and irredeemable preference shares with discretionary dividends are usually equity; dividends go through equity.
The effective interest method spreads the true cost or return over the life of the instrument.
The rate that exactly discounts all future cash flows back to the opening carrying amount. It includes transaction costs and any discount or premium.

manas.q: What is the effective interest rate?

children.note: Opening balance + interest at EIR − cash paid or received = closing balance. Repeat each year until the closing equals the amount redeemed.

manas.q: What are the columns of an amortised cost table?

children.note: The coupon (nominal) rate gives the cash; the EIR gives the income or expense in profit. The difference unwinds into the balance.

manas.q: What is the difference between the coupon rate and the EIR?

children.note: Exams usually give it. At work use Excel IRR or RATE on the cash flows, or trial and error.
IFRS 9 asks you to provide for losses you expect, not wait for a customer to default.
Provide for credit losses expected in future, weighted by probability, using past, current and forecast information.

manas.q: What impairment model does IFRS 9 use?

children.note: No big rise in credit risk since the start: provide 12-month expected losses. Interest on the gross amount.

manas.q: What loss allowance is needed in Stage 1?

children.note: Credit risk has increased significantly: provide lifetime expected losses. Interest still on the gross amount.

manas.q: What triggers Stage 2 and what allowance applies?

children.note: There is evidence of loss (e.g. default). Lifetime losses, and interest is now on the net amount after the allowance.
For trade receivables without a significant financing part, always provide lifetime losses, often using a provision matrix by age.

manas.q: What is the simplified approach for trade receivables?

children.note: Dr Impairment loss (profit or loss) / Cr Loss allowance. The allowance is deducted from the asset in the balance sheet.
Rates and prices below are made up for practice (illustrative), not real market rates.

children.topic: Bond at amortised cost: the facts
children.note: 1 Jan 2025 a company buys a 3-year KES 1,000,000 bond for KES 950,000 plus KES 10,000 broker fees. Coupon 6% (KES 60,000) paid each 31 Dec; repaid at par 31 Dec 2027.
950,000 + 10,000 costs = KES 960,000. Held to collect and SPPI passes, so amortised cost. Dr Financial asset 960,000 / Cr Bank 960,000.
The rate that turns 60,000, 60,000 and 1,060,000 back into 960,000 is about 7.54% (7.5392% exact, found by computer).
Opening 960,000 + interest 72,377 − cash 60,000 = closing 972,377.
Opening 972,377 + interest 73,310 − cash 60,000 = closing 985,687.
Opening 985,687 + interest 74,313 − cash 60,000 = 1,000,000; the KES 1,000,000 repaid clears it to nil. Interest uses the exact EIR, rounded to the shilling.
Total interest 220,000 = cash in 1,180,000 − paid 960,000. 2025: Dr Financial asset 72,377 / Cr Interest income 72,377; Dr Bank 60,000 / Cr Financial asset 60,000.
Company issues 100,000 8% preference shares of KES 100 each at par (KES 10,000,000), redeemable at par in 5 years. No issue costs.
Redemption cannot be avoided, so IAS 32 says liability, not equity. Dr Bank 10,000,000 / Cr Financial liability 10,000,000.
8% × 10,000,000 = KES 800,000. Issued and redeemed at par with no costs, so EIR = 8%. Dr Finance cost 800,000 / Cr Bank 800,000.
Had they been irredeemable with optional dividends: Cr Share capital (equity), and dividends Dr Retained earnings, not finance cost.
A pharmacy wholesaler has receivables of KES 2,000,000 and uses loss rates from its own history (illustrative).
Allowance 12,000 + 15,000 + 20,000 + 40,000 = KES 87,000. If none existed: Dr Impairment loss 87,000 / Cr Loss allowance 87,000. Net receivables 1,913,000.
Bought 10,000 listed shares at KES 50 (500,000) for trading, plus KES 5,000 broker fees. Year-end price KES 56 (illustrative).
Dr Investment 500,000 / Cr Bank 500,000. Fees are expensed because FVTPL: Dr Profit or loss 5,000 / Cr Bank 5,000.
Fair value 10,000 × 56 = 560,000. Gain 60,000: Dr Investment 60,000 / Cr Profit or loss 60,000.
Where marks are usually lost.
Interest in profit is at the EIR on the opening balance, not the coupon. The coupon is only the cash.
Add them to amortised cost assets, deduct them from liabilities; expense them only for FVTPL.
A "preference share" can be a liability. Look at whether cash must be paid.
Gains on equity at FVOCI stay in equity even on sale; only FVOCI debt is recycled to profit.
IFRS 9 wants expected losses now, even on new, healthy receivables.
The final closing balance must equal the redemption amount; fix any small rounding in the last year and say so.
Try each one before opening the answer bubbles. Figures are illustrative.
1 Jan 2025 a company issues a KES 2,000,000 loan note at par, costs KES 100,000, coupon 8% yearly, repaid at par in 3 years. EIR about 10.01%. Find 2025 finance cost and closing balance.
1,900,000 × 10.01096% = KES 190,208 (to the shilling). Dr Finance cost 190,208 / Cr Liability 190,208.
1,900,000 + 190,208 − 160,000 coupon = KES 1,930,208. It reaches 2,000,000 by end of 2027 (last year adjusted by KES 1 for rounding).
(a) trade receivables, (b) shares held for trading, (c) bonds held to collect and sell, (d) a strategic 5% stake in a supplier.
(a) Amortised cost: collect cash, SPPI passes. (b) FVTPL: held for trading.
(c) FVOCI debt: collect and sell, SPPI passes. (d) FVTPL by default, or FVOCI if the irrevocable election is made at the start.
A SACCO has a performing KES 400,000 loan. 12-month expected loss is 2%; lifetime is 7%. What allowance?
No significant rise in risk, so Stage 1: 400,000 × 2% = KES 8,000. If risk rose (Stage 2): 400,000 × 7% = KES 28,000.

nodeData.note: How to add a parent and the companies it controls into one group balance sheet: control, goodwill, non-controlling interest, fair values and removing trading inside the group.

children.note: When one company controls another, the owners want one set of figures for the whole family of companies. That combined set is called the group (consolidated) accounts.
The company that controls another company. Example: Pamoja Ltd owns most of the shares in Simba Ltd and runs it, so Pamoja is the parent.

manas.q: What is a parent company?

children.note: A company that is controlled by another company (the parent). It is still a separate legal company with its own books.

manas.q: What is a subsidiary?

children.note: The group is the parent and all the companies it controls, seen together as one business (a single economic entity), as IFRS 10 describes.

manas.q: What does 'group' mean in consolidated accounts?

children.note: The parent's own books only show 'Investment in Simba'. Owners and lenders need to see all the land, stock, cash and debts the group really controls.
Under IFRS 10, a parent that controls subsidiaries presents consolidated statements. Kenyan listed and large companies follow full IFRS (source: ifrs.org, IFRS 10).

children.topic: Where this fits in the paper
children.note: Topics 1 to 7 taught single-company figures (PPE, leases, tax, financial instruments). Here we add companies together. Topic 9 does the group profit or loss and associates.
You consolidate a company when you control it. Control, not just share percentage, is the basis for consolidation under IFRS 10.

An investor controls a company when it has (1) power over its key activities, (2) exposure to variable returns from it, and (3) the ability to use that power to affect those returns (source: IFRS 10).

manas.q: What are the three parts of control under IFRS 10?

children.note: Usually owning over 50% of the voting shares gives control. Example: Pamoja owns 80% of Simba's shares, so Pamoja controls Simba.

manas.q: What share of voting rights usually gives control?

children.note: Control can exist with less than half the shares, e.g. an agreement that lets you appoint most of the board. Look at the real power, not just the number.
Some investment funds (investment entities) do not consolidate the companies they invest in. They measure them at fair value through profit or loss instead (source: IFRS 10).
Holding about 20% to 50% with real influence but no control usually makes an associate. Associates are not added line by line; they are covered in topic 9.
The consolidated statement of financial position (SOFP) adds the parent's and subsidiary's assets and liabilities line by line, then makes a few adjustments.
Add all of the subsidiary's assets and liabilities to the parent's, even if the parent owns only 80%. The group controls all of them.

manas.q: If the parent owns 80%, how much of the subsidiary's assets go into the group SOFP?

children.note: The parent's 'Investment in subsidiary' is removed. It is replaced by goodwill and the subsidiary's net assets.
Group share capital is the parent's share capital only. The subsidiary's share capital is cancelled in the goodwill working.

manas.q: Whose share capital appears in the group SOFP?

children.note: W1 group structure, W2 net assets of the subsidiary, W3 goodwill, W4 non-controlling interest, W5 group retained earnings. Learn this order.

manas.q: What are the five standard workings for a group SOFP?

children.note: Write who owns what and since when. Example: Pamoja owns 80% of Simba since 1 Jan 2025, so NCI is 20%.
Show the subsidiary's share capital, reserves and fair value adjustments at two dates: acquisition date and reporting date. The difference is post-acquisition growth.
Goodwill is the extra the buyer pays above the fair value of what it gets. It stands for things like customers, staff skills and reputation.
Goodwill = price paid (consideration) + NCI at acquisition − fair value of the subsidiary's net assets at acquisition (source: IFRS 3).

manas.q: What is the formula for goodwill on acquisition?

children.note: What the parent gives (cash, shares, later payments) is measured at fair value on the acquisition date (source: IFRS 3).

manas.q: How is the consideration measured under IFRS 3?

children.note: The subsidiary's identifiable assets and liabilities are measured at their fair value on the acquisition date, not at book value (source: IFRS 3).
If the price is less than the fair value of net assets, check the numbers again. If it is still lower, the gain goes to profit or loss at once (source: IFRS 3).

manas.q: How is a gain on bargain purchase treated?

children.note: Goodwill is not depreciated. Instead it is tested for impairment (loss of value) every year under IAS 36 Impairment of Assets.

manas.q: Is goodwill amortised under IFRS?

children.note: Proportionate method: all of the loss reduces group retained earnings. Fair value method: split it between group retained earnings and NCI by their shares.
NCI is the part of the subsidiary owned by outside shareholders, not the parent. It appears inside equity in the group SOFP.
If Pamoja owns 80% of Simba, the other 20% belongs to outsiders. Their share is the non-controlling interest (older name: minority interest).

manas.q: What is non-controlling interest?

children.note: NCI is shown in equity, separately from the equity of the parent's owners. It is not a liability.

manas.q: Where is NCI shown in the group SOFP?

children.note: NCI at acquisition = NCI % × fair value of the subsidiary's net assets. This gives 'partial' goodwill, the parent's part only.

manas.q: How is NCI measured under the proportionate share method?

children.note: NCI at acquisition = fair value of the NCI shares (often given in the question, or share price × NCI shares). This gives 'full' goodwill.

manas.q: How is NCI measured under the fair value method?

children.note: IFRS 3 lets the group choose either method for each acquisition. Read the question carefully to see which one is asked.
NCI at acquisition + NCI % of post-acquisition growth in net assets − NCI share of goodwill impairment (fair value method only).

manas.q: How do you work out NCI at the reporting date?

children.note: Only profits made after the parent bought the subsidiary belong to the group. Profits made before are 'bought' and go into the goodwill sum.
Reserves the subsidiary had on the acquisition date. They are part of the net assets bought, so they go in the goodwill working, not group reserves.

manas.q: What happens to pre-acquisition reserves?

children.note: Growth in the subsidiary's reserves after the acquisition date. The parent's share goes to group retained earnings; the rest goes to NCI.

manas.q: What happens to post-acquisition reserves?

children.note: Parent's retained earnings + parent % of subsidiary's post-acquisition growth − unrealised profit (parent as seller) − parent's share of goodwill impairment.

manas.q: What goes into group retained earnings?

children.note: If bought part way through the year, assume profit is earned evenly unless told otherwise. Split the year's profit into before and after the purchase date.
On acquisition the subsidiary's assets are brought to fair value in the group accounts, even if the subsidiary's own books still show old cost.
Group accounts must show what the group really paid for each asset. Example: Simba's land cost KES 5m long ago but is worth KES 7m today.
Add the extra value to PPE and to W2 net assets at both dates. Land is not depreciated, so the uplift stays the same each year.
If plant is uplifted, the group charges extra depreciation on the uplift over its remaining life. This reduces PPE and post-acquisition reserves.

manas.q: What follows a fair value uplift on depreciating plant?

children.note: The uplift becomes part of the group's cost of the asset, then normal IAS 16 depreciation rules apply, as you learned in topic 1.
The group cannot owe money to itself or make profit by selling to itself. These intra-group items are removed.
If Simba owes Pamoja KES 700,000, cancel it: Dr Payables 700 / Cr Receivables 700 (KES '000). Neither appears in the group SOFP.

manas.q: How are intra-group receivables and payables treated?

children.note: If the parent's receivable is bigger because cash is on the way, first add the cash to group cash: Dr Cash / Cr Receivables. Then cancel the rest.
If goods sent have not arrived, add them to group inventory: Dr Inventory / Cr Receivables (or payables side). Then the balances agree and cancel.
Profit on goods sold inside the group that are still in the group's stock at year end. Remove it: Dr Retained earnings / Cr Inventory.

manas.q: What is provision for unrealised profit (PURP)?

children.note: Mark-up is profit as % of cost; margin is profit as % of selling price. Mark-up 25% means profit = 25/125 of the selling price.

manas.q: What is the difference between mark-up and margin?

children.note: Parent sold: whole PURP reduces group retained earnings. Subsidiary sold: reduce the subsidiary's post-acquisition profit in W2, so NCI shares the cut.

manas.q: If the subsidiary is the seller, who bears the PURP?

children.note: Loans between group companies cancel the same way. A dividend the subsidiary owes the parent is cancelled against the parent's receivable.
Two examples in KES '000. Example A is a simple 100% purchase. Example B has NCI, fair values, intra-group items and impairment, and fully balances.
Pamoja pays 15,000 for all of Simba. Simba's net assets: share capital 10,000 + retained earnings 3,000 = 13,000. Fair values equal book values.
Goodwill = 15,000 − 13,000 = 2,000. No NCI because Pamoja owns 100%.
Pamoja: investment 15,000 + other assets 35,000 = 50,000; share capital 30,000, RE 12,000, liabilities 8,000. Simba: assets 16,000; SC 10,000, RE 3,000, liabilities 3,000.
Goodwill 2,000 + assets 51,000 = 53,000. Share capital 30,000 + RE 12,000 + liabilities 11,000 = 53,000. It balances.
Pamoja bought 80% of Simba on 1 Jan 2025 for 20,000 cash. Then Simba had SC 10,000, RE 6,000. NCI fair value then: 4,500. SOFP date: 31 Dec 2026.
At acquisition land was worth 2,000 more and plant 1,000 more (5 years left). Simba owes Pamoja 700. Pamoja sold Simba goods for 2,400 at 20% mark-up; half still in stock. Goodwill impaired 600.

Pamoja: PPE 50,000, investment 20,000, inventory 8,000, receivables 6,000, cash 3,000 = 87,000; SC 40,000, RE 30,000, payables 9,000, loan 8,000. Simba: PPE 18,000, inv 5,000, rec 3,000, cash 1,500 = 27,500; SC 10,000, RE 11,000, payables 4,000, loan 2,500.
At acquisition: 10,000 + 6,000 + land 2,000 + plant 1,000 = 19,000. At year end: 10,000 + 11,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 − extra depreciation 400 = 23,600. Growth = 4,600.
Plant uplift 1,000 ÷ 5 years = 200 a year × 2 years = 400.
20,000 + NCI 4,500 − net assets 19,000 = 5,500. Less impairment 600 = 4,900 in the group SOFP.
Profit in the sale = 2,400 × 20/120 = 400. Half still in stock, so PURP = 200. Pamoja was the seller, so all 200 comes off group RE and off inventory.
Goodwill 4,900; PPE 50,000 + 18,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 − 400 = 70,600; inventory 12,800; receivables 8,300 (after cancelling 700); cash 4,500. Total 101,100.

children.topic: B: group SOFP – equity and debts
children.note: Share capital 40,000; retained earnings 33,000; NCI 5,300; payables 12,300 (after cancelling 700); loans 10,500. Total 101,100. It balances.
NCI at start = 20% × 19,000 = 3,800; goodwill = 23,800 − 19,000 = 4,800, less 600 = 4,200. RE 32,880 (all impairment to parent), NCI 4,720. Totals 100,400 both sides.
These slips cost the most marks in group balance sheet questions.
Wrong. Add 100% of the subsidiary's assets and liabilities, then show the outsiders' share as NCI.
Wrong. Only the parent's share capital goes in group equity. The subsidiary's is used up in the goodwill working.

children.topic: Using book values, not fair values
children.note: Goodwill must use fair values at acquisition. Forgetting the uplift, or its extra depreciation, throws out PPE, goodwill and reserves.
Read the words carefully. A 25% mark-up on cost is a 20% margin on sales.
Use the subsidiary's reserves at the acquisition date for goodwill, and the growth since then for group reserves and NCI.
Intra-group receivables and payables must be removed from both sides, after adjusting for cash or goods in transit.
Try each question, then open the bubbles below it for the answer steps. Figures in KES '000.
P pays 9,000 for 75% of S. Fair value of S's net assets is 10,000. NCI uses the proportionate method. Find goodwill.
S (80% owned) sold goods to P for 1,200 at a 25% margin. One third is still in P's stock. Find PURP and who bears it.
Profit = 1,200 × 25% = 300. One third unsold: PURP = 100. Reduce inventory by 100.
S was the seller, so cut S's post-acquisition profit by 100: group RE bears 80, NCI bears 20.
P owns 45% of S's shares. By agreement P appoints 4 of the 6 directors who run S. Should P consolidate S?
Yes. P has power over S's key activities through the board, so P controls S even with under 50% of the shares (IFRS 10).
NCI fair value at acquisition 3,000. NCI holds 30%. S's net assets grew 2,000 since acquisition. No impairment. Find NCI.

maps.title: CA23 · 9. Group accounts: profit or loss and associates

nodeData.topic: Group accounts: profit or loss and associates
nodeData.note: How a group shows one combined profit for the year, and how it shows companies it influences but does not control (associates and joint ventures). Builds on topic 8, the group balance sheet.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A group is a parent plus the companies it controls. Owners want to see the profit the whole group earned, not just the parent's own profit.
IFRS 10 treats the parent and its subsidiaries as one single economic entity. So the group profit statement shows what that one big business earned from outsiders.

manas.q: What does 'single economic entity' mean in group accounts?

children.note: Under IFRS 10, control is the basis for consolidation. If the parent controls a company (a subsidiary), you add its income and expenses in full, line by line.

manas.q: What is the basis for consolidating a company under IFRS 10?

children.note: If the investor only has significant influence (an associate) or shares control (a joint venture), you do not add line by line. You show one line: share of profit.
Topic 8 covered control, goodwill and non-controlling interest (NCI) on the balance sheet. This topic uses the same ideas for the profit for the year.
Afya Holdings owns 80% of Dawa Pharmacy Ltd and 30% of Maabara Labs Ltd. Dawa is a subsidiary (added line by line); Maabara is an associate (one line).

children.topic: Building the group profit or loss
children.note: The consolidated statement of profit or loss starts with parent plus subsidiary, then removes anything that is only trading inside the group.
Add 100% of the parent's and 100% of the subsidiary's revenue, cost of sales, expenses and tax, even if the parent owns only 80%. The NCI share is taken out at the bottom.

manas.q: Do you add 100% or only the parent's % of a subsidiary's revenue and costs?

children.note: If the subsidiary was bought during the year, include only its income and expenses after the date control began. Bought 1 April with a 31 Dec year end means 9/12.

manas.q: How do you treat a subsidiary bought part way through the year in the group P&L?

children.note: Sales between parent and subsidiary are not sales to outsiders. Take the full amount out of group revenue and out of group cost of sales.

manas.q: How do you cancel intra-group sales in the consolidated P&L?

children.note: If goods sold inside the group are still in the buyer's stock at year end, the profit on them is not yet earned by the group. Add the URP to cost of sales (and reduce inventory).

manas.q: What is unrealised profit (URP) and where does it go in the group P&L?

children.note: If the parent was the seller, the URP comes off the parent's profit only. If the subsidiary was the seller, it comes off the subsidiary's profit, so the NCI shares in it.

manas.q: When does unrealised profit affect the NCI share of profit?

children.note: Mark-up is profit as a % of cost; margin is profit as a % of selling price. A 25% mark-up equals a 20% margin. On a KES 600 sale, profit is 120 either way.

manas.q: What is the difference between mark-up and margin?

children.note: If the subsidiary's assets were valued up at acquisition (topic 8), charge the extra depreciation in the group P&L. It reduces the subsidiary's profit, so the NCI shares it.
Any goodwill impairment for the year is an expense in the group P&L, usually in operating expenses. Only the current year's charge goes in, not past years'.

manas.q: Where does this year's goodwill impairment go in the consolidated P&L?

children.note: If NCI is measured at its share of net assets, the parent bears all goodwill impairment. If NCI is at fair value, the NCI bears its % of the impairment too.
A dividend from the subsidiary to the parent is just cash moving inside the group. Remove it from the parent's investment income; only outside dividends stay.
Interest on intra-group loans and management fees appear as income for one company and expense for the other. Remove both sides; group profit does not change.
At the bottom, show profit for the year attributable to: owners of the parent, and non-controlling interest. The two must add up to group profit.

manas.q: Into which two parts is consolidated profit for the year split?

children.note: NCI share = NCI % × subsidiary's profit after tax (post-acquisition), after subsidiary-side adjustments: URP where the sub sold, extra FV depreciation, and impairment if NCI at fair value.

manas.q: How do you calculate the NCI share of profit for the year?

children.note: If there is other comprehensive income (e.g. a revaluation gain under IAS 16), total comprehensive income is split between parent owners and NCI the same way.
Some investments give influence but not control. IAS 28 says these are shown using the equity method, not by adding line by line.
An associate is a company over which the investor has significant influence: power to take part in its financial and operating policy decisions, but not control or joint control.

manas.q: What is an associate under IAS 28?

children.note: IAS 28 presumes significant influence if the investor holds 20% or more of the voting power, unless it can be clearly shown otherwise. Below 20% presumes no influence.

manas.q: What shareholding is presumed to give significant influence?

children.note: Clues include a seat on the board, taking part in policy decisions, big transactions between the two, swapping managers, or providing key technical know-how.
A joint venture is an arrangement where two or more parties share control and have rights to its net assets. IFRS 11 requires joint ventures to use the equity method too.

manas.q: How does IFRS 11 require a joint venture to be accounted for?

children.note: Start with the cost of the investment, then add your share of the associate's profit (or take off your share of losses) after you bought it.

manas.q: What is the equity method in simple words?

children.note: Investment in associate = cost + share of post-acquisition profit − dividends received − impairment. Shown as one non-current asset line.

manas.q: What is the formula for investment in associate on the group balance sheet?

children.note: Show 'Share of profit of associate' as one line, usually just before group profit before tax. Do not add the associate's revenue or costs line by line.

manas.q: How does an associate appear in the consolidated P&L?

children.note: Dividends received are not income in the group P&L. They reduce the investment, because you have already counted your share of the profit they came from.
If the investment has lost value, the impairment loss reduces the investment and is charged in the group P&L, usually netted in the share of profit line.
Sales to or from an associate are NOT cancelled from group revenue. The associate is outside the group, so these are real sales to an outsider.

children.topic: URP with an associate: your share only
children.note: Only the investor's % of unrealised profit is removed. If you hold 30%, remove 30% of the URP, not all of it.

manas.q: How much unrealised profit is removed on trading with an associate?

children.note: An associate is not consolidated line by line, so there is no non-controlling interest for it. You only ever show your own share.
Five examples in KES '000. Every total has been checked: try each one yourself first, then compare.

Duka Group: P owns 80% of S from years ago. P: revenue 5,000, COS 3,000, expenses 800, tax 300. S: revenue 2,000, COS 1,200, expenses 300, tax 100. P sold S goods for 400 (cost 300); half still in S's stock. Goodwill impairment this year 20; NCI at share of net assets.
Expenses = 800 + 300 + 20 impairment = 1,120. Profit before tax = 2,750 − 1,120 = 1,630. Tax = 300 + 100 = 400. Profit for the year = 1,230.
S's profit after tax = 2,000 − 1,200 − 300 − 100 = 400. P sold the goods, so no URP in S. NCI = 20% × 400 = 80. Owners of the parent = 1,230 − 80 = 1,150.

children.topic: If NCI were at fair value
children.note: NCI also bears 20% of the 20 impairment = 4. NCI = 80 − 4 = 76; owners of the parent = 1,230 − 76 = 1,154. Group profit stays 1,230.

P (year end 31 Dec) bought 75% of Matatu Movers Ltd on 1 April. Matatu's full year: revenue 1,600, COS 960, expenses 320, tax 80 (profit 240). P: revenue 4,000, COS 2,400, expenses 700, tax 200 (profit 700).
Matatu after 1 April: revenue 1,200, COS 720, expenses 240, tax 60, profit 180 (= 240 × 9/12).
Revenue 5,200; COS 3,120; gross profit 2,080; expenses 940; profit before tax 1,140; tax 260; profit for the year 880 (= 700 + 180).
NCI = 25% × 180 = 45. Owners of the parent = 880 − 45 = 835. NCI is only on the post-acquisition 9 months.
P owns 70% of S. S sold goods to P for 600 at a 25% mark-up on cost; P still holds ¼ at year end. S's profit after tax is 500.
Cost = 600 ÷ 1.25 = 480, so profit = 120. Still in stock: 120 × ¼ = 30. Add 30 to group cost of sales; take 600 out of revenue and COS.
S was the seller, so adjust S's profit: 500 − 30 = 470. NCI = 30% × 470 = 141.
Dr Cost of sales (group P&L) 30 / Cr Inventories (group SOFP) 30. Debits equal credits: 30 = 30.
On 1 Jan 2024 P paid 3,000 for 30% of Maabara Labs (significant influence). Maabara's profit: 2024 500, 2025 1,000. Maabara paid a 400 dividend in 2025. Impairment in 2025: 50.
Share of profit of associate = 30% × 1,000 − 50 impairment = 250, shown as one line. The 120 dividend P received (30% × 400) is NOT income in the group P&L.
3,000 cost + 150 (2024 share) + 300 (2025 share) − 120 dividend − 50 impairment = 3,280. Same answer.
P (owns 30% of Maabara) sold goods to Maabara for 500 at a 25% mark-up on cost. Maabara still holds 40% of them at year end.
Cost = 500 ÷ 1.25 = 400, profit = 100. Still in stock: 100 × 40% = 40. P's share: 30% × 40 = 12.
Dr Cost of sales 12 / Cr Investment in associate 12. Do NOT remove the 500 sale from group revenue; Maabara is not in the group.
These slips cost the most marks in group P&L questions.
Wrong: 80% of the subsidiary's revenue. Right: 100% of every line, then split the profit at the bottom between parent owners and NCI.
For a mid-year acquisition, include only the months after control. Pre-acquisition profit belongs in goodwill (topic 8), not in group profit.

children.topic: Removing only the profit, not the sale
children.note: Cancel the whole intra-group sale from revenue and cost of sales, then add the URP to cost of sales. These are two separate steps.
Read the question carefully. 25% on cost is 20% of selling price. Using the wrong base gives the wrong URP.
If the parent sold the goods, NCI does not share the URP. Only adjust the NCI share when the subsidiary was the seller.
Sales to an associate stay in group revenue. Only the investor's share of URP comes out.
Dividends from an associate or subsidiary are not group income. Remove them from investment income to avoid double counting.
Only this year's impairment goes in this year's P&L. Earlier years' losses are already in opening retained earnings.
Try each question, then open the bubble to check the steps. Figures in KES '000.
P revenue 8,000; S revenue 3,000; during the year P sold goods to S for 500. What is group revenue?
8,000 + 3,000 − 500 = 10,500. Intra-group sales are removed in full, whether or not the goods are still in stock.
P owns 90% of S. S's profit after tax is 600. Extra FV depreciation is 40 and URP on S's sales to P is 20. Find the NCI share.
600 − 40 − 20 = 540. Both items are on the subsidiary's side, so they reduce S's profit.
S was bought on 1 October; group year end 31 December. S's revenue for the full year is 2,400 (earned evenly). How much goes into group revenue?
P bought 25% of A for 2,000. Since then A's retained profit has risen by 800. This year A made 400. Find the investment and this year's P&L line.
2,000 + 25% × 800 = 2,200 on the group balance sheet.
Share of profit of associate = 25% × 400 = 100, shown as one line.
