nodeData.note: How to read a set of accounts and judge how a business is really doing. You compare years, turn figures into percentages and ratios, explain what changed, and know where the numbers can mislead. This pulls together all the earlier topics of the paper.

children.note: Accounts are full of numbers, but numbers alone say little. Analysis turns them into answers: is the business making money, can it pay its bills, and is it safe to lend to or invest in?
Analysis is comparing figures so they tell a story: this year against last year, one company against another, or one figure against another (a ratio).

manas.q: What is financial statement analysis?

children.note: Owners and investors (will I earn a return?), banks and lenders (will I be repaid?), suppliers (will they pay me?), staff, the government and KRA, and managers who run the business.

1) Is it profitable? 2) Can it pay short-term bills (liquidity)? 3) Does it use its assets and cash well (efficiency)? 4) Is it carrying too much debt (gearing)? Investors add a fifth: what do I earn per share?
A ratio alone means little. Compare it with last year, with a competitor, with the industry average, or with the budget. The change and the reason for it are what matter.

Everything you learnt earlier changes the figures: revaluing PPE, capitalising intangibles, when revenue is recognised, leases on the balance sheet, tax, provisions, financial instruments and group accounts. A good analyst knows how each one moves the ratios.

IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements replaces IAS 1 for years starting on or after 1 January 2027 (early use allowed). It makes the profit or loss statement more alike across companies, which makes comparing them easier.
Profit or loss must show 'operating profit' and 'profit before financing and income taxes'. Today companies choose their own subtotals, so the same label can mean different things.

manas.q: Which two subtotals does IFRS 18 require in profit or loss?

children.note: If managers quote their own measure in public (for example 'adjusted profit'), IFRS 18 makes them explain it in the notes and show how it links back to the IFRS figures. Analysts should still check what was left out.
Two simple tools first: trend (horizontal) and common-size (vertical) analysis. Then the ratios, in five families. Learn each formula and, more importantly, what it tells you.
Put two or more years side by side and work out the change in shillings and in percent for each line. Formula: (this year − last year) ÷ last year × 100.

manas.q: What is horizontal (trend) analysis?

children.note: Revenue rose from KES 500m to KES 600m: (600 − 500) ÷ 500 × 100 = 20%. Then ask why: new branches, higher prices or more customers?

children.topic: Look for lines that move apart
children.note: If revenue grows 20% but profit falls, costs grew faster. If receivables grow faster than sales, customers are paying more slowly.
Show every line as a percentage of one base figure: revenue for profit or loss, total assets for the balance sheet. This lets you compare a small duka with a big supermarket.

manas.q: What is common-size (vertical) analysis?

children.note: Cost of sales KES 420m ÷ revenue KES 600m = 70% this year, against 68% last year. So each KES 100 of sales now costs KES 2 more to buy in.
These ratios show how much profit the business squeezes out of its sales and out of the money invested in it.
Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100. Shows how much is left from each sale after the cost of the goods. Falls if prices are cut or buying costs rise.

manas.q: Formula for gross profit margin?

children.note: Operating profit (profit before interest and tax) ÷ revenue × 100. Shows profit after running costs such as rent, salaries and depreciation.

manas.q: Formula for operating profit margin?

children.note: Operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100. Capital employed = equity + non-current liabilities (long-term debt). Shows the return earned on all long-term money put in.

manas.q: Formula for ROCE, and what is capital employed?

children.note: Profit after tax ÷ equity × 100. Shows the return earned for the shareholders only. Debt can push ROE up, but adds risk.

manas.q: Formula for return on equity?

children.topic: Liquidity: can it pay its bills?
children.note: Liquidity is about the short term: can the business pay suppliers, salaries and tax due in the next year from its current assets?
Current assets ÷ current liabilities, shown as 'x : 1'. Above 1 means more short-term assets than short-term bills. Too high can mean idle stock or cash.

manas.q: Formula for the current ratio?

children.note: (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. Leaves out stock because it may take time to sell. A tougher test of whether bills can be paid.

manas.q: Formula for the quick (acid test) ratio?

children.note: There is no single right answer. A supermarket sells for cash and can live with a low current ratio; a builder needs more. Compare with the same industry and with last year.

children.topic: Efficiency: how well it uses assets
children.note: These ratios show how fast stock sells, how fast customers pay, how slowly the business pays suppliers, and how hard its assets work.
Inventory ÷ cost of sales × 365. About how many days stock sits on the shelf before it is sold. Rising days can mean slow or expired stock.

manas.q: Formula for inventory days?

children.note: Trade receivables ÷ revenue × 365 (use credit sales if given). How many days customers take to pay. Rising days mean slower collection or weak credit control.

manas.q: Formula for receivable days?

children.note: Trade payables ÷ cost of sales (or credit purchases) × 365. How many days the business takes to pay suppliers. Very high can mean cash trouble.

manas.q: Formula for payable days?

children.note: Revenue ÷ capital employed (some use total assets; say which). Shows how many shillings of sales each shilling of capital produces.

manas.q: Formula for asset turnover?

children.note: Inventory days + receivable days − payable days. How long cash is tied up between paying for goods and getting paid by customers. Shorter is usually better.

manas.q: How do you work out the cash conversion cycle?

children.note: Operating margin × asset turnover = ROCE (when both use capital employed). So a fall in ROCE comes from lower margins, slower asset use, or both.
Gearing measures how much of the business is paid for by borrowing. More debt means fixed interest to pay and more risk if profit falls.
Debt ÷ (debt + equity) × 100, where debt is interest-bearing long-term borrowing, including lease liabilities. Another version is debt ÷ equity. State the one you use.

manas.q: Formula for the gearing ratio?

children.note: Operating profit ÷ finance costs, shown as 'times'. How many times profit could pay the interest bill. Low cover warns of trouble if profit drops.

manas.q: Formula for interest cover?

children.note: Under IFRS 16 (topic 4) a lessee shows a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. So renting shops now adds debt, raises gearing and capital employed, and can lower ROCE versus the old rules.
These are the ratios shareholders and the stock market watch. They use the share price and the number of shares.
Profit after tax for ordinary shareholders ÷ number of ordinary shares. IAS 33 Earnings per Share sets the detailed rules (for example a weighted average of shares).

manas.q: Formula for earnings per share (EPS)?

children.note: Share price ÷ EPS. How many years of current earnings buyers will pay for. A high P/E shows the market expects growth.

manas.q: Formula for the P/E ratio?

children.note: Dividend per share ÷ share price × 100. The cash return a buyer gets at today's price, like interest on a deposit.

manas.q: Formula for dividend yield?

children.note: Profit after tax (or EPS) ÷ dividends (or dividend per share). How many times the dividend could be paid from this year's profit. Low cover means little is kept for growth.

manas.q: Formula for dividend cover?

children.note: A made-up Nairobi pharmacy chain, Afya Pharmacy Ltd, with two years of figures in KES million. We compute every ratio, then explain it. Year-end figures are used, not averages.
In 2026 Afya opened four new branches in leased premises and took a bank loan. A rival chain cut prices. More sales now come from medical insurers, who pay later than walk-in customers.

2026 vs 2025. Revenue 600 vs 500. Cost of sales (420) vs (340). Gross profit 180 vs 160. Operating expenses (108) vs (90). Operating profit 72 vs 70. Finance costs (12) vs (6). Profit before tax 60 vs 64. Tax (given) (18) vs (19). Profit after tax 42 vs 45.
100 million ordinary shares of KES 1 both years. Dividends paid: KES 22m in 2026, KES 20m in 2025. Share price at year end: KES 5.04 (2026) and KES 6.30 (2025).
2026 vs 2025. PPE incl. right-of-use assets 260 vs 200. Inventory 105 vs 70. Receivables 50 vs 35. Cash 5 vs 25. Total assets 420 vs 330.
Share capital 100 vs 100. Retained earnings 140 vs 120. Loan and lease liabilities 100 vs 50. Trade payables 70 vs 50. Tax payable 10 vs 10. Total 420 vs 330 — it balances.
Opening 120 + profit 42 − dividends 22 = closing 140. Capital employed = equity + long-term debt: 240 + 100 = 340 (2026); 220 + 50 = 270 (2025).

Revenue +20%, gross profit +12.5%, operating profit +2.9%, profit after tax −6.7%. Inventory +50%, receivables +43%, cash −80%, debt +100%. Cost of sales 70% of revenue (68%); operating expenses 18% both years.
Current ratio (105+50+5)/80 = 160/80 = 2.0:1 (130/60 = 2.17:1). Quick ratio 55/80 = 0.69:1 (60/60 = 1.0:1). Quick ratio fell because cash dropped while stock grew.
Gearing 100/340 = 29.4% (50/270 = 18.5%). Debt to equity 100/240 = 41.7% (22.7%). Interest cover 72/12 = 6.0 times (70/6 = 11.7 times). Debt and interest doubled.
12.0% × 1.765 = 21.2% = ROCE 2026. 14.0% × 1.852 = 25.9% = ROCE 2025. The fall in ROCE comes mainly from the lower margin.
Exam marks come from explaining, not just calculating. For each ratio say what happened, the likely reason, and what it means for the reader.

To / From / Date / Subject. Short introduction. Then headings: profitability, liquidity, efficiency, gearing, investor view. End with a conclusion and, if asked, a recommendation. Put the ratio table in an appendix.

manas.q: What is the layout of a short analysis report?

children.note: Example: 'Gross margin fell from 32% to 30% (what), probably because Afya matched a rival's price cuts (why). If this continues, profit will keep shrinking even as sales grow (so what).'

Sales grew 20% thanks to new branches, but profit after tax fell 6.7%. Lower prices cut gross margin, and new branch costs and doubled interest ate the rest. ROCE fell from 25.9% to 21.2% as new branches are not yet fully earning.

Cash fell from KES 25m to 5m. Stock now sits 91 days, up from 75, maybe from stocking new branches or slow lines. Insurers pay more slowly. The quick ratio of 0.69 means Afya leans on suppliers, who now wait 61 days.

Gearing rose to 29.4%, partly from new bank debt and partly from shop leases now on the balance sheet (IFRS 16). Interest cover of 6 times is still comfortable. The P/E fell to 12, so the market is less hopeful.
Afya is growing but less profitable and shorter of cash. Managers should cut slow-moving stock, chase insurer claims, and watch borrowing until the new branches mature.

Revaluing PPE (IAS 16) raises equity and depreciation, so ROCE falls. Capitalised development costs (IAS 38) lift profit now. Group accounts include NCI in equity and only a share of associate profit, so check what the ratio includes.
Good answers list what else you need: industry averages, a cash flow statement, branch-by-branch figures, the age of stock, the terms of the new loan, and figures from more than two years.
Ratios are only as good as the figures behind them. Always say where the numbers might mislead.
Making the year-end picture look better than it really is, for example collecting a big debt just before the year end or delaying purchases, then reversing it after. It flatters liquidity.

manas.q: What is window dressing?

children.note: Two firms can choose different policies: cost vs revaluation for PPE, inventory cost formulas, depreciation lives. Their ratios are then not like for like.

manas.q: Why do accounting policy choices limit comparisons?

children.note: Old assets at historical cost look cheap against today's profits, so ROCE looks high. Sales growth in shillings may just be price rises, not more customers.
A big gain on selling land, a restructuring cost or an impairment can swing one year's profit. Strip them out to see the normal trend, and check IAS 37 provisions (topic 6).
A school uniform shop or a farm supplier has a busy season. A year end in the quiet season shows low stock and receivables, so the ratios do not reflect the rest of the year.
A single year-end figure may not be typical. Averages of opening and closing balances are better when you have them. Say which you used.
Use cost of sales for inventory and payable days, and revenue for receivable days. Use operating profit (before interest) for ROCE, but profit after tax for ROE.
Most marks are for comments. Do not list ratios without a reason. Link ratios together, e.g. cash fell because inventory and receivable days grew.
Use the facts in the question (new branches, a new loan, a price war). Examiners put them there to explain the changes in the ratios.
Try each one before opening the answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: Work out the cash cycle
children.note: Inventory KES 60m, receivables KES 40m, payables KES 30m, revenue KES 400m, cost of sales KES 240m. Find the cash cycle in days.
Inventory 60/240×365 = 91.3 days. Receivables 40/400×365 = 36.5 days. Payables 30/240×365 = 45.6 days.
91.25 + 36.5 − 45.625 = 82.1 days. Cash is tied up for about 82 days.
Operating profit KES 45m, revenue KES 300m, equity KES 150m, long-term loans KES 75m. Find ROCE, operating margin and asset turnover.
A shop chain starts applying IFRS 16 and adds lease liabilities of KES 80m. Debt was KES 120m, equity KES 300m. What happens to gearing?
Gearing rises although the business is no riskier in substance; the leases were always there. Explain this when comparing with older years or with firms using other rules.

children.topic: Q4: Explain a falling quick ratio
children.note: Quick ratio fell from 1.0 to 0.69. Give two possible reasons and one risk.
Reasons: cash used to buy stock and open branches; customers paying more slowly. Risk: if suppliers demand payment quickly, the business may not have the cash and may need an overdraft.

Accounting Stuff walks through the main ratio families with a simple company.
A short explainer of trend and common-size analysis.
An ACCA lecture on interpreting financial statements with ratios.
OpenTuition ACCA FR lecture on why ratios can mislead.
FOG Accountancy Tutorials: a long lesson on accounting ratios step by step.
A worked example of inventory, receivable and payable days.
Free places to read further on ratios and on the standards behind the figures.
A list of common ratios and their families.
Overview of horizontal, vertical and ratio analysis.
How the cash cycle is measured and used.

nodeData.note: An audit is an independent check of a business's accounts by a qualified outsider, who then gives an opinion on whether they can be trusted. This first topic of Auditing and Assurance covers what an audit is, why people need one, the key ideas behind it and the steps an auditor follows.

children.note: Start here: who needs an audit, and why someone outside the business has to do it.
An audit is an independent examination of an organisation's financial statements by a qualified auditor, who then gives a written opinion on whether they are fairly shown.

manas.q: What is an audit?

children.note: In a company, shareholders own the business but directors and managers run it day to day. Owners cannot watch everything, so they need someone independent to check the managers' report on how the money was used. This is called the agency idea.

manas.q: What is the agency idea behind audits?

children.note: Fifty shareholders own a private hospital in Nairobi, but a hired CEO and finance team run it. The auditor checks the accounts the managers prepare, so owners who never visit the wards can still trust the numbers.
Shareholders, banks and SACCOs lending money, suppliers giving credit, KRA, regulators and future investors all lean on audited accounts when they make decisions.

manas.q: Name four groups who rely on audited accounts.

children.note: A bank lending KES 50 million to a business wants to know the profit and assets are real. Audited accounts lower the bank's risk, which can mean easier and cheaper loans.

children.topic: The auditor does not prepare accounts
children.note: Management writes the financial statements; the auditor only checks them and gives an opinion. Mixing the two jobs would mean checking your own work.

Many people think an audit proves the accounts are 100% right or that the auditor must find every fraud. Neither is true. The difference between what the public expects and what an audit really does is called the expectation gap.

manas.q: What is the audit expectation gap?

children.note: An audit is one kind of assurance engagement. Learn the three parties and the two levels of assurance.
Assurance is the extra confidence users get when an independent expert checks information against agreed rules (criteria) and reports what they found.
Every assurance engagement has three parties: the practitioner who checks, the responsible party whose information is checked, and the intended users who read the report.

manas.q: Name the three parties in an assurance engagement.

children.note: The independent professional, such as an audit firm, who gathers evidence and gives the conclusion or opinion.
The people responsible for the information being checked, usually the directors who prepared the financial statements.
The people the report is written for, such as shareholders, lenders and regulators, who will make decisions using it.
The subject matter is what is checked, for example the financial statements. The criteria are the yardstick, for example IFRS or IFRS for SMEs.
A high but not absolute level of confidence. The auditor does enough work to reduce the risk of a wrong opinion to an acceptably low level. A full audit gives reasonable assurance.

manas.q: What is reasonable assurance?

children.note: A lower, meaningful level of confidence from less work, mostly asking questions and comparing numbers. A review of half-year accounts usually gives limited assurance.

manas.q: What is limited assurance?

children.note: Reasonable assurance is given in positive words: the accounts give a true and fair view. Limited assurance uses negative words: nothing has come to our attention that suggests they are wrong.

manas.q: How is the wording of reasonable and limited assurance different?

children.note: The opinion says whether the accounts give a true and fair view, or present fairly in all material respects. Both mean the accounts are free from big errors and follow the reporting rules, not that every shilling is exact.

manas.q: What does 'true and fair' mean?

children.note: What the auditor is trying to achieve and the attitude they need while doing it.

In plain words: get reasonable assurance that the accounts as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether from error or fraud, so the auditor can give an opinion, and then report as the ISAs require.

manas.q: What is the overall objective of the auditor under ISA 200?

children.note: A misstatement is anything in the accounts that is wrong, missing or badly shown. An error is a mistake; fraud is done on purpose to cheat or mislead.

manas.q: What is the difference between error and fraud?

children.note: A misstatement is material if it is large enough, alone or added to others, to change the decisions of people using the accounts. Small slips that change nothing are immaterial. ISA 320 deals with this.

manas.q: When is a misstatement material?

children.note: Materiality is about amount and also nature. A small payment to a director that was hidden, or a bribe, can be material even if the shilling amount is tiny.

Auditors often start from a percentage of a key figure, like 5% of profit before tax or 0.5–1% of revenue. These are habits of the profession, not set by law, and the auditor uses judgement to pick one.

manas.q: Give two common benchmarks for overall materiality.

children.note: A lower figure than overall materiality, used when testing individual areas. It leaves a safety margin so that many small undetected errors do not add up to a material one.

manas.q: What is performance materiality?

children.note: A questioning mind. The auditor stays alert to signs of error or fraud and does not simply believe what management says without evidence.

manas.q: What is professional scepticism?

children.note: Using training, knowledge and experience to make sensible decisions during the audit, such as setting materiality or deciding how much evidence is enough.

manas.q: What is professional judgement?

children.note: The auditor must be, and be seen to be, independent of the client. This is covered in topic 2, Professional ethics.
Why even a good audit cannot promise the accounts are perfect.
Inherent limitations are reasons built into every audit that stop it giving absolute assurance. That is why it gives reasonable, not total, assurance.

manas.q: Why can an audit not give absolute assurance?

children.note: Auditors usually test a selection of items rather than every transaction, so some errors can be missed. Sampling is covered in topic 4.

children.topic: Evidence persuades, it does not prove
children.note: Most audit evidence points towards an answer rather than proving it beyond doubt.
Many figures, like bad debts or the life of an X-ray machine, are estimates. There is no single right answer to check against.
Forged documents, or staff working together (collusion), can hide fraud from even a careful auditor.
Directors and management are responsible for preventing and detecting fraud through good controls. The auditor's job is to consider the risk of fraud causing a material misstatement (ISA 240).

manas.q: Who is responsible for preventing and detecting fraud?

children.note: An audit must be done in a sensible time at a sensible cost, so the auditor cannot chase every small item forever.

children.topic: Types of audit and Kenya rules
children.note: External vs internal audit, and who sets the rules for auditors in Kenya.
Done by an independent firm appointed by the shareholders. It gives an opinion on the financial statements to the owners.

manas.q: What is an external audit?

children.note: A team inside the organisation (or outsourced) that checks controls, risks and how well things run, and reports to management or the audit committee.

manas.q: What is internal audit?

children.note: External auditors are appointed by shareholders, must be independent, follow the ISAs and report on the accounts. Internal auditors serve management, can cover any area of operations and their work is not required by company law.
External: shareholders at the general meeting. Internal: management or the board.
External: the shareholders. Internal: management and the audit committee.
External: the financial statements. Internal: controls, risks, efficiency and anything management asks.
In Kenya, companies must generally have their yearly accounts audited by a registered, practising auditor under the Companies Act 2015. Check the Companies Act 2015 and ICPAK for the current details.

manas.q: What is a statutory audit?

children.note: Some small companies can be exempt from the audit requirement if they meet the conditions in the law. The conditions change, so check the Companies Act 2015 and ICPAK before relying on it.
The Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Kenya (ICPAK), set up under the Accountants Act, registers accountants, licenses auditors to practise and checks the quality of their work.

manas.q: Who regulates auditors in Kenya?

children.note: KASNEB examines and awards the CPA qualification; ICPAK then registers and licenses qualified accountants.
The International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB) writes the International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) and quality management standards (ISQMs). Kenya follows the ISAs.

manas.q: Who issues the International Standards on Auditing?

children.note: Government bodies in Kenya are audited by the Office of the Auditor-General, not by private firms appointed by shareholders.

children.topic: The audit process at a glance
children.note: Five big steps from start to finish. Later topics in this paper go deeper into each.
Before starting, the auditor and client agree the terms in writing: the scope, each side's duties and the fee basis. This is covered by ISA 210.

manas.q: What is an engagement letter?

children.note: Understand the business, set materiality and spot where errors are most likely. See topic 3, Risk and internal control.
Test controls and check balances and transactions with documents, confirmations and counts. See topic 4, Audit evidence and sampling.
Review the work, check events after the year end, ask management for written representations and judge whether uncorrected errors are material.
Give the opinion to the shareholders. Report types are covered in topic 5, Audit reports.
Agree, plan, test, finish, report: engagement letter, planning and risk, evidence, completion, report.

manas.q: List the five main stages of an audit in order.

children.note: Two worked examples: setting materiality with real numbers, and choosing the right level of assurance.
Uzima Hospital Ltd (made-up name): revenue KES 480,000,000 and profit before tax KES 36,000,000 for the year.

children.topic: Option A: 5% of profit before tax

children.note: For a profit-making hospital the owners care about profit, so the auditor picks Option A: overall materiality KES 1,800,000. A charity or mission hospital might use revenue or expenses instead. This is judgement, not a legal rule.
Say the auditor uses 75% of overall materiality: 75% × KES 1,800,000 = KES 1,350,000. Areas are tested using this lower figure.
The pharmacy stock is overstated by KES 2,100,000. That is above KES 1,800,000, so it is material and must be corrected, or the opinion is affected.
Decide whether each job gives reasonable assurance, limited assurance or none.
A full statutory audit of a SACCO's year-end accounts gives reasonable assurance, with a positive opinion.
A matatu company's bank asks for a review of six-month accounts. Mostly enquiry and analysis, so limited assurance with negative wording.
Preparing (compiling) accounts is not an assurance engagement at all; no assurance is given because no independent check is done.
An internal audit team checks drug stock controls and reports to management. Useful, but it is not the independent statutory audit for shareholders.
Points that cost marks again and again.
Never say an audit guarantees the accounts are correct. It gives reasonable assurance only.

children.topic: Trap: auditor must find all fraud
children.note: Preventing and detecting fraud is management's responsibility. The auditor looks for material misstatement, including from fraud.
The directors prepare the financial statements; the auditor gives an opinion on them.
Benchmark percentages are rules of thumb, not law. Always say judgement is used and nature matters as well as size.

children.topic: Trap: mixing up reasonable and limited
children.note: Audit = reasonable assurance, positive opinion. Review = limited assurance, negative wording.
Internal auditors are employees or work for management, so they are not independent of the company the way external auditors are.
Do not quote audit-exemption limits or section numbers unless you have checked the current Companies Act 2015.
Try each question before opening the answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: Explain why companies need audits
children.note: Typical 4-mark question.
Shareholders own the company but directors run it, so owners cannot check everything themselves.

children.topic: Step 2: risk of bias or error
children.note: Managers may make mistakes or show results in a better light because their pay or jobs depend on it.
An independent auditor's opinion gives users reasonable assurance, so shareholders and lenders can rely on the accounts.

children.topic: Q2: Materiality for a duka chain
children.note: Profit before tax KES 12,500,000; revenue KES 210,000,000. Calculate materiality and judge an error of KES 400,000.
0.5% to 1% of KES 210,000,000 = KES 1,050,000 to KES 2,100,000. Profit is the key figure for owners, so use KES 625,000.
KES 400,000 is below KES 625,000, so not material by size alone. But check its nature (e.g. fraud) and add it to other errors before concluding.

children.topic: Q3: Distinguish external and internal audit
children.note: Typical 6-mark question: give three differences.
External auditors are appointed by shareholders; internal auditors by management or the board.
External auditors report to shareholders on the accounts; internal auditors report to management and the audit committee.
External audit is required by company law for most companies; internal audit usually is not.

nodeData.note: Ethics is the set of rules that keeps accountants and auditors honest, fair and trusted. This map covers the IESBA Code of Ethics that ICPAK members in Kenya follow: five principles, five threats, and how to deal with them, with Kenyan examples.

children.note: An audit (topic 1) is only useful if people trust the auditor. Ethics is what earns that trust.
Banks, KRA, SACCO members and shareholders rely on accounts the auditor has checked. If the auditor is not honest or not independent, the audit opinion is worth nothing.
The standards of right behaviour that a profession expects from all its members, beyond simply obeying the law.

manas.q: What are professional ethics?

children.note: The International Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants (including International Independence Standards). It is written by IESBA, a global board, and used in many countries.

manas.q: Which code of ethics do accountants in Kenya follow?

children.note: ICPAK is set up under the Accountants Act. It registers accountants, follows the IESBA Code for its members, runs Code of Ethics training and can discipline members who break the rules.
KASNEB sets and marks the CPA exams. ICPAK looks after qualified members and their conduct. Passing exams alone does not make you a member.
Accountants in practice (auditors, tax advisers) and accountants in business (a finance officer at a hospital or a SACCO accountant). Ethics applies to both.
The Code gives principles plus a way of thinking. You cannot just tick boxes; you must use judgement for each new situation.

manas.q: Is the IESBA Code rules-based or principles-based?

children.note: Every professional accountant must follow these five principles at all times. Memory aid: 'I O P C P'.
Be straightforward and honest in all work. Never be linked to a report you know is false or misleading.

manas.q: What does the principle of integrity require?

children.note: A duka owner asks you to leave KES 300,000 of cash sales out of the books to cut tax. Agreeing would break integrity.
Do not let bias, a conflict of interest or pressure from others override your professional judgement.

manas.q: What does the principle of objectivity require?

children.note: You audit a matatu SACCO where your uncle is chairman. Your judgement may be bent by family loyalty.
Keep your knowledge and skills up to date, and work carefully, fully and on time, following the right standards.

manas.q: What does professional competence and due care mean?

children.note: Taking on a bank audit when nobody in your firm knows bank regulation breaks this principle unless you get the skills first.
Keep client information secret and never use it for your own gain, unless the client agrees or the law or a professional duty requires you to disclose.

manas.q: What does the principle of confidentiality require?

children.note: When the client gives permission; when the law requires it (for example anti-money-laundering reporting or a court order); or for a professional duty such as an ICPAK quality review.

manas.q: When may an accountant disclose confidential information?

children.note: Telling a friend that a hospital client is about to lose a big insurance contract, so he sells its shares, is a serious breach.
Obey the law and avoid anything that would bring the profession into disrepute, including false or exaggerated advertising.

manas.q: What does professional behaviour require?

children.note: Posting on social media that your firm 'guarantees a clean audit opinion' is unprofessional and misleading.
The Code's conceptual framework: identify threats, evaluate them, then address them. Use this for any ethical problem.
Ask what in this situation could push me to break a principle. The Code groups threats into five types.

manas.q: What are the three steps of the conceptual framework?

children.note: Self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity and intimidation. Memory aid: 'SSAFI'.

manas.q: Name the five threats in the IESBA Code.

children.note: Your own money or other interest could affect your judgement. Example: the auditor owns shares in the client SACCO.

manas.q: What is a self-interest threat?

children.note: You check work that you or your firm did earlier. Example: your firm wrote the hospital's accounts and now audits them.

manas.q: What is a self-review threat?

children.note: You promote the client's position so far that you are no longer neutral. Example: speaking for an audit client in a tax dispute with KRA.

manas.q: What is an advocacy threat?

children.note: A long or close relationship makes you too trusting. Example: the same partner has audited a Nairobi hospital for many years and is friends with the CEO.

manas.q: What is a familiarity threat?

children.note: Real or felt pressure stops you acting objectively. Example: a client director says he will sack your firm if you qualify the opinion.

manas.q: What is an intimidation threat?

children.note: Decide whether the threat is at an acceptable level. Look at how big it is and what is already in place to reduce it.

children.topic: Reasonable and informed third party test
children.note: Imagine a sensible outsider who knows all the facts. Would they conclude you still follow the principles? If not, the threat is too high.

manas.q: What is the reasonable and informed third party test?

children.note: If the threat is not acceptable, you must do one of three things.
Eliminate the circumstance that creates the threat. Example: the audit junior sells the SACCO shares.
Take actions that bring the threat down to an acceptable level. Example: an independent partner reviews the work.

manas.q: What is a safeguard?

children.note: If nothing reduces the threat enough, refuse the job or resign from it.
Use different staff for different services; have an independent review; rotate senior staff off a long-running client; get advice from ICPAK or a colleague; tell those charged with governance.
An accountant in a company can face threats as well, such as a boss pressing them to inflate profit for a bank loan. The same three steps apply.
Auditors and assurance providers need independence on top of the five principles. It is covered in the International Independence Standards part of the Code.
Actually thinking freely and being able to give an honest opinion without being influenced.

manas.q: What is independence of mind?

children.note: Avoiding facts that would make an informed outsider believe your judgement may be compromised.

manas.q: What is independence in appearance?

children.note: A direct financial interest in an audit client creates a self-interest threat so big that safeguards cannot fix it. It must be sold or the person removed.
Borrowing from or lending to an audit client is generally not allowed unless it is a normal loan from a bank or SACCO on normal terms.
A close relative in a senior post at the client creates familiarity and self-interest threats. The team member may have to leave the audit.
If an audit partner moves to the client as finance director, the firm faces familiarity and intimidation threats on the next audit.
Senior people who stay on one audit for many years become too friendly. The Code requires rotation of key partners on public interest entities (check the current Code for the time limits).
Accept only if trivial and inconsequential. A free weekend at the coast from a hotel client is not trivial.
Preparing accounts, valuations or internal audit for an audit client can create self-review threats. Some services are banned for public interest entities.
Relying heavily on one client's fees, overdue fees and contingent (success-based) fees all create self-interest threats. Contingent fees for audits are not allowed.

manas.q: Why are contingent fees not allowed for an audit?

children.note: Being in a court case with an audit client creates self-interest and intimidation threats; the firm usually needs to step down.
Use 'threat → why → what to do' for each case.
An audit senior holds shares worth KES 80,000 in Upendo SACCO, which the firm audits.
Self-interest: a good result for the SACCO raises her own dividend.
She must sell the shares before working on the audit, or be removed from the team. Note the action on the audit file.
The same partner has led the audit of Afya Bora Hospital for many years and goes to the CEO's family events.
Familiarity: he may trust management too easily and miss problems.
Rotate the partner off the audit and bring in an independent quality reviewer.
Mama Njeri's duka is a small client. Your firm wrote up her books and now audits them.
Self-review: the team may not challenge numbers the firm itself produced.
Use separate staff for each job and make sure the owner, not the firm, approves the accounts.
Firm's total fees KES 20,000,000; one client pays KES 5,000,000. Share = 5,000,000 ÷ 20,000,000 = 25% of income.
Self-interest and intimidation: losing a quarter of income would hurt, so the firm may avoid upsetting the client.
Have an independent partner review the work, and reduce reliance on the client over time.
A matatu company's director says: 'Sign a clean report or we find new auditors.'
Intimidation.
Do not give in. Discuss with the audit committee or board, and resign if the pressure continues.
A client has not paid last year's fee of KES 400,000 and asks you to start this year's audit.
Self-interest: unpaid fees act like a loan to the client, so you want it to survive.
Get the old fee paid before signing the new report, or consider declining.
Points where students lose marks.

children.topic: Naming a threat with no reason
children.note: Saying 'self-interest threat' alone earns little. Explain why the facts create it and how big it is.
'Be careful' or 'remain professional' are not safeguards. Give a real action: remove the person, rotate, review, decline.
Self-review is about checking your own work. Familiarity is about being too close to people.
When evaluating a threat, refer to how an informed outsider would see it.
Some threats, like owning shares in an audit client, cannot be reduced; the only answer is to remove the cause or resign.
Sharing client data with a bank or friend without consent is a breach, even with good intentions.
Short exam-style questions; open each to see the answer steps.
State and briefly explain the fundamental principles of the IESBA Code.
Integrity (honest), objectivity (no bias), competence and due care (skilled and careful), confidentiality (keep secrets), professional behaviour (obey law, protect the profession).
You are the audit manager of Tumaini SACCO. Your sister has just become its finance manager. Identify the threats and actions.
Familiarity and self-interest: you may not challenge her work and her success affects your family.
Tell the engagement partner and remove yourself from the audit team.
Distinguish independence of mind from independence in appearance.
Mind is being truly unbiased inside. Appearance is avoiding facts that would make an informed outsider doubt you. Auditors need both.
Your audit client asks your firm to represent it before the Tax Appeals Tribunal. What threats arise?
Advocacy (arguing the client's side) and self-review if the tax amounts affect figures you audit. Use a separate team or decline the tax work.

nodeData.note: Before testing numbers, an auditor asks: where could the accounts be wrong, and does the business have good checks to stop mistakes? This topic covers audit risk, materiality, understanding the business, internal control and how the auditor responds. It builds on topic 1 (what an audit is) and topic 2 (ethics).

children.note: An auditor cannot check every receipt. So they find the risky areas and spend most time there. This is called a risk-based audit.
The auditor plans the work around where errors or fraud are most likely, instead of checking everything equally. It saves time and gives better evidence.

manas.q: What is a risk-based audit?

children.note: An audit gives a high level of comfort, not a guarantee. Testing samples and relying on judgement means some errors may still be missed.

children.topic: Link to topic 1: the audit opinion
children.note: Topic 1 showed the auditor gives an opinion on whether accounts are true and fair. Risk work decides how much evidence is needed to support that opinion.
Ethics asks the auditor to keep a questioning mind. When assessing risk, do not simply accept what management says; look for evidence.
The International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board issues the ISAs. Its 2026 Handbook was published on 30 September 2026. ICPAK adopts the ISAs for use in Kenya.
Audit risk is broken into parts so the auditor can see which part they can control. The result tells them how much testing to do.
The risk that the auditor gives the wrong opinion, for example a clean opinion when the accounts are materially wrong. The auditor aims to keep it acceptably low.

manas.q: What is audit risk?

children.note: Audit risk = inherent risk × control risk × detection risk. Inherent risk × control risk together are called the risk of material misstatement (RMM).

manas.q: State the audit risk model.

children.note: The chance an item is wrong before any controls are considered, because of its nature. Cash, estimates and complex items carry high inherent risk.

manas.q: What is inherent risk?

children.note: The chance that the business's own checks fail to prevent or catch an error. Weak controls mean high control risk.

manas.q: What is control risk?

children.note: The chance that the auditor's own tests miss an error. It is the only part the auditor controls, by doing more or better testing.

manas.q: What is detection risk?

children.note: Inherent risk and control risk combined. It exists in the business whether or not there is an audit; the auditor can only assess it, not change it.

manas.q: What is the risk of material misstatement (RMM)?

children.note: The higher the RMM, the lower detection risk must be, so the auditor does more substantive testing. Low RMM allows less testing.

manas.q: How do RMM and detection risk relate?

children.note: Materiality is the size of error that would change a reader's decision. The auditor uses it to plan work and judge errors found. Covered in ISA 320.
An error or omission is material if it could change the decisions of people who use the accounts. It depends on size and on the nature of the item.

manas.q: When is a misstatement material?

children.note: A small amount can still be material, for example a director's loan, a bribe, or an error that turns a profit into a loss.
Auditors pick a base such as profit before tax, revenue, total assets or equity, then take a percentage. The figures are judgement, not fixed rules.
A lower amount than overall materiality, used for individual tests. It leaves a safety margin because small errors can add up.

manas.q: What is performance materiality?

children.note: Errors below a very small amount are not collected or added up. Anything above it goes on the list of misstatements found.

children.topic: Revisit as the audit goes on
children.note: If final figures differ a lot from the draft used at planning, the auditor recalculates materiality and checks whether more work is needed.
ISA 315 (Revised 2019) Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement tells the auditor to learn the business well enough to spot where accounts could be wrong.
Understand the business, its environment, its reporting framework and its internal control, then identify and assess the risks of material misstatement.

manas.q: What does ISA 315 (Revised 2019) require?

children.note: Industry, competition, laws, KRA rules, ownership, financing and how the business makes money. A matatu SACCO faces different risks from a pharmacy.
Ask management and staff (enquiry), compare figures and ratios (analytical procedures), and watch and inspect (observation and inspection).

manas.q: Name the risk assessment procedures.

children.note: The revised ISA 315 grades inherent risk on a scale from low to high, looking at factors such as complexity, uncertainty, change and fraud pressure.
Risks at the top end of the scale that need special attention, such as fraud in revenue or big estimates. The auditor must do specific work on them.

manas.q: What is a significant risk?

children.note: The engagement team meets to talk about where the accounts could be wrong, including fraud, so everyone understands the risks.
The auditor records the understanding gained, risks found and how they were assessed in the audit file.
Internal control is the set of checks management uses to run the business properly, protect assets and produce reliable accounts. ISA 315 groups it into five components.
The policies and checks set by those in charge to give reasonable comfort about reliable reporting, efficient operations and following the law.

manas.q: What is internal control?

children.note: The attitude at the top: honesty, a competent team, clear responsibilities and an active board. A good "tone at the top" makes other controls work.

manas.q: What is the control environment?

children.note: How management itself spots business risks, decides how serious they are and acts on them.
How management checks over time that controls still work, for example internal audit reviews or a supervisor checking reconciliations.
How transactions are captured, processed and reported, and how staff learn their roles. Includes the accounting software and the M-Pesa statement feed.
The actual checks: approvals, reconciliations, physical locks, IT passwords, and segregation of duties.

manas.q: Give examples of control activities.

children.note: Control activities, Risk assessment, Information system and communication, Monitoring, control Environment. A study trick, not an official term.

manas.q: List the five components of internal control.

children.note: Controls can fail through human error, staff working together to cheat (collusion), or management overriding them. Small businesses also have few staff.
Segregation of duties means no single person handles a transaction from start to finish. It is one of the strongest control activities.
Authorising, recording, keeping the asset (custody) and checking (reconciling). Ideally different people do each.

manas.q: Which duties should be segregated?

children.note: The shopkeeper serves and takes cash, but the owner counts the till each evening and compares it to the sales book. The person holding cash does not do the count alone.
One person orders drugs, another receives and signs the delivery note, and a third pays the supplier. Stock counts are done by someone other than the storekeeper.
The cashier receives till payments, but the owner downloads the till statement and reconciles it to sales daily. Only the owner can withdraw from the till.
A small duka may have one worker. The owner then compensates with close personal supervision, daily checks and surprise counts.
ISA 330 tells the auditor to design tests that answer the risks found. There are two kinds: tests of controls and substantive procedures.
For high risk overall, use more experienced staff, more supervision, more surprise in tests and more work near year end.
Tests that check whether a control actually worked through the year. Done only when the auditor plans to rely on that control.

manas.q: What is a test of controls?

children.note: Tests that look for errors in the figures themselves. Two types: tests of detail and substantive analytical procedures.

manas.q: What are substantive procedures?

children.note: Even with strong controls, ISA 330 requires some substantive procedures on each material class of transactions, balance and disclosure.

manas.q: Can an auditor rely only on tests of controls?

children.note: Pick 25 supplier payments and check each has a manager's signed approval. This tests the approval control, not the amounts.
Ask the bank to confirm the year-end balance directly to the auditor, then agree it to the cash book. This tests the figure itself.
Strong controls: test them and reduce detail testing. Weak or untested controls: go fully substantive with larger samples.
After the audit, the auditor writes to management and those charged with governance about control weaknesses found.
A letter (also called a report to management) listing weaknesses in internal control, their effects and recommendations. ISA 265 covers communicating deficiencies.

manas.q: What is a management letter?

children.note: For each point: the weakness, what could go wrong (implication), and what to do (recommendation). Management's reply is often added.

manas.q: What is the usual layout of a management letter point?

children.note: Weakness: till not reconciled to sales. Implication: theft or missed sales go unnoticed. Recommendation: owner reconciles daily and signs.
Serious weaknesses must be reported in writing to those charged with governance, such as the board or audit committee.

children.topic: Not a substitute for the opinion
children.note: The letter helps management improve. It does not change the audit opinion and is not a full list of every weakness.
Real numbers make the ideas easy to remember. All figures are invented for practice.
An ILLUSTRATIVE example only, not a rule. Profit before tax KES 40,000,000; revenue KES 250,000,000. The auditor tests possible benchmarks.
5% × KES 40,000,000 = KES 2,000,000. Many firms use a percentage of profit for profit-making businesses; the percentage is the auditor's judgement.
1% × KES 250,000,000 = KES 2,500,000. Revenue is steadier when profit swings. Auditor chooses KES 2,000,000 as more prudent.
Using 75% for illustration: 75% × KES 2,000,000 = KES 1,500,000. Tests are planned at this lower level.
Using 5% for illustration: 5% × KES 2,000,000 = KES 100,000. Errors below this are ignored; above it they are listed.
Illustration only: target AR 5%, IR 100%, CR 50%. DR = 0.05 ÷ (1.0 × 0.5) = 0.10, so detection risk can be 10%. In practice risks are usually graded low/medium/high.
If CR rises to 100%: DR = 0.05 ÷ (1.0 × 1.0) = 0.05. Lower detection risk means more substantive testing and bigger samples.
Sales of KES 180,000 recorded in the wrong year. It is above KES 100,000 trivial, so it is listed, but below KES 2,000,000 so not material alone.

children.topic: Adjusting entry for the cut-off error
children.note: If management corrects it: Dr Revenue KES 180,000 / Cr Trade receivables KES 180,000. Both sides equal KES 180,000.
Common ways candidates lose marks on this topic.
Inherent risk is about the item itself; control risk is about the business's checks. Say which one, and why.
The auditor cannot change inherent or control risk. They respond by lowering detection risk through more work.
Ask: am I checking that a check happened (control) or that the number is right (substantive)? Name the test correctly.
Percentages are judgement, not laws. In the exam, show your workings and say the figure is a guide.
"Improve controls" scores little. Give a specific weakness, a clear risk and a practical fix for that business.
Try each one, then open the bubbles to check your answer steps.

children.topic: Q: Define the parts of audit risk
children.note: Four to six marks style question.
AR = IR × CR × DR, and say IR × CR = risk of material misstatement.
IR: risk from the nature of the item. CR: risk controls fail. DR: risk the auditor's tests miss errors.
IR high for cash sales in a duka; CR high if no one counts the till; DR lowered by larger samples.
A pharmacy has one storekeeper who orders, receives and counts drugs. Identify the weakness and recommend.
No segregation of duties: one person controls ordering, receipt and records of stock.
Drugs could be stolen or fake orders made and hidden in the stock records.
Split ordering and receiving; have an independent person do monthly stock counts and compare to records.

children.topic: Q: Test of control or substantive?
children.note: Classify: (a) check invoices bear approval; (b) circularise receivables; (c) observe the till count.
Both are tests of controls: they check that an approval or a count actually happens.
Substantive test of detail: it gathers evidence that the receivable amounts exist and are correct.

children.note: AmandaLovesToAudit shows how to tell the two kinds of test apart.

nodeData.note: Auditors cannot just trust what managers say. They gather proof (audit evidence) to back their opinion, and since they cannot check every item, they test a sample. This topic builds on risk and internal control: the risks you found decide how much proof you need.

children.note: Audit evidence is all the information the auditor uses to reach the opinion on the financial statements. ISA 500 Audit Evidence sets the rules.

Any information that supports or contradicts the figures: invoices, bank letters, what the auditor sees at a stock count, and answers from staff. It includes records from the accounting system and from outside sources.

manas.q: What is audit evidence?

children.note: The audit report is only as strong as the proof behind it. Without enough good proof, the auditor cannot give an opinion and may have to modify the report.
Sufficiency is about how much evidence. Higher risk of misstatement means more evidence; better quality evidence means you may need a little less.

manas.q: What does 'sufficient' mean in ISA 500?

children.note: Appropriateness is about quality, made of two parts: relevance and reliability. Lots of weak evidence cannot make up for poor quality.

manas.q: What does 'appropriate' mean in ISA 500?

children.note: Does the test actually address the assertion at risk? Checking goods received notes to the ledger tests completeness, not existence, so the direction of the test matters.
Can you trust the source and form? Reliability depends on where the evidence came from, how it was obtained and its form.
Some evidence is stronger than others. Learn the general rules below; they are guides, not absolute laws.

manas.q: Which kinds of audit evidence are more reliable?

children.note: A letter straight from the client's bank is stronger than the client's own cash book, because an outsider has no reason to bend it.
Proof the auditor gets directly, like recalculating depreciation or watching a stock count, beats proof handed over by the client.
A written document or signed confirmation is stronger than a verbal answer to a question.
Original documents beat photocopies, scans or faxes, which can be altered more easily.

children.topic: Good controls make inside evidence stronger
children.note: Client-produced records are more reliable when the client's internal controls over them work well, as tested in the risk and control topic.
Assertions are the hidden claims managers make when they sign the accounts. Auditors design tests for each assertion that could be wrong.
A claim by management, stated or implied, that the figures are right in a specific way, for example that receivables really exist and are fully collectible.

manas.q: What is a financial statement assertion?

children.note: Claims about sales, purchases and expenses during the year.

manas.q: Name the assertions about classes of transactions.

children.note: The recorded sales or expenses really happened and belong to the business. Test from the ledger back to documents.
Everything that happened was recorded. Test from documents, like delivery notes, forward to the ledger.
Amounts are correctly calculated, recorded in the right year, and posted to the right account. Cut-off matters around year-end, such as a sale on 31 December delivered on 2 January.
Claims about assets, liabilities and equity at the reporting date.

manas.q: Name the assertions about account balances.

children.note: The asset or liability is real at year-end. A receivable of KES 2 million must be owed by a real customer.
The business owns or controls the asset, and the liabilities really belong to it. Goods held for another firm are not your inventory.
All balances are included, and at the right amount, for example inventory at lower of cost and net realisable value under IAS 2, receivables after doubtful debts.
The notes and headings are complete, accurate, correctly classified and easy to understand, such as related party notes and contingent liabilities.
Completeness, Existence, Accuracy, Valuation, Occurrence, Presentation. Add rights and obligations, cut-off and classification to get the full list.
ISA 500 lists the main audit procedures. Many exam answers are just: name the procedure, say what you do, and say which assertion it tests.
Looking at documents or physical assets, such as reading a lease agreement or seeing a delivery van. Seeing an asset proves existence, not ownership or value.

manas.q: What is inspection as an audit procedure?

children.note: Watching a process being done, like the client's stock count or how cash is banked. It only proves what happened while you watched.

manas.q: What is observation as an audit procedure?

children.note: Getting a written reply directly from a third party, such as a bank or customer. ISA 505 External Confirmations covers how to control the request.

manas.q: What is external confirmation and which ISA covers it?

children.note: The customer is asked to reply in every case, agreeing or giving their own balance. Stronger, used for high-risk or large balances.
The customer replies only if they disagree. Weaker, because silence may just mean the letter was ignored; use only when risk is low.
The auditor sends the letters and gets replies directly. If management refuses to let you write to a customer, find out why and treat it as a risk sign.
Checking the maths yourself, for example re-adding the receivables list or recomputing depreciation on vehicles.

manas.q: What is recalculation?

children.note: Doing a client control again yourself, such as redoing a bank reconciliation, to see if it works.

manas.q: What is reperformance?

children.note: Comparing figures and ratios with expectations, last year or the industry, and chasing odd movements. ISA 520 Analytical Procedures covers their use as substantive tests.

manas.q: What are analytical procedures and which ISA covers them?

children.note: Asking people inside or outside the business. Answers alone are rarely enough, so back them up with other proof.

manas.q: Why is inquiry alone not enough evidence?

children.topic: Tests of control vs substantive tests
children.note: Tests of control check that a control works (like reperforming an approval). Substantive tests look for errors in the figures themselves, through detailed tests and analytical procedures.
Receivables, inventory and cash are tested in nearly every Kenyan audit and in many KASNEB questions.
Main risks: customers who do not exist and debts that will not be paid.
Send positive confirmation letters to a sample of debtors, for example hardware shops buying on credit from a Nairobi distributor. Tests existence.
Check cash received from customers in January and February after a December year-end. Payment after year-end is good proof the debt existed and was collectible.
Review the aged receivables list for old balances and discuss them with the credit controller. Tests valuation and the allowance for expected losses.
Main risks: stock that does not exist, is not owned, or is worth less than cost.
Under ISA 501, auditors attend the count when inventory is material, such as at a hospital pharmacy. Watch the counters and do test counts.
Floor to sheet tests completeness (items on shelves are listed). Sheet to floor tests existence (items listed are really there).
Compare cost to recent selling prices. Expired drugs or damaged goods must be written down to net realisable value under IAS 2.
Cash is easy to steal, so it is high risk even when small.
Ask the client's banks to confirm balances, loans and securities directly to the auditor. Very reliable external evidence.
Redo the year-end reconciliation and trace uncleared cheques and deposits to the January bank statement.
Get M-Pesa till or paybill statements for business lines and agree them to the cash book. Count petty cash on a surprise basis, in the presence of the custodian.
Sampling means testing less than 100% of a population so that every item has a chance of being picked, and then concluding on the whole. ISA 530 Audit Sampling sets the rules.
Applying a test to fewer than all the items in a population, chosen so that each sampling unit could be selected, to draw a conclusion about the whole population.

manas.q: What is audit sampling under ISA 530?

children.note: For a few big or risky items, test them all (100%). Picking only the largest items is targeted testing, not sampling, so you cannot project to the rest.
Statistical sampling uses random selection and probability maths to measure sampling risk. Non-statistical relies on judgement; both are allowed by ISA 530.

manas.q: What is the difference between statistical and non-statistical sampling?

children.note: The method must give a sample that represents the population.
Use a random number generator or tables so each item has an equal chance of selection.
Divide population size by sample size to get an interval, pick a random start, then take every nth item. Watch for patterns in the population.

manas.q: How does systematic selection work?

children.note: Each shilling is a sampling unit, so bigger balances are more likely to be picked. Good for testing overstatement of assets like receivables.

manas.q: What is monetary unit sampling?

children.note: The auditor picks items without a conscious bias or pattern. Not allowed for statistical sampling.
Picking one block, such as all March invoices. Rarely suitable for sampling because one block cannot represent the whole year.
The risk that your sample conclusion differs from what testing everything would show. It falls as sample size rises.

manas.q: What is sampling risk?

children.note: Any risk not caused by sampling: using the wrong procedure, misreading evidence, or missing an error you looked at. Reduce it by training and supervision.

manas.q: What is non-sampling risk?

children.note: Bigger sample: higher risk of misstatement, lower tolerable misstatement, more expected errors, or more assurance wanted from the test. Smaller sample: good controls and other evidence on the same assertion.
Errors in the sample must be scaled up to estimate the error in the whole population, then compared with the tolerable misstatement.

manas.q: Why must sample misstatements be projected?

children.note: The largest error in a population the auditor can accept, set below performance materiality for that area.
Projected error = sample error ÷ sample value × population value. Use when errors are roughly in proportion to item size.
A truly one-off error proven not to represent the rest may be left out of the projection. ISA 530 expects this to be rare and well proven.
Working papers are the audit file: the record of what was planned, done, found and concluded. ISA 230 Audit Documentation sets what to record.
They show the audit followed the ISAs, help the reviewer supervise, and defend the firm if later questioned by ICPAK quality reviewers or in court.

manas.q: Why does an auditor keep working papers?

children.note: The file should let an experienced auditor with no link to the job understand what was done, the results, and the big judgements.

manas.q: What is the 'experienced auditor' test in ISA 230?

children.note: Client, year-end, who prepared and reviewed it and when, the objective, the items tested (identifying features), results, and a conclusion.
The permanent file holds long-term items like the company constitution and lease agreements. The current file holds this year's tests and evidence.
The papers belong to the audit firm, and the file should be finalised soon after the report, usually within 60 days. Keep them confidential, normally for at least five years.
Real numbers in KES. Every figure below has been recalculated.
Ledger shows Mama Njeri Hardware owing KES 200,000; her reply says KES 150,000. She paid KES 50,000 on 30 December and it reached the client's bank on 3 January.
No error. At 31 December the money had left the customer but not reached the client, so the ledger KES 200,000 is right. Check the January bank statement shows KES 50,000 received on 3 January.
Credit sales KES 146 million, year-end receivables KES 24 million. Last year receivables days were 45.
24 ÷ 146 × 365 = 60 days, up from 45. Customers are paying slower, so look harder at doubtful debts and possible fake sales.
A list of 400 debtor balances, sample of 40. Interval = 400 ÷ 40 = 10. Pick a random start between 1 and 10, say 7, then take items 7, 17, 27 and so on.
Receivables of KES 24,000,000, sample of 40 shillings. Interval = KES 600,000. With a random start of KES 250,000, pick the balances containing shilling 250,000, 850,000, 1,450,000 and so on.
Population KES 24,000,000. Sample of 40 balances worth KES 3,000,000 found overstatements of KES 45,000. Tolerable misstatement is KES 500,000.
45,000 ÷ 3,000,000 = 1.5% of the sample value is wrong.
1.5% × 24,000,000 = KES 360,000 likely error in the whole receivables balance.
KES 360,000 is below KES 500,000 tolerable, but close. Allow for sampling risk: consider a bigger sample or asking the client to adjust the known KES 45,000.
Under MUS with an interval of KES 600,000, a picked balance booked at KES 200,000 is really KES 180,000. Taint = 20,000 ÷ 200,000 = 10%, so projected error = 10% × 600,000 = KES 60,000.
Common slips first, then short questions in KASNEB style.
Marks come from saying what you do AND why (which assertion). 'Circularise receivables to confirm existence' scores; 'circularise' alone may not.
Ledger to documents tests occurrence or existence; documents to ledger tests completeness. Mixing these up is a classic lost mark.
Never compare the sample error alone (KES 45,000) with tolerable misstatement. Project it to the population first.
Haphazard picks have no formal method, so they cannot support statistical sampling.

children.topic: Q1: Rank evidence for a receivable
children.note: Rank: client's sales invoice, customer's confirmation sent to the auditor, and a director's verbal assurance.
1st customer confirmation (external, direct to auditor, written); 2nd sales invoice (internal, written); 3rd verbal assurance (internal, spoken).
Give three procedures to test that inventory exists at a pharmacy.
Attend and observe the count; do sheet to floor test counts; inspect goods held by third parties or get a confirmation from the warehouse holding them.
Payables KES 8,000,000; sample worth KES 2,000,000 shows understatement of KES 30,000. Find the projected error.
30,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 1.5%; 1.5% × 8,000,000 = KES 120,000 projected understatement. Compare with tolerable misstatement.
