nodeData.note: The audit report is the auditor's final product: a short letter telling shareholders, members or the board whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. Before writing it, the auditor finishes the audit, weighs up the errors found and decides which kind of opinion fits.

children.note: The last stage before signing. The auditor checks events after year end, whether the entity can keep going, gets written promises from management and adds up all the errors found.
Earlier topics gathered evidence item by item. Now the auditor steps back and asks: taken together, is the picture fair? A mistake here leads straight to a wrong opinion.
ISA 560 Subsequent Events covers things that happen between the year-end date and the date the auditor signs, and even after signing.

Events that give more evidence about something that already existed at year end. The figures must be changed. Example: a SACCO borrower declared bankrupt in February for troubles that began before 31 December.

manas.q: What is an adjusting event after the reporting period?

children.note: Events caused by conditions that arose after year end. Figures stay the same, but a material one is disclosed in the notes. Example: a hospital pharmacy fire in February.

manas.q: What is a non-adjusting event after the reporting period?

children.note: The auditor must actively look for such events: read board minutes, ask management, review later management accounts and check recent legal letters.

manas.q: What must the auditor do about events up to the date of the auditor's report?

children.note: After the report date the auditor has no duty to keep searching. But if a fact comes to light that would have changed the report, the auditor discusses it with management and may need a new report.

Going concern means the entity is expected to keep operating for the foreseeable future and not close down. ISA 570 (Revised 2024) was published by the IAASB on 9 April 2025; check its effective date on iaasb.org.
Accounts are normally prepared assuming the business will carry on. If it is about to close, assets would be valued very differently, so this assumption matters.

manas.q: What is the going concern assumption?

children.note: Loans in default, members withdrawing deposits fast, losing a key licence or supplier, big unpaid KRA demands, or net current liabilities. A SACCO failing liquidity rules is a classic sign.
Reviews management's own assessment and cash-flow forecasts, questions the assumptions with professional scepticism, and checks loan agreements and lender support letters.
If serious doubt remains but the basis is still right and the notes explain it well, the opinion stays unmodified and the report adds a separate going concern uncertainty section.

manas.q: How is a material uncertainty about going concern reported when disclosure is adequate?

children.note: The 2024 revision puts more weight on scepticism and on management's assessment, and calls for the report to say more about going concern conclusions. Read the standard on iaasb.org for the detail.
Weak or missing disclosure of the uncertainty gives a qualified or adverse opinion. If the entity is clearly not a going concern but uses that basis anyway, the opinion is adverse.
ISA 580 Written Representations: a signed letter from management confirming certain things to the auditor, dated close to the report date.
That management prepared the accounts properly, gave the auditor all information and recorded all transactions. It may also confirm specific points such as no hidden guarantees.

manas.q: What must management confirm in written representations?

children.note: A letter is weak evidence on its own. The auditor cannot accept a promise in place of counting stock or checking a bank balance.
Refusing to sign raises doubts about management's honesty. The auditor may disclaim an opinion, because it affects the whole audit.
ISA 450 Evaluation of Misstatements: keep a list of all errors found, ask management to correct them, then judge whether what is left is material.
A difference between what the accounts show and what they should show, in amount, classification, presentation or disclosure.

manas.q: What is a misstatement?

children.note: A small cut-off below which errors need not be listed, often a small percentage of materiality. Anything above it goes on the schedule.
The auditor tells management about all listed errors and asks them to fix them. Uncorrected ones are reported to the board and listed in the representation letter.
Several small errors can add up to a material amount. The auditor judges both each error and the total, and also the nature, such as an error that turns a loss into a profit.

manas.q: Under ISA 450, what does the auditor assess about uncorrected misstatements?

children.note: ISA 700 (Revised) sets out how the auditor forms an opinion and the layout of the report. A clean report is called an unmodified opinion.
The auditor concludes the accounts are fairly presented in all material respects under the reporting framework, such as IFRS or IFRS for SMEs.

manas.q: What is an unmodified audit opinion?

children.note: The report follows a set order so readers anywhere can find things quickly.

manas.q: What are the main parts of the auditor's report under ISA 700?

children.note: A heading showing it is an independent auditor's report, addressed usually to the shareholders or, for a SACCO, its members.
The opinion comes at the very top, naming the entity and the statements audited and saying whether they are fair.
Says the audit followed ISAs, that the auditor is independent and met ethics rules (the IESBA Code, adopted by ICPAK), and has enough evidence.
Where they apply, these sections follow the basis for opinion. They are covered in the next branch.
One part explains that management and the directors prepare the accounts; another explains what the auditor does and the limits of an audit.
In Kenya, company audit reports usually add a section on matters the Companies Act 2015 requires the auditor to report on, such as proper books being kept.
The engagement partner is named for listed entities, the report is signed, dated and the city given, for example Nairobi.
Not earlier than the day the auditor has enough evidence, including that the directors have approved the accounts.

manas.q: When can the auditor's report be dated?

children.note: A high but not total level of assurance. The report never says the accounts are 100% correct.
Some reports carry extra sections that add information without changing the opinion.
ISA 701: the matters the auditor thought were most important in this year's audit, chosen from what was discussed with those charged with governance.
Required for listed entities, such as companies on the Nairobi Securities Exchange. Others can include them voluntarily or if law requires.

manas.q: Which audits must include key audit matters?

children.note: Start from matters discussed with the board; pick those needing most attention, such as high-risk areas or big judgements; then select the most significant.
Why the matter was significant and how the audit dealt with it. Example: a bank's loan loss provisions.
A KAM is not a qualification and must not be used instead of one. A matter causing a qualified opinion goes in the basis for opinion, not in KAMs.

manas.q: Can a key audit matter replace a modified opinion?

children.note: A paragraph pointing readers to something already properly disclosed in the accounts that is vital to understanding them. The opinion is not modified.

manas.q: What is an emphasis of matter paragraph?

children.note: A major court case with an uncertain result, or a big fire at a hospital after year end that is correctly disclosed.
The auditor only points to the note; it never adds new information about the entity's accounts.
A paragraph about something NOT in the accounts that helps readers understand the audit or the report, for example that last year's accounts were audited by another firm.

manas.q: What is an other matter paragraph?

children.note: ISA 720 (Revised): the auditor reads the rest of the annual report, such as the chairman's statement, and checks it is consistent with the accounts and what the auditor knows.
Reads and considers it; does not audit it. If something is wrong and management refuses to fix it, the report says so in the other information section.

manas.q: What is the auditor responsibility for other information under ISA 720?

children.note: A SACCO chairman's report says loans grew 20%, but the audited figures show 8%. The auditor asks for the statement to be corrected.
ISA 705 (Revised): if the auditor finds material misstatements or cannot get enough evidence, the opinion is modified.
Either the accounts are wrong (material misstatement), or the auditor could not get enough evidence (inability, sometimes called limitation of scope).

manas.q: What are the two causes of a modified opinion?

children.note: Material means big enough to change a reader's decision. Pervasive means the problem spreads across many areas or goes to the heart of the accounts.
Affects many items, is a large part of the accounts, or a disclosure so basic that readers cannot understand the statements without it.

manas.q: When is a misstatement pervasive?

children.note: Two questions decide the opinion: what is the cause, and is it material only or also pervasive?
Qualified opinion: the accounts are fair except for the stated matter.

manas.q: Material but not pervasive misstatement gives which opinion?

children.note: Adverse opinion: the accounts do not give a true and fair view.

manas.q: Material and pervasive misstatement gives which opinion?

children.note: Qualified opinion: except for the possible effects of the matter the auditor could not check.

manas.q: Inability to get evidence, material not pervasive, gives which opinion?

children.note: Disclaimer of opinion: the auditor does not express an opinion at all.

manas.q: Inability to get evidence, material and pervasive, gives which opinion?

children.note: The opinion heading changes, for example to Qualified Opinion, and the basis section explains the problem and, where possible, its money effect.
Before issuing a modified report, the auditor tells those charged with governance and explains the wording planned.
Auditors must report to those charged with governance, such as the audit committee or SACCO supervisory committee, not just to shareholders.
The people who oversee the entity's direction and accountability, usually the board or its audit committee.

manas.q: Who are those charged with governance?

children.note: The auditor's responsibilities, planned scope and timing, significant findings, uncorrected errors and, for listed entities, an independence confirmation.

manas.q: What does ISA 260 require the auditor to communicate?

children.note: Significant weaknesses in internal control found during the audit must be reported in writing, explaining the risk and suggesting a fix.

manas.q: What does ISA 265 require?

children.note: In practice these points go in a letter. Example: the SACCO lets one clerk both approve and pay out loans; split these duties.
Real numbers in KES. Follow each step and check the totals yourself.
Ukulima SACCO's profit before tax is KES 48,000,000. The auditor uses 5% of profit as overall materiality: KES 2,400,000.
Set lower to leave a safety margin: 75% x 2,400,000 = KES 1,800,000.
5% x 2,400,000 = KES 120,000. Errors below this are not listed.
Uncorrected errors found: interest income overstated KES 900,000; loan impairment under-provided KES 1,300,000. Total KES 2,200,000, below 2,400,000.
2,200,000 is below materiality, but close. The auditor asks for correction and considers more testing, as undetected errors could push it over.
A further KES 400,000 of unrecorded expenses is found. Total now 900,000 + 1,300,000 + 400,000 = KES 2,600,000, above 2,400,000.
Material, but limited to income and loans, so not pervasive: qualified opinion. Correct profit would be 48,000,000 - 2,600,000 = KES 45,400,000.
Dr Interest income 900,000; Dr Impairment expense 1,300,000; Dr Expenses 400,000 / Cr Interest receivable 900,000; Cr Loan loss allowance 1,300,000; Cr Accruals 400,000. Both sides KES 2,600,000.
Afya Bora Hospital, materiality KES 6,000,000. A fire destroyed pharmacy stock records; closing stock of KES 35,000,000 cannot be checked.
Cause: inability to get evidence. Material (35m is above 6m) but only one area: qualified opinion, except for possible effects.
If revenue, expenses and stock records were all lost, the problem is pervasive: disclaimer of opinion.

SACCO year end 31 Dec 2025. On 20 Feb 2026 a borrower owing KES 3,000,000, already struggling in December, is declared bankrupt. Adjusting: Dr Impairment expense 3,000,000 / Cr Loan loss allowance 3,000,000.
Common slips first, then short questions to test yourself.

children.topic: Trap: KAM is not a qualification
children.note: Students put a qualifying matter in the KAM section. Wrong: it goes in the basis for qualified opinion.
An emphasis of matter only points to something properly disclosed. If disclosure is missing, think modified opinion.
Do not jump to adverse or disclaimer for every large error. Ask whether it spreads across the accounts.
Wrong figures lead to qualified or adverse. Missing evidence leads to qualified or disclaimer. Never write adverse for missing evidence.
A client refuses to let you confirm receivables of KES 8m; materiality is KES 3m; nothing else is wrong. Which opinion?
Cause: inability to get evidence. 8m is above 3m, so material. Only one balance, so not pervasive. Qualified opinion, except for possible effects.
A matatu company has a serious going concern doubt, fully explained in note 2. What does the report include?
Basis is still right and disclosure adequate, so opinion unmodified, with a material uncertainty related to going concern section pointing to note 2.
A listed company charged no depreciation on all its assets; the effect is huge across the accounts. Which opinion?
Cause: misstatement. Huge and across many figures, so pervasive. Adverse opinion. Also tell the audit committee under ISA 260 first.

maps.title: CA25 · 1. Costs and how they behave

nodeData.note: What management accounting is, how costs are grouped, and how they change as output changes. Learn to split mixed costs with the high-low method and build a cost card.

children.note: Accounting that helps managers inside the business plan, control and decide. This topic is the starting point for the whole paper.
Management accounting gives managers the numbers they need to run the business day to day: what things cost, what to charge, where money is wasted.

manas.q: What is management accounting?

children.topic: How it differs from financial accounting
children.note: Financial accounting (CA11) reports the past to outsiders in a fixed format under IFRS. Management accounting looks forward, has no required format, and is for people inside.

manas.q: Give three differences between management and financial accounting.

children.note: Financial reports: shareholders, banks, KRA. Management reports: owners, managers, supervisors.
Financial statements must follow IFRS or IFRS for SMEs and the Companies Act. Management reports follow no law; they just need to be useful.

manas.q: Is management accounting governed by IFRS?

children.note: Financial accounts cover a year and the whole business. Management accounts can be weekly, per product, per branch, and include forecasts.
Planning: budgets and targets. Control: compare actual with plan and fix problems. Decision making: price a job, drop a product, buy or make.

manas.q: What are the three main uses of management accounting information?

children.note: Cost accounting records and works out the cost of products, services and departments. Management accounting uses those costs to advise managers.
A duka owner pricing sugar, a SACCO pricing a loan product, or a hospital setting a lab test fee all need to know their true costs first.
Before we classify costs we need to know what we are costing and where the costs are gathered.
Anything we want to know the cost of: a loaf, a matatu trip, a lab test, a customer, a branch.

manas.q: What is a cost object?

children.note: A unit of output used to measure cost, e.g. per loaf, per passenger-km, per patient-day, per 1,000 litres of water.

manas.q: What is a cost unit?

children.note: Made of two measures, such as passenger-km for a matatu or tonne-km for a lorry. Common in service businesses.

manas.q: Give an example of a composite cost unit.

children.note: A place, department or machine where costs are collected, e.g. the baking room, the hospital lab, the workshop. A manager is answerable for its costs.

manas.q: What is a cost centre?

children.note: A profit centre is answerable for costs and revenue (a branch). An investment centre also controls capital spending (a whole division).
Each cost is given a code (e.g. 410-02 = flour, bakery) so it is posted to the right centre and type. Good coding makes reports reliable.
Costs can be classified in several ways. Each way answers a different manager question.
A direct cost can be traced straight to one unit; an indirect cost is shared by many units and must be spread.
Direct materials (flour in bread), direct labour (baker paid per batch), direct expenses (hire of a special mould for one order).

manas.q: What are the three types of direct cost?

children.note: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses. You met it in CA11 manufacturing accounts.

manas.q: What is prime cost?

children.note: Costs that cannot be traced to one unit: factory rent, supervisor salary, oven electricity. Production overheads are spread over units later (topic 3).

manas.q: What are overheads?

children.note: Product costs are part of making goods and sit in inventory until sold. Period costs are charged to profit in the period they happen.
Direct costs plus production overheads. They are valued in closing inventory (IAS 2 Inventories requires production overheads to be included).

manas.q: What is a product cost?

children.note: Selling, distribution and admin costs, e.g. sales staff pay, delivery van fuel, office rent. They are expensed straight away.

manas.q: What is a period cost?

children.note: Grouping by department activity: production, selling, distribution, administration, finance, research. This is how a costed profit statement is laid out.
Grouping by how the cost reacts when activity goes up or down: fixed, variable, semi-variable, stepped. This is the key idea for the rest of the paper.
A controllable cost can be changed by the manager in charge. Judge a manager only on costs they control.
Cost behaviour shows how total cost changes as activity (output, hours, km) changes.
Stay the same in total whatever the output, within a range.

manas.q: What is a fixed cost?

children.note: Rent of the bakery KES 80,000 a month is paid whether you bake 2,000 or 8,000 loaves.
KES 80,000 over 2,000 loaves is KES 40 each; over 8,000 loaves it is KES 10 each. Total fixed, per unit falling.

manas.q: What happens to fixed cost per unit as output rises?

children.note: A flat horizontal line on a graph of total cost against output.
Rise in total in step with output; cost per unit stays the same.

manas.q: What is a variable cost?

children.note: Flour and other ingredients KES 30 per loaf: 2,000 loaves = KES 60,000; 8,000 loaves = KES 240,000.
Fuel of about KES 20 per km: more trips, more fuel. Per km stays flat, total rises.
A straight line from zero rising with output.
Have a fixed part and a variable part.

manas.q: What is a semi-variable cost?

children.note: Analyser lease KES 300,000 a month (fixed) plus reagents KES 300 per test (variable).
Total cost y = a + bx, where a = fixed cost, b = variable cost per unit, x = activity level.

manas.q: What is the cost equation for a semi-variable cost?

children.note: A Safaricom business line with a fixed monthly charge plus a charge per extra minute is semi-variable.
Fixed over a range, then jump up to a new level when capacity runs out.

manas.q: What is a stepped fixed cost?

children.note: One matatu and driver can serve up to about 1,200 passengers a week. Above that you need a second vehicle and driver, so cost steps up.
Looks like a staircase: flat, jump, flat, jump.
The band of activity over which our fixed and variable assumptions hold. Outside it, rent may rise or bulk discounts may change cost per unit.

manas.q: What is the relevant range?

children.note: A forecast far outside the levels in your data is unreliable; the cost pattern may be different there.
To plan, we must separate a semi-variable cost into its fixed and variable parts. Three methods are examined.
Use the highest and lowest activity levels only.

manas.q: What are the steps of the high-low method?

children.note: Choose by ACTIVITY (output), not by cost. Write down cost at each.
b = (cost at high − cost at low) ÷ (high activity − low activity).

manas.q: What is the high-low formula for variable cost per unit?

children.note: a = total cost at high − (b × high activity). Check it also works at the low level.
Quick and easy. But it uses only two points, which may be unusual months, so it can mislead.
Plot every month on a graph (activity across, cost up) and draw a line of best fit by eye. Where it meets the cost axis is the fixed cost.
Uses all the data and shows odd points. But the line is a judgement, so two people get different answers.
The maths version of the best-fit line, from CA15. It uses all data and gives one exact answer.
b = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) ÷ (nΣx² − (Σx)²); a = (Σy ÷ n) − b(Σx ÷ n).

manas.q: What are the least squares formulas for b and a?

children.note: The correlation coefficient r near +1 means activity explains cost well; r² shows how much of the change in cost is explained.
Turning totals into cost per unit so managers can price and plan.

children.topic: Cost per unit falls as output rises
children.note: Variable cost per unit is flat but fixed cost is spread over more units, so total cost per unit falls. This is why big bakeries can sell cheaper.
A list showing the standard cost of one unit, layer by layer: materials, labour, expenses, then overheads.

manas.q: What is a cost card?

children.note: Direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses = prime cost; + variable production overhead; + fixed production overhead = full production cost.

manas.q: What is the layout of a cost card?

children.note: Real numbers in KES. All arithmetic checked.
High = April 8,000 loaves, KES 380,000. Low = May 3,000 loaves, KES 230,000.
140,000 + 30 × 7,000 = 140,000 + 210,000 = KES 350,000. 7,000 is inside the range seen, so it is reliable.
b ≈ KES 29.47 per loaf, a ≈ KES 142,984. At 7,000 loaves: about KES 349,307, close to the high-low KES 350,000.
Bakery: fixed KES 140,000, variable KES 30 per loaf. At 4,000 loaves: 140,000 ÷ 4,000 = 35 + 30 = KES 65 each. At 7,000: 20 + 30 = KES 50 each.
Timber KES 1,800; labour 3 hrs × KES 400 = 1,200; direct expenses 100 → prime cost KES 3,100.
Variable overhead 3 hrs × KES 100 = 300; fixed overhead 3 hrs × KES 250 = 750. Full production cost = 3,100 + 300 + 750 = KES 4,150.
Errors examiners see every sitting.
Always pick the highest and lowest ACTIVITY, even if another month has a higher cost.
Fixed costs are fixed in TOTAL. Per unit they fall as output rises; variable is the opposite.
If a stepped fixed cost jumps between the low and high points, remove the step first, then use high-low.
Forecasting far beyond your data (e.g. 20,000 loaves from data of 3,000–8,000) can give a wrong cost.
Delivery van fuel and office rent are period costs. They never go into inventory value.
Oven electricity is an overhead but rises with baking hours, so it can be variable. Direct/indirect and fixed/variable are separate questions.
Try each one, then open the steps.
A lab did 2,400 tests at KES 1,020,000 and 1,500 tests at KES 750,000. Find the cost equation and the cost of 2,000 tests.
A matatu ran 6,000 km costing KES 210,000 and 9,000 km costing KES 285,000. Find cost per km and fixed cost.
Classify: (a) security guard salary, (b) sugar in a bakery, (c) electricity with a standing charge, (d) supervisors, one per 10 workers.
(a) fixed, (b) variable, (c) semi-variable, (d) stepped fixed.

nodeData.note: How a business buys, stores, issues and values its materials, and how it pays and accounts for its workers. These are usually the two biggest direct costs, so controlling them protects profit.

children.note: Materials and labour make up most of prime cost (Topic 1). Good control stops waste, theft, stock-outs and paying for hours that produce nothing.
In a bakery, flour and bakers' pay; in a furniture workshop, timber and carpenters. Small savings on each add up to big profit gains.
Too much stock ties up cash and spoils; too little stops production. Poor labour records mean paying for idle hours or ghost workers.
Each step from ordering to issuing has its own document, so every bag or box can be traced and someone is answerable for it.
A request from the stores or a department asking the buying office to buy goods. It starts the process.
The buying office's official order to the supplier, stating item, quantity, price and delivery date. In Kenya often called an LPO (local purchase order).

manas.q: What is a purchase order?

children.note: Written by stores when goods arrive, recording what was actually received and its condition. It is matched to the order and the invoice before paying.

manas.q: What is a goods received note (GRN)?

children.note: Pay the supplier only when the purchase order, GRN and supplier invoice agree on item, quantity and price. This stops paying for goods never received.
A form a production department uses to take materials out of stores for a job. It is the authority to issue stock and is charged to that job.

manas.q: What is a materials requisition note?

children.note: Kept by the storekeeper at the shelf. Shows quantities only: received, issued and balance.

manas.q: What is a bin card?

children.note: Kept by the cost office. Shows quantities AND values (price and amount) for receipts, issues and balance. It should agree with the bin card on quantity.

manas.q: How does a stores ledger card differ from a bin card?

children.note: Counting stock to check records. Periodic: everything at once, e.g. year end. Continuous: a few items counted each day so all are checked through the year.
When the same item was bought at different prices, we must choose which price to charge to production. The choice changes both cost of issues and closing stock value.
Issues are priced at the oldest prices first. Closing stock is valued at the most recent prices.

manas.q: What is the FIFO method of pricing issues?

children.note: After every receipt, work out a new average: total value ÷ total units in stock. Issues are priced at that average until the next receipt.

manas.q: How is the cumulative weighted average price worked out?

children.note: One average for the whole period: (opening value + purchases value) ÷ (opening units + units bought). Simple, but only known at period end.

manas.q: What is the periodic weighted average price?

children.note: Issues at the newest prices first. You may meet it in exam questions, but IAS 2 Inventories does not allow LIFO for financial statements.

manas.q: Is LIFO allowed under IAS 2?

children.note: Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Use specific identification for unique items; for interchangeable items use FIFO or weighted average.

manas.q: How does IAS 2 value inventory?

children.note: FIFO charges older, cheaper prices to production, so profit and closing stock are higher. Weighted average gives figures in between.
Set levels so you reorder in time and never hold far too much. Exams use usage per week and lead time (weeks from ordering to delivery).
The time between placing an order and the goods arriving.
Reorder level = maximum usage × maximum lead time. Order when stock falls to this level, so you do not run out even in the worst case.

manas.q: What is the formula for the reorder level?

children.note: Minimum level = reorder level − (average usage × average lead time). Stock should not normally fall below it. It is the safety or buffer stock.

manas.q: What is the formula for the minimum stock level?

children.note: Maximum level = reorder level + reorder quantity − (minimum usage × minimum lead time). Stock above this is wasteful.

manas.q: What is the formula for the maximum stock level?

children.note: Buffer stock protects against a delay or a busy week, but it ties up cash, takes space and may expire, e.g. drugs in a hospital pharmacy.
The order size that makes total ordering cost plus holding cost as low as possible. The idea was developed by Ford W. Harris in 1913.
EOQ = √(2 × Co × D ÷ Ch). Co = cost of placing one order; D = yearly demand in units; Ch = cost of holding one unit for a year.

manas.q: What is the EOQ formula?

children.note: Costs per order: admin, phone and M-Pesa charges, transport, receiving and checking. Bigger orders mean fewer orders, so lower ordering cost.
Costs of keeping stock: storage space, insurance, spoilage, theft, and interest on cash tied up. Bigger orders mean more stock held, so higher holding cost.
At the EOQ, yearly ordering cost equals yearly holding cost, and total cost is lowest.
Demand is steady and known, lead time is known, price does not change with order size, and no stock-outs. Real life is messier.
If a supplier gives a discount for big orders, compare total cost (purchase + ordering + holding) at the EOQ and at each discount level, and choose the lowest.
Labour cost depends on how workers are paid and on hours that are not productive. Workers may be paid by time, by output, or a mix.
Pay = hours worked × rate per hour. Simple and fair for careful work, but no reward for working faster.

manas.q: How is pay worked out under a time rate?

children.note: Pay = units made × rate per unit. Rewards speed, but quality may suffer and inspection is needed.

manas.q: How is pay worked out under a piece rate?

children.note: Extra pay for beating a target, e.g. for hours saved. Can be individual or a group bonus for a team.
Overtime pay has two parts: basic rate for the extra hours, plus the premium (the extra above basic). Only the premium is treated specially.

manas.q: What is the overtime premium?

children.note: Normally the premium is an indirect cost (production overhead), because it is luck which job happened to be done in the extra hours.

manas.q: How is overtime premium usually treated?

children.note: If overtime was worked because a customer asked for a rush job, the premium is charged directly to that job.

manas.q: When is overtime premium a direct cost?

children.note: Hours paid but not worked, e.g. machine breakdown, power cut, waiting for materials. Normal idle time goes to overhead; abnormal idle time goes to the income statement.

manas.q: How is idle time treated?

children.note: Gross pay is reduced by employee tax and other statutory deductions before net pay. Rates change often, so always check the current KRA rate.
Ratios show how hard and how well workers are used, and how fast staff leave.
Labour turnover = number of leavers replaced ÷ average number of employees × 100%. High turnover means hiring and training costs.

manas.q: What is the formula for labour turnover rate?

children.note: Low pay, poor conditions, better jobs elsewhere. Costs: adverts, interviews, training, lost output and more waste while new staff learn.
Efficiency = standard hours of actual output ÷ actual hours worked × 100%. Above 100% means workers were faster than standard.

manas.q: What is the labour efficiency ratio?

children.note: Capacity = actual hours worked ÷ budgeted hours × 100%. Shows how much of the planned working time was used.

manas.q: What is the capacity ratio?

children.note: Production volume = standard hours of actual output ÷ budgeted hours × 100%. Also equals efficiency × capacity.

manas.q: What is the production volume ratio?

children.note: In a cost ledger, materials and wages pass through control accounts before reaching work in progress (WIP) or overheads.
Dr Materials (stores) control; Cr Payables (or Bank).
Dr Work in progress; Cr Materials control. Indirect materials such as cleaning oil: Dr Production overhead control; Cr Materials control.
Dr Wages control with gross pay; Cr Bank with net pay; Cr Statutory deductions payable with amounts withheld.
Direct labour: Dr WIP. Indirect labour, overtime premium and normal idle time: Dr Production overhead control. Office staff: Dr Admin overhead. Cr Wages control.
Real numbers in KES. All arithmetic checked.
1 Nov opening 100 bags @ KES 3,000. 5 Nov buy 200 @ 3,300. 10 Nov issue 200. 18 Nov buy 100 @ 3,400. 25 Nov issue 120. Total bought plus opening: 400 bags, KES 1,300,000.
A hospital pharmacy uses 24,000 boxes of gloves a year. Each order costs KES 2,500; holding one box for a year costs KES 120.
Orders: 24,000 ÷ 1,000 = 24 × 2,500 = 60,000. Holding: average stock 500 × 120 = 60,000. Total KES 120,000 a year.
20 orders × 2,500 = 50,000; holding 600 × 120 = 72,000; total 122,000. Higher, so 1,000 is better.

children.topic: Stock levels: cement at a hardware
children.note: Usage per week: minimum 300, average 400, maximum 500 bags. Lead time: 2 to 4 weeks (average 3). Reorder quantity 3,000 bags.
Worked 50 hours in a week; basic week 40 hours at KES 400; overtime at time-and-a-half.
Basic for all hours 50 × 400 = 20,000; premium 10 × 200 = 2,000. Total KES 22,000.
Direct labour KES 20,000 (to WIP). Premium KES 2,000 to production overhead, unless a customer asked for the overtime.
Budgeted hours 2,000; actual hours worked 1,800; output worth 1,900 standard hours.
Efficiency 1,900 ÷ 1,800 = 105.6%. Capacity 1,800 ÷ 2,000 = 90%. Production volume 1,900 ÷ 2,000 = 95%.
Efficiency × capacity: 105.6% × 90% = 95% (exactly 19/18 × 0.9 = 0.95). Matches the production volume ratio.
Gross wages KES 1,000,000: direct 700,000; indirect 150,000; overtime premium 50,000; normal idle time 30,000; office staff 70,000.
Dr Wages control 1,000,000; Cr Bank (net pay) and Cr Statutory deductions payable, which together total 1,000,000.
Dr WIP 700,000; Dr Production overhead 230,000 (150,000 + 50,000 + 30,000); Dr Admin overhead 70,000; Cr Wages control 1,000,000.
Errors examiners see often.

children.topic: Mixing up bin card and ledger
children.note: The bin card has quantities only. The stores ledger card has quantities and values.
Under cumulative weighted average, work out a new average after EVERY receipt, not after issues.
LIFO may appear in cost questions, but it is not allowed under IAS 2 for financial statements.

children.topic: Charging all overtime pay as overhead
children.note: Only the PREMIUM goes to overhead. The basic rate for overtime hours is still direct labour.
Reorder level uses MAXIMUM usage × MAXIMUM lead time. The minimum level uses averages.
Keep D and Ch on the same time basis (usually per year). Monthly demand with yearly holding cost gives a wrong answer.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Opening 40 units @ KES 500; bought 60 @ KES 550; issued 70. Find issue cost and closing stock under FIFO and periodic average.
Yearly demand 12,000 packets; ordering cost KES 300 per order; holding cost KES 20 per packet a year. Find the EOQ and orders a year.
12,000 ÷ 600 = 20 orders. Ordering 20 × 300 = 6,000 equals holding 300 × 20 = 6,000.
A worker did 45 hours; basic week 40 hours at KES 300; overtime at time-and-a-half. Split the pay.
Direct labour 45 × 300 = KES 13,500. Premium 5 × 150 = KES 750 to overhead. Gross pay KES 14,250.
A factory started the year with 110 workers and ended with 90. It replaced 15 leavers. Find the turnover rate.
Average workers (110 + 90) ÷ 2 = 100. Turnover 15 ÷ 100 × 100% = 15%.

nodeData.note: Overheads are shared running costs like rent and power. Learn how to charge them to departments, move service costs to production, and load them onto each unit with a rate.

children.note: Overheads are the running costs you cannot pin to one product or job. They still have to be paid for, so we share them out fairly.
Costs that cannot be traced straight to one unit: factory rent, supervisor pay, machine repairs, electricity for the whole workshop.

manas.q: What is an overhead?

children.note: Indirect costs of the factory or workshop: indirect materials (glue, nails), indirect labour (cleaners, supervisors) and indirect expenses (rent, power, depreciation of machines).

manas.q: What are production overheads?

children.note: Admin, selling and distribution costs: office salaries, adverts, delivery van fuel. They are period costs and are charged to profit when incurred.

manas.q: What are non-production overheads?

children.note: To know the full cost of a product, set a fair price, and value closing inventory. IAS 2 Inventories says inventory cost includes a fair share of production overheads.

manas.q: Why must production overheads be included in inventory value?

children.note: Prime cost (direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses) plus a share of production overheads = full production cost.
The method of putting all production overheads, fixed and variable, into the cost of units. This whole topic shows how it is done.

manas.q: What is total absorption costing?

children.note: First charge overheads to cost centres, then move service centre costs to production centres, then load them onto units with a rate.

manas.q: What are the three stages of overhead analysis?

children.note: Getting every overhead shilling into a cost centre, either whole or shared by a fair base.
Charging a whole overhead to one cost centre because it clearly belongs there, e.g. the stores keeper's salary goes all to Stores.

manas.q: What is overhead allocation?

children.note: Splitting a shared overhead between cost centres using a fair base, e.g. factory rent shared by floor area.

manas.q: What is overhead apportionment?

children.note: Pick the base that best shows which centre causes or uses the cost. There is no single right answer, but it must be sensible and easy to measure.
Share by floor area (square metres) each centre takes up.

manas.q: Fair base for factory rent?

children.note: Share by kilowatt-hours used (from sub-meters) or by machine hours.
Share by the cost or value of machines in each centre.

manas.q: Fair base for machine depreciation?

children.note: Share by number of employees in each centre.
Share by volume of space (cubic metres) where height differs a lot.
Production centres make the product (machining, assembly). Service centres help them (stores, maintenance, canteen). Units only pass through production centres.

manas.q: What is a service cost centre?

children.note: A table with one column per cost centre and one row per overhead. Each row shows the base used. The column totals must add back to total overheads.
Service centre costs must move into production centres, because only production centres handle units.
Stores and maintenance do not make tables or beds, so we cannot absorb their cost into units directly. We pass it on to the centres they serve.
Share each service centre's cost straight to production centres only, and ignore any work service centres do for each other.

manas.q: What is the direct method of reapportionment?

children.note: Service centres are closed one at a time. The first one shares to everyone it serves, including the other service centre; later ones share only forward.

manas.q: What is the step-down method?

children.note: Usually the service centre that does the most work for other service centres, or the one with the biggest cost.
Fully recognises that service centres serve each other. Done by repeated distribution or by simultaneous equations.

manas.q: What is the reciprocal method?

children.note: Keep sharing service costs back and forth by the given percentages until what is left is tiny, then share the remainder to production centres only.
Let s and t be each service centre's total cost after receiving its share from the other. Write two equations, solve, then share s and t out.

manas.q: How does the algebraic method work?

children.topic: All methods give the same total
children.note: Whatever method is used, total overheads in production centres equal total overheads to start with. Only the split between them changes.
Loading production centre overheads onto each unit or job with a rate.
Adding overhead into the cost of each unit using an overhead absorption rate (OAR).

manas.q: What is overhead absorption?

children.note: OAR = budgeted overheads of the centre ÷ budgeted level of activity (units, labour hours or machine hours).

manas.q: What is the overhead absorption rate formula?

children.note: Use only when the centre makes one identical product, e.g. a bakery making one loaf type. Unfair if products differ.

manas.q: When is a rate per unit suitable?

children.note: Best for a centre where work is mainly by hand, like assembly or upholstery. Longer jobs pick up more overhead.

manas.q: When use a labour hour rate?

children.note: Best for a centre where machines do most of the work, like a sawmill or CNC machining. Machine-heavy jobs carry more overhead.

manas.q: When use a machine hour rate?

children.note: Percentage of direct labour cost, direct material cost or prime cost. Easy but weak, since price changes alter the overhead charged.
Use one rate for each production centre (departmental rates), not one blanket rate for the whole factory. It gives fairer job costs.

manas.q: Why prefer departmental rates to a blanket rate?

children.note: Rates are set at the start of the year from budgets, so actual results rarely match exactly.
Actual overheads are only known at year end, but jobs must be costed and priced now. So the rate is worked out in advance from budgets.

manas.q: Why are absorption rates predetermined?

children.note: Absorbed = predetermined OAR × ACTUAL activity (actual hours or units).

manas.q: How is absorbed overhead calculated?

children.note: Absorbed is more than actual overhead. Too much cost was charged to units, so profit is increased by the difference at period end.

manas.q: What is over-absorption?

children.note: Absorbed is less than actual overhead. Too little was charged to units, so the shortfall is an extra expense that reduces profit.

manas.q: What is under-absorption?

children.note: Actual overhead spending differed from budget, or actual activity (hours, units) differed from budget, or both.
Actual: Dr Production overhead control / Cr Bank or payables. Absorbed: Dr Work in progress / Cr Production overhead control. The balance left goes to profit or loss.
Dr Production overhead control / Cr Over-absorbed overheads (to profit or loss).
Dr Under-absorbed overheads (to profit or loss) / Cr Production overhead control.
Activity-based costing shares overheads using many cost drivers instead of one hourly rate. It is covered later, in CA34S3.
Mti Bora Furniture in Industrial Area has two production centres, Machining (M) and Assembly (A), and two service centres, Stores (S) and Maintenance (T). Budgeted overheads KES 2,300,000.
Charged straight to centres: M 440,000; A 320,000; S 82,000; T 158,000. Total KES 1,000,000.
Shared costs KES 1,300,000: rent 600,000 (area 500/300/100/100 m²), power 240,000 (kWh 6,000/2,000/500/1,500), depreciation 300,000 (machine value), supervision 160,000 (staff 12/20/4/4).
Machines KES 2.0m/0.6m/0.1m/0.3m, so depreciation M 200,000, A 60,000, S 10,000, T 30,000. Supervision at KES 4,000 a head: M 48,000, A 80,000, S 16,000, T 16,000.
M 1,132,000; A 688,000; S 180,000; T 300,000. Total 2,300,000, which agrees with the budget.
Stores serves M 50%, A 30%, T 20%. Maintenance serves M 60%, A 20%, S 20%.
Round 1 leaves M 1,423,600, A 809,200 and S 67,200 to share again. After five rounds the figures settle at M 1,467,000 and A 833,000.
Using the reciprocal totals. Machining (machine-led): 1,467,000 ÷ 9,000 machine hours = KES 163 per machine hour. Assembly (hand work): 833,000 ÷ 9,800 labour hours = KES 85 per labour hour.

children.topic: Step 5: cost of a dining table
children.note: Materials 6,000 + labour 2,500 = prime cost 8,500. Overheads: 3 machine hrs × 163 = 489 and 5 labour hrs × 85 = 425. Full production cost KES 9,414.
Machining: 9,400 actual hrs × 163 = 1,532,200 absorbed vs 1,500,000 actual, over-absorbed 32,200. Assembly: 9,500 × 85 = 807,500 vs 820,000 actual, under-absorbed 12,500.
Dr Overhead control 32,200 / Cr P&L 32,200 (Machining). Dr P&L 12,500 / Cr Overhead control 12,500 (Assembly). Net over-absorption of KES 19,700 adds to profit.
Errors that cost marks in overhead questions.
Absorbed overhead uses ACTUAL hours × the budget rate. Budget hours are only for setting the rate.
Over-absorbed ADDS to profit; under-absorbed REDUCES profit. Remember: under = not enough charged, so top up the expense.
After every stage the centre totals must add back to total overheads. Always do a check total.
In step-down and reciprocal methods, service centres pass cost to each other. The direct method is the only one that ignores this.
Machine hours for a machine centre and labour hours for a hand-work centre. Exam questions often hint at which one fits.
Admin and selling costs are not put into inventory value under absorption costing. Only production overheads are.
Try each one, then open the steps.
A Nakuru hospital pays rent KES 900,000. Floor area: Lab 200 m², Pharmacy 100 m², Wards 300 m². Apportion the rent.
A hospital lab budgets overhead KES 3,600,000 for 12,000 tests. It does 13,000 tests and spends KES 3,750,000. Find the result.
13,000 × 300 = 3,900,000 absorbed. Actual 3,750,000. Over-absorbed KES 150,000.
Dr Overhead control 150,000 / Cr P&L 150,000. Profit rises by KES 150,000.
Give two reasons why a workshop may under-absorb overheads.
Actual overhead spending was higher than budget (e.g. KPLC tariff rise), or actual hours worked were fewer than budget (e.g. power cuts, fewer orders).

nodeData.note: Two ways to put a cost on each unit made. Learn what each includes, how to lay out both profit statements, and why their profits differ by the fixed overhead held in stock.

children.topic: 1. Two ways to cost a unit
children.note: Both methods count materials, labour and variable overhead. They disagree on one thing only: does fixed production overhead go into the cost of each unit, or is it charged in full each period?
Only variable costs go into a unit: direct materials, direct labour, direct expenses and variable production overhead. All fixed costs are charged to profit in the period they happen.

manas.q: What goes into a unit's cost under marginal costing?

children.note: US and Wikipedia books say variable costing or direct costing. KASNEB and ACCA usually say marginal costing. Same idea.

manas.q: What is another name for marginal costing?

children.note: Every production cost goes into a unit, including a share of fixed production overhead using the absorption rate (OAR) from topic 3. Also called full or total absorption costing.

manas.q: What goes into a unit's cost under absorption costing?

children.note: The extra cost of making one more unit. In exams it equals variable production cost per unit.

manas.q: What is marginal cost?

children.note: Under BOTH methods, selling, distribution and admin costs never go into inventory. They are period costs (topic 1).
Fixed production overhead: a period cost under marginal costing, a product cost under absorption costing. Everything else is treated the same.

manas.q: What is the only cost treated differently by marginal and absorption costing?

children.note: The choice changes the value of closing inventory, and so changes reported profit whenever production and sales are not equal.
The key number in marginal costing and in later decision topics.
Sales minus ALL variable costs (production and selling). It is what each sale 'contributes' first to paying fixed costs and then to profit.

manas.q: What is contribution?

children.note: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit. It stays the same per unit whatever the output, within the relevant range.

manas.q: How do you find contribution per unit?

children.note: Profit = total contribution − total fixed costs. Once fixed costs are covered, each extra sale adds its full contribution to profit.

manas.q: How is profit found from contribution?

children.note: A shop sells a crate of soda for KES 1,000 that costs KES 750 to buy. Contribution is KES 250 a crate. With rent KES 50,000 a month it must sell 200 crates to break even.
Contribution is the base for break-even (CVP) analysis, limiting factors and make-or-buy decisions later in this paper.
Each method has its own layout. Learn both formats; exams often ask for both side by side.
Sales − variable cost of sales (opening + variable production − closing, all at variable cost) − variable selling = contribution; − all fixed costs = profit.

manas.q: What is the layout of a marginal costing profit statement?

children.note: Sales − cost of sales (opening + production − closing, at full cost) ± under/over-absorbed overhead = gross profit; − selling and admin = profit.

manas.q: What is the layout of an absorption costing profit statement?

children.note: Marginal: closing stock at variable production cost per unit. Absorption: at full production cost per unit (variable + fixed OAR).

manas.q: How is closing inventory valued under each method?

children.note: Only the absorption statement needs it. Under-absorbed overhead is added to cost of sales; over-absorbed is taken off. See topic 3 for how to work it out.
The marginal statement shows contribution, not gross profit, and fixed production overhead appears as one actual figure below contribution.
A Thika juice maker over two months where production ≠ sales. All figures checked with code; the two profits reconcile exactly.

Price KES 220 a carton. Variable production cost KES 100 (materials 60, labour 30, variable overhead 10). Variable selling KES 10 per carton sold. Fixed production overhead KES 600,000 a month; fixed selling and admin KES 150,000 a month.
Month 1: made 10,000, sold 8,000 (closing stock 2,000). Month 2: made 9,000, sold 10,000 (stock falls to 1,000). No opening stock in month 1.
Budgeted normal output 10,000 cartons. OAR = 600,000 ÷ 10,000 = KES 60 a carton. Full production cost = 100 + 60 = KES 160 a carton.
Sales 8,000 × 220 = 1,760,000. Variable COS: production 1,000,000 − closing 2,000 × 100 = 200,000 → 800,000. Variable selling 80,000. Contribution 880,000.
Contribution 880,000 − fixed production 600,000 − fixed selling and admin 150,000 = KES 130,000. Check: 8,000 × KES 110 contribution = 880,000.
Sales 10,000 × 220 = 2,200,000. Variable COS: opening 200,000 + production 900,000 − closing 100,000 = 1,000,000. Variable selling 100,000. Contribution 1,100,000.
1,100,000 − 600,000 − 150,000 = KES 350,000. Marginal profit follows SALES: more sold, more profit.
Sales 1,760,000. COS: production 10,000 × 160 = 1,600,000 − closing 2,000 × 160 = 320,000 → 1,280,000. Absorbed 600,000 = actual, so no adjustment. Gross profit 480,000.
Gross profit 480,000 − variable selling 80,000 − fixed selling and admin 150,000 = KES 250,000.
Absorbed 9,000 × 60 = 540,000 but actual fixed overhead was 600,000. Under-absorbed KES 60,000 is added: COS 1,660,000. Gross profit 2,200,000 − 1,660,000 = 540,000.
Gross profit 540,000 − variable selling 100,000 − fixed selling and admin 150,000 = KES 290,000.
Month 1: absorption 250,000, marginal 130,000. Month 2: absorption 290,000, marginal 350,000. Two months together: absorption 540,000, marginal 480,000.
The gap between the two profits is always the fixed overhead carried into or out of stock.
Difference in profit = change in inventory units × fixed overhead absorption rate per unit.

manas.q: How do you reconcile marginal and absorption profits?

children.note: When production > sales, some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing stock, so absorption profit is higher.

manas.q: Which method shows higher profit when inventory rises?

children.note: When sales > production, last period's fixed overhead in opening stock is released into this period's cost, so absorption profit is lower.

manas.q: Which method shows higher profit when inventory falls?

children.note: If opening and closing stock are the same number of units (and the rate is the same), both methods give the same profit.
Total gap 60,000 = the 1,000 cartons still in stock × 60. Over the life of a business, with all stock sold, total profits are the same; only timing differs.
Start with marginal profit; add fixed overhead in closing stock; subtract fixed overhead in opening stock; result = absorption profit. Works in either direction.
Each method has a job. Know the arguments for and against.

IAS 2 Inventories says inventory cost includes costs of conversion, which takes in a systematic share of fixed production overhead based on normal capacity. So published accounts use absorption costing.

manas.q: Which costing method does IAS 2 require for inventory in financial statements?

children.note: Small Kenyan companies using IFRS for SMEs follow the same idea in its inventories section: fixed production overhead goes into stock.
For pricing a special order, break-even, or choosing which product to push, managers look at contribution. Fixed costs usually do not change with the decision.
Simple; no arbitrary sharing of fixed overhead; no under/over-absorption; profit moves with sales; managers cannot boost profit just by making stock.

manas.q: Give two advantages of marginal costing.

children.note: Not allowed for published inventory; may under-price if managers forget fixed costs must still be covered; splitting mixed costs can be hard.
Meets IAS 2; reminds managers that fixed costs must be recovered in price; smooths profit when a business builds stock for a busy season.

manas.q: Give two advantages of absorption costing.

children.note: Profit can be raised by over-producing and building stock; OARs rest on budgets and estimates; under/over-absorption confuses non-accountants.

manas.q: Give two disadvantages of absorption costing.

children.note: Where marks are lost in this topic.
Absorption statements use the OAR on actual production. If actual overhead differs, adjust: add under-absorbed, deduct over-absorbed. Marginal statements never need it.

children.topic: Valuing stock at the wrong cost
children.note: Marginal stock = variable production cost only (no fixed, no selling cost). Absorption stock = variable production + fixed OAR. Never put selling costs in stock.

children.topic: Variable selling in cost of sales
children.note: Variable selling cost depends on units SOLD, not made. Show it after cost of sales in both formats.

children.topic: Using the wrong rate in reconciliation
children.note: Use the fixed production OAR per unit, not the actual overhead ÷ actual output, unless the question says so.

children.topic: Fixed overhead per unit in marginal
children.note: Do not spread fixed costs per unit in a marginal statement. Show the whole actual fixed overhead below contribution.
Stock UP → absorption profit higher. Stock DOWN → marginal profit higher. Say it out loud before you sign the answer.
If the OAR changes, opening stock carries last period's rate. Value opening and closing stock at their own rates when reconciling.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Marginal profit KES 400,000. Opening stock 3,000 units, closing 5,000 units. Fixed OAR KES 50 a unit. Find absorption profit.
Stock rose by 5,000 − 3,000 = 2,000 units, so absorption profit is higher.
Variable production cost KES 80 a unit, fixed OAR KES 40, variable selling KES 5. Closing stock 1,500 units. Value it both ways.
1,500 × 80 = KES 120,000. Selling cost is ignored.
Budgeted fixed overhead KES 500,000 for 20,000 units. Actual output 22,000 units; actual fixed overhead KES 520,000. Find the adjustment.
Absorbed 550,000 > actual 520,000: over-absorbed KES 30,000. Deduct it from cost of sales in the absorption statement, which raises profit.
A firm makes and sells 12,000 units, with no opening or closing stock. Will the two profits differ?
No. Stock does not change, so no fixed overhead moves between periods and both profits are equal.

nodeData.note: How a business plans the coming year in numbers: sales, production, materials, labour, overheads and cash. Then how flexible budgets help managers control costs fairly.

children.topic: 1. What a budget is and why
children.note: A budget is the plan for the coming period written in numbers. It builds on cost behaviour (topic 1) and costing methods (topics 2–4).
A budget is a plan for a set period (usually a year, split into months) showing expected sales, costs, cash and resources.

manas.q: What is a budget?

children.note: Making a budget forces managers to think ahead: how much will we sell, what will we need, where could problems come from.
Sales, production, buying and finance must agree. The bakery cannot sell 12,000 packets if production plans for 8,000.
Each month actual results are compared with the budget. Big gaps are looked into and fixed.
A budget tells every manager what is expected of them. A fair target can push people to do better.
Plan, coordinate, communicate, control, motivate. Some books add "authorise spending" and "evaluate performance".

manas.q: What are the main purposes of budgeting?

children.note: A forecast is a best guess of what will happen. A budget is the plan the business commits to, often built from forecasts.

manas.q: What is the difference between a budget and a forecast?

children.note: Budgeting is a yearly cycle run by a committee, guided by a manual, and starting from the factor that limits the business most.
Senior managers from each area (sales, production, finance, HR) who agree and approve the budget. The chief accountant often coordinates.

manas.q: What does the budget committee do?

children.note: Usually an accountant who collects the figures, sets the timetable and puts the budgets together for the committee.
A guide that sets out the timetable, who prepares what, the formats to use and how approval works.

manas.q: What is a budget manual?

children.note: The one thing that limits activity, so it must be budgeted first. Usually it is sales demand.

manas.q: What is the principal budget factor?

children.note: Sales demand for a bakery, oven capacity at peak season, skilled nurses in a hospital, or the loan fund available to a SACCO.
Every other budget depends on it. If you start anywhere else, the plans will not fit together.
Set goals → find the principal budget factor → prepare the sales budget → other functional budgets → cash budget → master budget → approve → compare actual with budget.

manas.q: What are the steps in the budget cycle?

children.note: Usually the financial year, broken into months or quarters so that control can happen during the year.
Each department budget feeds the next one. Learn the order and the two key formulas.
Units expected to be sold × selling price, month by month. It is usually the first budget.

manas.q: What is the sales budget?

children.note: Units to make = sales + closing inventory of finished goods − opening inventory of finished goods.

manas.q: What is the formula for the production budget?

children.note: Materials used = units to produce × material per unit. Measured in kg, metres or litres.

manas.q: How is the materials usage budget worked out?

children.note: Materials to buy = usage + closing material inventory − opening material inventory. Then × price per kg to get KES.

manas.q: What is the formula for the materials purchases budget?

children.note: Hours needed = units to produce × hours per unit. Cost = hours × rate per hour, plus any overtime or idle time.
Variable overheads change with activity; fixed overheads stay flat. Note which items are non-cash, such as depreciation.
Period costs such as sales staff pay, delivery fuel and office rent. They do not go into the production cost.
Planned spending on long-term assets, such as a new oven or a delivery van. It affects the cash budget.
A month-by-month plan of cash coming in and going out. It shows when the business may run short or have spare cash.
A profitable business can still fail if it runs out of cash. The cash budget warns early so you can arrange an overdraft or delay buying.

manas.q: Why is a cash budget important?

children.note: Receipts − payments = net cash flow. Opening balance + net cash flow = closing balance. Each closing balance is next month's opening.

manas.q: What is the layout of a cash budget?

children.note: Cash sales arrive at once. Credit sales arrive later, e.g. 40% this month and 60% next month. Bad debts never arrive.

manas.q: How do credit sales affect a cash budget?

children.note: Suppliers may be paid a month later; wages usually the same month. Use the date cash leaves, not the date the cost is incurred.
Depreciation, provisions and bad debts written off are not cash. Do not put them in the cash budget.

manas.q: Is depreciation included in a cash budget?

children.note: Loans received, asset sales and share issues come in; asset purchases, loan repayments, dividends and tax go out. Any tax shown in an example is illustrative.
The master budget brings it all together. Then you choose how flexible the budget is and how it is built.
The summary: budgeted income statement, budgeted statement of financial position and cash budget for the period.

manas.q: What does the master budget contain?

children.note: Prepared for one level of activity only. It does not change if actual output is different.

manas.q: What is a fixed budget?

children.note: Shows costs and revenue at several activity levels, using cost behaviour: fixed costs stay, variable costs move with output.

manas.q: What is a flexible budget?

children.note: After the period, redraw the budget at the ACTUAL output. Compare actual with this flexed budget to judge managers fairly.

manas.q: Why do we flex a budget before comparing it with actual results?

children.note: Take last year's figures and add a percentage for inflation or growth. Quick, but carries past waste forward.

manas.q: What is incremental budgeting?

children.note: Start from nil: every activity must justify its cost before it gets money. Finds waste, but takes much time and effort.

manas.q: What is zero-based budgeting?

children.note: Instead of adding 8% to last year's marketing spend, a SACCO asks: which campaigns actually brought members? Only those get funded.
Kept 12 months ahead by adding a new month (or quarter) as each one ends. Stays up to date, but needs constant work.

manas.q: What is a rolling (continuous) budget?

children.note: Top-down (imposed): bosses set the budget. Bottom-up (participative): managers who will run it help build it.
Budgets affect behaviour. A good budget motivates; a bad one causes games and stress.
Letting managers help set their budget gives better information and more commitment. It takes longer.

manas.q: What are the benefits of participative budgeting?

children.note: Padding a budget: asking for more cost or setting lower sales than expected, so the target is easy to beat.

manas.q: What is budgetary slack?

children.note: Too easy gives no push; too hard and people give up. A target that is hard but reachable works best.
Under incremental budgets, managers may waste money in the last month so next year's budget is not cut.
Budgets should make each manager's aim match the aim of the whole business, not just their own department.

manas.q: What is goal congruence?

children.note: Mkate Tamu bakes biscuit packets selling at KES 50. Budget for Jan–Mar. Sales: Jan 10,000, Feb 12,000, Mar 11,000, Apr 13,000 packets. All tables checked.
Closing finished packets = 10% of next month's sales. Opening Jan = 1,000.
Each packet uses 0.2 kg of flour at KES 80 per kg. Flour in store: 500 kg at start; closing Jan 600, Feb 560, Mar 600 kg.
0.05 hours per packet at KES 250 an hour. Jan 510 hrs = KES 127,500; Feb 595 hrs = KES 148,750; Mar 560 hrs = KES 140,000.
Variable KES 4 per packet baked. Fixed KES 120,000 a month, of which KES 20,000 is depreciation (not cash). Cash overheads: Jan 140,800; Feb 147,600; Mar 144,800.
Sales: Dec KES 450,000; Jan 500,000; Feb 600,000; Mar 550,000. 40% paid at once, 60% next month. Receipts: Jan 470,000; Feb 540,000; Mar 580,000.
Flour paid one month later (Dec purchases KES 160,000). Wages and cash overheads same month. New oven KES 150,000 paid in Feb. Totals: Jan 428,300; Feb 617,550; Mar 472,000.
Opening Jan 50,000. Jan +41,700 → 91,700. Feb −77,550 → 14,150. Mar +108,000 → 122,150. February is tight: arrange an overdraft or delay the oven.
Variable cost per packet: flour 16 + labour 12.50 + overhead 4 = KES 32.50. Contribution 17.50 × 33,000 sold = 577,500 − fixed 360,000 = KES 217,500 profit.
The bakery budgeted 10,000 packets: sales KES 500,000, variable costs KES 300,000 (KES 30 each), fixed KES 100,000, profit KES 100,000. It actually sold 12,000.
Sales KES 588,000, variable costs KES 372,000, fixed KES 104,000. Actual profit KES 112,000.
Actual 112,000 vs fixed budget 100,000 looks KES 12,000 better. But more packets were sold, so this hides the real picture.
Actual 112,000 vs flexed 140,000: KES 28,000 worse. Prices were lower and costs higher than planned. Topic 6 splits this into variances.
Errors examiners see every sitting.
Production = sales + CLOSING − OPENING. Adding opening inventory is the most common slip.
The materials and labour budgets are based on units PRODUCED, not units sold.
Depreciation is not a cash payment. Only the asset purchase itself goes in the cash budget.

children.topic: Using the sale date for cash
children.note: Credit sales and credit purchases go in the month cash moves, not the month of the sale or purchase.

children.topic: Comparing actual with a fixed budget
children.note: If output changed, flex the budget first. Otherwise variable costs look over- or under-spent unfairly.
Each month's closing cash becomes next month's opening. Check the chain rolls forward.
Try each one, then open the steps.
A Gikomba workshop expects to sell 400 chairs. Opening inventory 60 chairs, closing inventory wanted 80. How many to make?
Each chair needs 4 metres of timber at KES 450. Opening timber 300 m, closing 250 m. Find purchases for 420 chairs.
Sales: March KES 800,000, April KES 1,000,000. 30% cash, 65% next month, 5% bad debts. Find April receipts.
April cash 30% × 1,000,000 = 300,000 + 65% × 800,000 = 520,000. Total KES 820,000. The 5% bad debt never arrives.
Costs were KES 400,000 at 5,000 units and KES 550,000 at 8,000 units. Find the flexed cost at 6,500 units.

nodeData.note: Standard costing sets a "should cost" for each unit before work starts. Variances compare that plan with what really happened, so managers can see where profit was won or lost. This topic builds on costs, materials, labour, overheads, marginal/absorption costing and budgets.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Start here: the idea of a planned cost per unit, and why businesses bother to compare plan with actual.
The planned cost of making one unit, worked out in advance from expected prices, quantities and times. It is the "should cost" you compare real results against.

manas.q: What is a standard cost?

children.note: A table showing, for one unit, how much material, labour and overhead it should use and at what price. Adding the lines gives the standard cost per unit.

manas.q: What does a standard cost card show?

children.note: The difference between what should have happened (standard or budget) and what actually happened. Each variance is shown as a KES amount.

manas.q: What is a variance?

children.note: Favourable means profit is higher than planned (cost lower or revenue higher). Adverse means profit is lower than planned. F is good for profit, A is bad.

manas.q: What do favourable and adverse variances mean?

children.note: It helps with pricing, valuing inventory, budgeting and control. Managers look only at big variances instead of checking every shilling (management by exception).
Managers spend time only on variances that are large or keep repeating, and leave small ones alone. This saves time and focuses effort.

manas.q: What is management by exception?

children.topic: Where it fits in the paper
children.note: It joins earlier topics: material and labour costs (topic 2), overhead absorption (topic 3), marginal vs absorption profit (topic 4) and the budget (topic 5) it measures against.
How the numbers on the standard cost card are chosen.
Assumes perfect conditions: no waste, no breakdowns, no idle time. It is rarely met, so it can demotivate staff.

manas.q: What is an ideal standard?

children.note: Allows for normal waste, rest and small delays. Hard but reachable with good effort, so it usually motivates best.

manas.q: What is an attainable standard?

children.note: Based on today's working conditions as they are. Useful when things are unstable, but it does not push for improvement.

manas.q: What is a current standard?

children.note: Kept unchanged for many years so trends can be seen. It soon goes out of date for control purposes.

manas.q: What is a basic standard?

children.note: Material prices from suppliers and price lists, quantities from engineers or past records, labour times from time studies, rates from wage agreements, overheads from the budget.
Tumaini Ltd, Nakuru. Timber 5 m x KES 200 = 1,000; labour 3 hrs x 150 = 450; variable overhead 3 hrs x 50 = 150; fixed overhead 3 hrs x 100 = 300. Standard cost KES 1,900.
Each cost splits into a price part (paid more or less per unit of input) and a quantity part (used more or less input).
Material variances look at the price paid per kg or metre and the amount used.
(Actual quantity bought x standard price) minus actual cost. Shows whether we paid more or less per unit of material than planned.

manas.q: Formula for material price variance?

children.note: (Standard quantity for actual output minus actual quantity used) x standard price. Shows whether we used more or less material than the output needed.

manas.q: Formula for material usage variance?

children.note: Standard material cost of actual output minus actual material cost. It equals price variance plus usage variance.
Price: supplier change, bulk discounts, inflation, better or worse quality. Usage: waste, theft, poor machines, untrained staff, or the quality of material bought.
Labour variances look at the rate per hour and the hours used.
(Actual hours paid x standard rate) minus actual wages paid. Shows whether we paid a higher or lower rate per hour than planned.

manas.q: Formula for labour rate variance?

children.note: Hours paid but not worked x standard rate. Always adverse, because we paid for time that made nothing (power cuts, waiting for materials).

manas.q: What is the idle time variance and is it F or A?

children.note: (Standard hours for actual output minus actual hours worked) x standard rate. Uses hours WORKED, not hours paid, once idle time is split out.

manas.q: Formula for labour efficiency variance?

children.note: Rate: overtime premium, wage rise, using more skilled staff. Efficiency: training, motivation, machine faults, poor materials. Idle: breakdowns, power cuts, lack of orders.
Variable overhead usually follows labour or machine hours, so its variances mirror labour.
(Actual hours worked x standard variable overhead rate) minus actual variable overhead. Shows spending per hour above or below plan.

manas.q: Formula for variable overhead expenditure variance?

children.note: (Standard hours for actual output minus actual hours worked) x standard variable overhead rate. Same hours difference as labour efficiency.

manas.q: Formula for variable overhead efficiency variance?

children.note: Under absorption costing, fixed overhead is charged to units at a set rate, so two kinds of difference arise: spending and volume.
Budgeted fixed overhead minus actual fixed overhead. Pure over- or under-spending; output level does not matter.

manas.q: Formula for fixed overhead expenditure variance?

children.note: (Actual output minus budgeted output) x standard fixed overhead per unit. Making more than planned spreads fixed cost wider, so it is favourable.

manas.q: Formula for fixed overhead volume variance?

children.note: (Actual hours worked minus budgeted hours) x standard fixed rate per hour. Working more hours than planned is favourable.

manas.q: What is the fixed overhead capacity variance?

children.note: (Standard hours for actual output minus actual hours worked) x standard fixed rate per hour. Capacity plus volume efficiency equals the volume variance.
Under marginal costing, fixed overhead is not charged to units, so there is no fixed overhead volume variance. Only the expenditure variance is reported.

manas.q: Which fixed overhead variance disappears under marginal costing?

children.topic: Sales variances and the operating statement
children.note: Sales variances explain the revenue side; the operating statement pulls every variance together.
(Actual selling price minus standard selling price) x actual units sold. Selling above the planned price is favourable.

manas.q: Formula for sales price variance?

children.note: (Actual units sold minus budgeted units sold) x standard profit per unit. Selling more than budget is favourable.

manas.q: Formula for sales volume variance under absorption costing?

children.note: Same unit difference, but multiplied by standard contribution per unit instead of standard profit.
A report that starts with budgeted profit, adds the sales volume variance to reach standard profit on actual sales, then adds or subtracts every other variance to arrive at actual profit.

manas.q: What does an operating statement do?

children.note: 1. Budgeted profit. 2. +/- sales volume variance. 3. = standard profit on actual sales. 4. +/- sales price variance. 5. +/- each cost variance (F added, A deducted). 6. = actual profit.
A variance shows where to look, not who is to blame. A favourable price for cheap timber may cause an adverse usage variance from extra waste.
One cause can create opposite variances: cheaper, less skilled staff give F rate but A efficiency. Judge the pair together before praising or blaming.

manas.q: Give an example of linked (interdependent) variances.

children.note: Investigate if it is large (for example over 5% of standard), keeps repeating, can be controlled, and the benefit of fixing it is worth the cost of checking.

Tumaini Ltd makes school desks. Standard cost KES 1,900, selling price KES 2,500, standard profit KES 600. Budget: make and sell 1,000 desks, budget profit KES 600,000. Fixed overhead budget KES 300,000 for 3,000 hours.
Made and sold 1,100 desks at KES 2,450. Timber 5,400 m cost 1,134,000. Labour 3,500 hrs paid cost 542,500; 100 hrs idle (power cut). Variable overhead 175,000. Fixed overhead 310,000.
Budget profit 600,000 + volume 60,000 F = 660,000. Less price 55,000 A = 605,000. Cost variances net 71,500 A (F 50,000; A 121,500). Actual profit 533,500.
F: material usage 20,000; fixed volume 30,000 = 50,000. A: material price 54,000; labour rate 17,500; idle 15,000; efficiency 15,000; var OH 5,000 + 5,000; fixed exp 10,000 = 121,500.
Standard contribution 2,500 - 1,600 = 900. Sales volume 100 x 900 = 90,000 F; no fixed volume variance. 600,000 + 90,000 - 55,000 - 101,500 = 533,500, same answer.
Cheap sales price and dearer timber hurt most. Extra sales and fuller use of the factory helped. Check the timber supplier and the power cuts first.
Errors that cost marks in KASNEB variance questions.

children.topic: Using budgeted output for cost variances
children.note: Always use standard quantity for ACTUAL output (flexed), never the original budget quantity. Comparing with the fixed budget mixes volume with efficiency.
Rate variance uses hours paid. Efficiency uses hours worked. Mixing them double-counts idle time.
If inventory is valued at standard, compute material price variance on quantity BOUGHT, not quantity used. Read the question carefully.
Always mark each variance F or A. A number without F/A gets few marks and breaks the reconciliation.
Absorption costing uses standard profit per unit; marginal costing uses standard contribution. Do not use selling price.
If your reconciliation misses actual profit, recheck the signs first, then whether a variance was left out or counted twice.
Standards go out of date fast with inflation, and focusing on cost can harm quality. Many modern firms add non-financial measures too.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Standard: 2 kg per unit at KES 50 per kg. 400 units made. Bought and used 850 kg for KES 41,650. Find price and usage variances.
850 x 50 = 42,500 should cost. Paid 41,650. Price variance = 850 F.
Standard 2 hrs per unit at KES 300. 920 units made. Paid 2,000 hrs costing KES 620,000; 100 hrs idle.
Should take 920 x 2 = 1,840 hrs; worked 1,900. 60 x 300 = 18,000 A. Total 68,000 A.
Budget 5,000 units at KES 800, standard profit KES 120 each. Sold 4,800 at KES 820.
Budget KES 200,000 for 10,000 units (KES 20 per unit). Made 9,000 units; actual fixed overhead KES 195,000.
(9,000 - 10,000) x 20 = 20,000 A. Under-absorbed by 15,000 in total.
