nodeData.note: How many units must we sell to cover all costs, and which choice makes more money this month? This topic uses contribution (from marginal costing, topic 4) to answer both questions.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Managers keep asking "how much must we sell?" and "should we do this or that?". Break-even and relevant costing give quick, number-based answers.
The break-even point is the level of sales where total revenue equals total cost, so there is no profit and no loss.

manas.q: What is the break-even point?

children.note: CVP looks at how costs and profit change when the number of units sold changes. Break-even is one part of it.

manas.q: What does CVP analysis study?

children.note: One-off choices such as make or buy, accept a special order or close a branch. Only the costs and income that change because of the choice matter.
Topic 4 split costs into variable and fixed and gave us contribution. Here we use that split for planning and decisions, not for valuing stock.
A duka owner pricing goods, a matatu SACCO checking a new route, a hospital pharmacy deciding whether to outsource. Same tools, different sizes.
Contribution is what each sale adds towards paying fixed costs and then to profit.
Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit. Fixed costs are left out.

manas.q: How do you work out contribution per unit?

children.note: Contribution per unit times units sold, or total sales minus total variable costs.
Profit = total contribution minus fixed costs. Once fixed costs are covered, every extra unit adds its full contribution to profit.

manas.q: How is profit found from contribution?

children.note: Contribution divided by sales, shown as a percentage. It tells you how many shillings of contribution each KES 1 of sales brings. Also called the P/V (profit-volume) ratio.

manas.q: What is the C/S ratio and what is its other name?

children.note: Price and variable cost per unit stay the same, fixed costs stay the same within the relevant range, all output is sold, and the sales mix is constant.

manas.q: Name four assumptions of break-even (CVP) analysis.

children.note: The core formulas. All of them divide fixed costs (plus any target profit) by contribution.
Fixed costs divided by contribution per unit.

manas.q: What is the formula for break-even point in units?

children.note: Fixed costs divided by the C/S ratio. Or break-even units times selling price; both give the same answer.

manas.q: What is the formula for break-even sales revenue?

children.note: How far sales can fall before a loss is made: budgeted (or actual) sales minus break-even sales, in units or KES.

manas.q: What is the margin of safety?

children.note: Margin of safety divided by budgeted sales, times 100. A higher percentage means a safer business.

manas.q: How is the margin of safety percentage worked out?

children.note: Units needed = (fixed costs + target profit) divided by contribution per unit. For KES, divide by the C/S ratio instead.

manas.q: How many units are needed to earn a target profit?

children.note: Profit also equals margin of safety in KES times the C/S ratio, because sales above break-even are all profit after variable costs.
Pictures of the same numbers. Exams may ask you to draw or read one.
Units (activity) along the bottom, KES up the side. Three lines: fixed cost, total cost and sales revenue.

manas.q: What lines appear on a break-even chart?

children.note: A flat line at the fixed cost amount. Total cost starts from where this line meets the KES axis and rises with variable costs.
Sales revenue and total cost cross at break-even. Gap to the right of it is profit; gap to the left is loss.
Draws variable cost first and fixed cost on top, so the gap between sales and variable cost shows contribution at every level.
One line showing profit or loss against sales. It starts at minus fixed costs at zero sales and crosses zero at break-even.

manas.q: Where does the P/V chart line start and cross the axis?

children.note: When a business sells several products, treat a fixed mix of them as one "batch".
Assume products are sold in a fixed ratio, such as 2 of A for every 1 of B. Break-even only holds while that mix holds.
Total contribution of the mix divided by total sales of the mix. Then break-even revenue = fixed costs divided by this ratio.

manas.q: How do you find break-even revenue for several products?

children.note: Selling more of the high-C/S product lowers the break-even revenue; selling more of the low-C/S product raises it.
For a decision, count only future cash flows that change because of the choice. Everything else is ignored.
A relevant cost is future, cash, and incremental (it differs between the options).

manas.q: What three features make a cost relevant?

children.note: Money already spent that cannot be got back, such as last year's market survey. It is the same whatever you choose now.

manas.q: What is a sunk cost and is it relevant?

children.note: A future cost you must pay anyway because of an earlier contract, like a signed lease. The decision cannot change it.

manas.q: What is a committed cost?

children.note: The benefit you give up by using a resource for this job instead of its best other use. It is a real cost of the choice.

manas.q: What is an opportunity cost?

children.note: Shared costs like head office rent spread across products. They usually stay the same, so they are not relevant unless they can be avoided.
If used regularly: relevant cost is replacement cost. If not needed elsewhere: the higher of scrap value or other-use value. The original price paid is sunk.
If workers are paid anyway and have spare time, using them costs nothing extra. If they must leave other work, include the lost contribution too.
When one resource is short (labour hours, machine hours, material), make the products that earn most per unit of that scarce resource.
A resource in short supply that stops the business meeting all demand. Sales demand itself can also be the limiting factor.

manas.q: What is a limiting (key) factor?

children.note: Work out how much of each resource full demand needs. Compare with what is available to see which one runs out.
Divide each product's contribution per unit by the scarce resource it uses, such as KES per labour hour.

manas.q: How are products ranked under a limiting factor?

children.note: Rank highest first. Give the scarce resource to the top product up to its demand, then the next, until it runs out.
If two or more resources are short at once, simple ranking fails and linear programming is used. That is covered at a higher level.
Make or buy, special orders and closing a segment all use the same relevant cost thinking.
Compare the extra cost of making (variable cost plus any avoidable fixed cost and opportunity cost) with the supplier's price.

manas.q: What costs are compared in a make-or-buy decision?

children.note: Supplier reliability, quality, keeping know-how in house, and whether freed staff and machines can be used for something better.
With spare capacity, accept if the price is above the extra (variable plus specific) cost. Fixed costs already covered are ignored.

manas.q: When should a one-off special order be accepted with spare capacity?

children.note: Regular customers may ask for the same low price; if there is no spare capacity, lost normal sales are an opportunity cost.
Close a product, route or branch only if the costs saved are more than the contribution lost. Shared fixed costs that will stay do not count.

manas.q: When should a loss-making segment be closed?

children.note: Effect on staff, on sales of other products bought together, on suppliers and on the firm's image in the community.
Real numbers in KES. Every figure has been checked.
Price KES 120, variable cost KES 70, fixed costs KES 200,000 a month. Contribution = KES 50. C/S = 50/120 = 41.67%. Break-even = 200,000/50 = 4,000 bottles = KES 480,000.
Budget 5,000 bottles (KES 600,000). Margin of safety = 1,000 bottles = KES 120,000 = 20%. Profit = 5,000 x 50 - 200,000 = KES 50,000 (also 120,000 x 41.67%).
Mix 2 A : 1 B. A: price 100, contribution 40. B: price 200, contribution 50. Batch: contribution 130, sales 400, C/S 32.5%. Fixed KES 260,000 / 130 = 2,000 batches = 4,000 A + 2,000 B = KES 800,000.
Make: materials 300 + labour 200 + variable overhead 100 = KES 600 (fixed overhead 150 stays anyway). Buy at KES 680. Make 5,000 units: saves 80 x 5,000 = KES 400,000.

children.topic: Make or buy with opportunity cost
children.note: Same case, but the machine could instead earn KES 500,000 contribution on another job. Make = 3,000,000 + 500,000 = KES 3,500,000; buy = KES 3,400,000. Now buying is better by KES 100,000.
Normal price KES 70, variable cost 45, full cost 55. Hotel wants 2,000 loaves at KES 50, extra delivery KES 6,000, spare capacity exists. Gain = 2,000 x 5 - 6,000 = KES 4,000, so accept.

Route C: fares 900,000, variable costs 650,000, contribution 250,000, route permits 100,000 (saved if closed), head office share 200,000. Shows a 50,000 loss, but closing loses 250,000 and saves 100,000: profit falls KES 150,000. Keep it.
Material in stock cost KES 40,000, no other use, scrap value 15,000: relevant 15,000. New material 25,000. Idle paid staff: 0. Lease already signed 8,000: ignore. Relevant cost = KES 40,000.
Where candidates lose marks on this topic.
Fixed cost per unit is not a real extra cost per unit. Use variable cost for contribution and decisions.
With a limiting factor, rank by contribution per scarce hour or kilo. In the workshop example, Z has the highest per unit but comes last.
Money already spent, like a past survey or the original price of old stock, never changes the decision.
If a resource has another use, the lost benefit must be added to the cost of the option that uses it.
Divide by contribution per unit for units, by the C/S ratio for KES. Do not divide fixed costs by price.
A segment may show a loss only because of shared costs. Check contribution and avoidable fixed costs before closing.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Find C/S ratio, break-even units and KES, and units for KES 100,000 profit.
Budget sales KES 2,000,000. Find break-even revenue, margin of safety and profit.
Variable cost to make is KES 420; absorbed fixed overhead KES 80 will not change. Supplier price KES 450. 4,000 units needed, no other use for capacity.
Make = KES 420 (ignore the 80 fixed). Buy = KES 450.
Make. Saving = 30 x 4,000 = KES 120,000.

nodeData.note: How Kenya's national and county governments raise, share, spend, borrow and account for public money, and what makes a good tax. Based on Chapter Twelve of the Constitution of Kenya 2010.

children.note: Public finance is how a government gets money, spends it and borrows it. It is the money side of running a country or a county.
The study of government money: what it collects (revenue), what it spends (expenditure) and what it borrows (debt), and how these affect people and the economy.

manas.q: What is public finance?

children.note: Money coming in: mainly taxes, plus fees and charges for services such as permits and parking.
Money going out: salaries of teachers and nurses, roads, hospitals, security, water and paying interest on loans.
When spending is more than income, the government borrows. Loans must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers.
Economists say it is about using resources well (allocation), sharing income fairly (distribution) and keeping the economy steady (stability).

manas.q: What are the three roles of public finance?

children.note: Taxes you compute, county fees a business pays and audits of public bodies all come from these rules. Many accountants work in government too.
Chapter Twelve of the Constitution of Kenya 2010 (Articles 201 onwards) sets the rules for all public money in Kenya.
Article 201: public finance must be open and accountable, and the public must take part in financial matters.

manas.q: Name the principles of public finance in Article 201.

children.note: Article 201: the tax burden must be shared fairly, revenue shared fairly between national and county governments, and marginalised groups helped.
Article 201: the costs and benefits of using resources and of borrowing must be shared fairly between people today and those in the future.
Article 201: public money must be used carefully and responsibly, with good financial management and clear reporting.
A county building a market with a loan must explain the plan in public, use the money well and report how it was spent. That is Article 201 in action.
Kenya has a national government and 47 county governments. Each spends money, so the Constitution says how revenue is shared and who may tax what.
Runs national services such as defence and national roads. It collects the big taxes and shares revenue with counties.
Run local services. They get a share of national revenue plus their own rates and fees.
Article 209 splits taxing powers between the two levels of government.
Article 209: only the national government may impose income tax, value-added tax (VAT), customs duties and excise tax.

manas.q: Which taxes may only the national government impose (Article 209)?

children.note: Article 209: counties may impose property rates, entertainment taxes and any other tax an Act of Parliament allows.

manas.q: Which taxes may a county impose under Article 209?

children.note: Article 209: both national and county governments may charge fees for services they provide, such as a county parking fee.
Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) is the government agency that assesses, collects and accounts for revenue due under Kenyan law. It collects; it does not make the law.

manas.q: What is the role of the Kenya Revenue Authority?

children.note: The Constitution sets up public funds. Money goes in, and it comes out only with legal approval.
Article 206: the main national fund. Money comes out only through an Appropriation Act, Articles 222/223, or a charge allowed by the Constitution or an Act.

manas.q: When may money be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund?

children.note: Article 207: each county has its own revenue fund. Taking money out needs approval from the Controller of Budget.

manas.q: What is a County Revenue Fund and who approves withdrawals?

children.note: Article 203(2): counties together get not less than 15% of all revenue collected by the national government, based on the latest audited accounts approved by the National Assembly.

manas.q: What is the minimum equitable share for counties?

children.note: Article 204: one half per cent (0.5%) of national revenue each year, for basic services like water, roads, health facilities and electricity in marginalised areas.

manas.q: What is the Equalisation Fund and how big is it?

children.note: Articles 215-216: the CRA advises on sharing revenue. It has a chairperson, 2 members nominated through National Assembly parties, 5 through Senate parties, and the finance PS.

manas.q: What is the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA)?

children.note: A budget is the government's plan for income and spending for a year. It goes round in a cycle every year.
Article 221: the Cabinet Secretary for finance gives revenue and spending estimates to the National Assembly at least two months before the financial year ends.

manas.q: When must budget estimates be submitted (Article 221)?

children.note: Parliament debates the estimates and passes an Appropriation Act. This law allows money to be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund (Article 206).

manas.q: What is an Appropriation Act?

children.note: Ministries and counties spend the approved money. Each withdrawal is first checked by the Controller of Budget.
Article 226: every public body has an accounting officer and its accounts are audited by the Auditor-General.
The Public Finance Management Act 2012 gives the detailed steps and dates for the budget process. The Constitution sets the main rules.
Both are independent offices, but they act at different times: one before money is spent, the other after.
Article 228: approves withdrawals from public funds before money is spent and reports every four months to each House. Term: 8 years, not renewable.

manas.q: What does the Controller of Budget do?

children.note: Article 229: audits public accounts after the year and reports within six months after the financial year ends. Term: 8 years, not renewable.

manas.q: What does the Auditor-General do?

children.note: Controller = gatekeeper before spending. Auditor-General = inspector after spending.
Governments borrow to fill the gap between income and spending. The Constitution puts limits on this.
Article 214: public debt is a charge on the Consolidated Fund, so repayments are paid without waiting for a new vote.

manas.q: How does the Constitution treat public debt (Article 214)?

children.note: Article 212: a county may borrow only if the national government guarantees the loan and the county assembly approves it.

manas.q: What two conditions apply before a county borrows?

children.note: Article 201 says borrowing costs must be fair to future generations, who will repay today's loans.
Before looking at Kenyan taxes, learn what makes a tax fair and workable, and the main ways to group taxes.
In The Wealth of Nations (1776) Adam Smith gave four maxims of a good tax.
People should pay in line with their ability to pay.

manas.q: What does the canon of equity mean?

children.note: The amount, time and way to pay should be clear, not left to the tax officer's whim.

manas.q: What does the canon of certainty mean?

children.note: Tax should be collected at a time and in a way easy for the taxpayer, e.g. PAYE deducted on payday.
The cost of collecting a tax should be small compared to what it raises.

manas.q: What does the canon of economy mean?

children.note: Taxes are grouped by who carries the burden.
Charged on a person's income or property and paid by that person, e.g. income tax or PAYE.

manas.q: What is a direct tax? Give an example.

children.note: Charged on goods and services and passed on to the buyer in the price, e.g. VAT, excise and customs duty.

manas.q: What is an indirect tax? Give an example.

children.note: Taxes are also grouped by how the rate changes as income grows.
The rate rises as income rises, so richer people pay a larger share. Kenya's PAYE bands (10% up to 35%) work like this (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026).

manas.q: What is a progressive tax?

children.note: Same rate for everyone whatever the amount, e.g. corporation tax on resident companies at 30% (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026).

manas.q: What is a proportional tax?

children.note: Takes a bigger share of a poor person's income than a rich person's. Taxes on basic goods often work this way.

manas.q: What is a regressive tax?

children.note: Simple calculations to make the rules real. All amounts are illustrative figures, not real budget data.
Suppose audited national revenue is KES 2,000 billion. Minimum county share = 15% × 2,000bn = KES 300 billion.
Use the latest audited revenue approved by the National Assembly. Here (illustrative figures): KES 2,000 billion.
2,000bn × 15% = KES 300bn. This is the floor; Parliament may give counties more, never less.
2,000bn × 0.5% = KES 10bn for basic services in marginalised areas (illustrative figures).
Made-up bands: 10% on the first KES 100,000, 30% above. Compare with a flat 15%. Two people: Wanjiku earns KES 80,000, Otieno KES 400,000.
Wanjiku pays 80,000 × 15% = KES 12,000. Otieno pays 400,000 × 15% = KES 60,000. Both pay 15% of income.
The progressive tax asks more of the higher earner (25% vs 10%); the flat tax asks the same 15% of both.

children.topic: Why a tax on basics is regressive
children.note: Both spend KES 20,000 on basics with 16% VAT: tax KES 3,200 each. That is 4% of Wanjiku's 80,000 but 0.8% of Otieno's 400,000 (illustrative figures; VAT 16% — check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026).
Mix-ups that cost marks in KASNEB questions on this topic.
The equitable share is not less than 15%. Do not write 'exactly 15%'. It is also based on audited revenue, not this year's guess.
The Equalisation Fund (0.5%) is separate from the 15% equitable share and serves marginalised areas only.
Controller of Budget approves before spending; Auditor-General audits after. Swapping them is a frequent error.
Income tax, VAT, customs and excise are national only. Counties use property rates, entertainment taxes and fees.

children.topic: KRA collects, Parliament makes tax law
children.note: KRA assesses and collects revenue; it does not decide tax rates. Rates come from Acts of Parliament.
Short exam-style questions. Try first, then open the steps.
Audited revenue is KES 1,800bn (illustrative figures). What is the least the counties must get?
Rule: not less than 15% of national revenue (Article 203(2)).
1,800bn × 15% = KES 270bn. Counties must get at least KES 270bn.
A county wants to pay a contractor from its County Revenue Fund. Who must approve?
The Controller of Budget (Articles 207 and 228). The Auditor-General later audits the payment.

children.topic: Q3: Can a county levy VAT?
children.note: A governor proposes a county VAT on hotel bills. Is it allowed?
No. VAT is national only under Article 209. The county could use entertainment tax or fees if an Act allows.
List and explain Adam Smith's four canons of taxation.
Equity (ability to pay), certainty (clear amount and date), convenience (easy time and way) and economy (cheap to collect).

maps.title: CA26 · 2. Income tax for individuals and PAYE

nodeData.topic: Income tax for individuals and PAYE
nodeData.note: How Kenya taxes a person's pay: who pays, what counts as pay, what comes off before tax, the bands and reliefs, and how an employer runs PAYE each month, with two full payslips.

children.note: Income tax is a tax on what a person earns. Whether Kenya taxes you, and on what, depends mainly on where you live and where the money comes from.
Income tax is money the government takes from what people and businesses earn in a year. It is the biggest single source of money for the Kenyan budget.

manas.q: What is income tax?

children.note: In topic 1 you saw that the government needs revenue to fund roads, schools and hospitals. Income tax, and PAYE in particular, is one of the main ways it collects that revenue.

A resident individual is someone who has a permanent home in Kenya and was here during the year, or who stays in Kenya long enough in a year (183 days or more is the usual test). Residents are taxed on their income from Kenya.

manas.q: Who is a resident individual for Kenyan income tax?

children.note: A non-resident does not meet the residence tests. Kenya still taxes the income they earn here, for example pay for work done in Kenya, often through withholding tax.
The main kinds of income the law taxes are: employment pay, business profits, rent, interest, dividends and some other gains. This topic focuses on employment income.

manas.q: Name the main sources of income taxed in Kenya.

children.note: Pay As You Earn (PAYE) is income tax on employment pay. The employer takes the tax out of each month's salary and sends it to KRA, so the worker pays a little every month instead of one big bill.

manas.q: What is PAYE?

children.note: The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) collects income tax for the government. Employers deal with KRA through the iTax online system.
Taxable pay is more than the basic salary. It includes cash extras and, above a limit, the value of things the employer gives you instead of cash.
Basic salary, wages, overtime, bonuses, commission, leave pay and cash allowances (house, transport, airtime) are all taxable employment income.

manas.q: Which cash payments count as employment income?

children.note: A benefit is something the employer gives you that is not cash, such as a company car, free housing or paid school fees. Non-cash benefits are taxable once they go above KES 5,000 a month (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When are non-cash benefits taxable?

children.note: Wanjiku gets free airtime and a gym pass worth KES 4,000 a month in total. This is not above KES 5,000, so it is left out of her taxable pay (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

Otieno's employer pays his house rent of KES 20,000 a month. This is well above KES 5,000, so the benefit is added to his taxable pay before PAYE is worked out (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

children.topic: Meals are exempt up to a limit
children.note: Meals the employer provides to staff are tax-free up to KES 5,000 a month. Anything above that is treated as taxable pay (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the tax-free limit for staff meals?

children.note: A few other items are tax-free under the Income Tax Act. In the exam, read the question carefully and only treat an item as exempt if the law or the question says so.
Some amounts come off your pay BEFORE tax is worked out. This lowers your taxable pay, so you pay less PAYE. KRA lists these as allowable deductions.
A deduction is taken off your pay before tax is calculated. A relief is taken off the tax itself after it is calculated. Mixing them up is a common exam error.

manas.q: What is the difference between a deduction and a relief?

children.note: NSSF is the national pension fund. The employee pays 6% of pensionable pay and the employer pays another 6%. The employee share reduces taxable pay (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What are the NSSF contribution rates?

children.note: Tier I is 6% of pay up to KES 9,000 (max KES 540). Tier II is 6% of pay from KES 9,001 to KES 108,000 (max KES 5,940). So the most an employee pays is KES 6,480 a month (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What are the NSSF Tier I and Tier II limits from Feb 2026?

children.note: The Social Health Insurance Fund replaced NHIF. Employees pay 2.75% of gross salary, with a minimum of KES 300 for pay below KES 6,000. KRA lists SHIF contributions as allowable deductions (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the SHIF rate for employees?

children.note: The employee pays 1.5% of gross monthly salary and the employer pays another 1.5%. KRA lists the levy as an allowable deduction (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the Affordable Housing Levy rate?

children.note: Contributions to a registered pension scheme are deductible up to KES 30,000 a month (KES 360,000 a year). Anything above the cap is not deductible (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the monthly limit for deductible pension contributions?

children.note: Contributions to a registered post-retirement medical fund are deductible up to KES 15,000 a month (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the deduction limit for a post-retirement medical fund?

children.note: Interest paid on a loan to buy or build your own home is deductible up to KES 30,000 a month. Only the interest counts, not the part of the payment that repays the loan (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the monthly limit for mortgage interest?

children.note: Kenya uses bands: the first slice of taxable pay is taxed at a low rate and each higher slice at a higher rate. Then reliefs are taken off the tax.
First KES 24,000 at 10%; next 8,333 at 25%; next 467,667 at 30%; next 300,000 at 32.5%; everything above 800,000 at 35% (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What are the monthly PAYE bands?

children.note: The first KES 24,000 of monthly taxable pay is taxed at 10%, so a full band 1 costs KES 2,400 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
The next KES 8,333 (pay from 24,001 to 32,333) is taxed at 25%. A full band 2 costs KES 2,083.25 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
The next KES 467,667 (up to 500,000) is taxed at 30%. Most middle-income workers reach this band (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Pay from 500,001 to 800,000 is taxed at 32.5%, and pay above 800,000 a month at 35% (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
The same bands for a year: first 288,000 at 10%; next 100,000 at 25%; next 5,612,000 at 30%; next 3,600,000 at 32.5%; above 9,600,000 at 35% (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What are the annual income tax bands?

children.topic: Only the slice is taxed higher
children.note: Moving into a higher band does not raise the tax on all your pay. Only the shillings inside that band get the higher rate. This is called a progressive tax.
Every resident individual gets KES 2,400 a month (KES 28,800 a year) taken off the tax worked out from the bands (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How much is personal relief?

children.note: If you pay premiums on a qualifying life, education or health policy, you get 15% of the premiums off your tax, up to KES 60,000 a year (KES 5,000 a month) (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How is insurance relief calculated?

children.note: Akinyi pays a life policy premium of KES 3,000 a month. Relief = 15% x 3,000 = KES 450 a month, which is below the cap, so her tax falls by KES 450 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Follow the same six steps every time and the answer will come out right.
Add up all cash pay for the month: basic salary, allowances, overtime, bonus, commission.

manas.q: What are the six steps of a PAYE computation?

children.note: Add the value of non-cash benefits that are above the KES 5,000 monthly limit. Leave out exempt items like meals within the limit (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Take off NSSF, SHIF, Housing Levy and, within their caps, pension, post-retirement medical fund and mortgage interest. The result is taxable pay.
Slice the taxable pay into the bands and multiply each slice by its rate. Add the slices together to get tax before relief.
Take off personal relief and any insurance relief. What remains is PAYE. If reliefs are bigger than the tax, PAYE is nil, not negative.
Net pay = gross cash pay minus NSSF, SHIF, Housing Levy, PAYE and any other deductions (pension, loans). This is what reaches the bank or M-Pesa.
The employer is KRA's collector. It must take tax out of pay, send it on time and file a return. Missing a step costs penalties.
Each month the employer works out PAYE for each employee and takes it out of pay before paying salaries.
PAYE for a month must be paid to KRA by the 9th of the following month. Payment can be made through banks or M-Pesa paybill 222222 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When must PAYE be paid to KRA?

children.note: The employer also files the monthly PAYE return on iTax by the 9th of the next month, listing each employee and the tax deducted (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
The levy (employee 1.5% plus employer 1.5%) is remitted within 9 working days after the end of the month (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
The employer deducts SHIF and sends it to the Social Health Authority through the KRA portal.
After the year, the employer gives each worker a P9 form showing pay and tax for the year. The worker uses it to file their own annual return.
Filing the PAYE return late costs 25% of the tax due or KES 10,000, whichever is higher (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the penalty for filing a PAYE return late?

children.note: Paying PAYE late costs a 5% penalty plus interest of 1% a month on the unpaid tax (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the penalty and interest for paying PAYE late?

children.note: An employer who does not deduct PAYE is charged 25% of the tax or KES 10,000, whichever is higher, and still owes the tax (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

Two full payslips using the Feb 2026 NSSF tiers, SHIF 2.75%, Housing Levy 1.5% (employee share), the monthly bands and personal relief of KES 2,400. Figures are rounded to the nearest shilling (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
A junior accountant in Nairobi earns KES 50,000 a month, all cash, with no benefits, pension or insurance.
Tier I: 6% x 9,000 = 540. Tier II: 6% x (50,000 - 9,000) = 2,460. Total employee NSSF = KES 3,000 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
SHIF = 2.75% x 50,000 = KES 1,375. Housing Levy = 1.5% x 50,000 = KES 750 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
8,245.85 - personal relief 2,400 = 5,845.85, rounded to KES 5,846 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
A finance manager earns KES 150,000 a month, all cash, with no benefits, pension or insurance.
Tier I: 540. Tier II: 6% x (108,000 - 9,000) = 5,940, because pay above 108,000 is ignored. Total = KES 6,480 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
SHIF = 2.75% x 150,000 = KES 4,125. Housing Levy = 1.5% x 150,000 = KES 2,250 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
35,926.85 - personal relief 2,400 = 33,526.85, rounded to KES 33,527 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

On top of gross pay the employer also pays its own NSSF share and its 1.5% Housing Levy. For payslip A that is 3,000 + 750 = KES 3,750; for B it is 6,480 + 2,250 = KES 8,730 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
First the traps examiners like to set, then three short questions to try.
Watch out for these when you compute PAYE.
Personal and insurance relief come off the TAX, not off the pay. Taking them off pay gives the wrong answer.

children.topic: Whole pay at the top rate
children.note: Do not multiply all of the taxable pay by 30%. Tax each band slice at its own rate (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Pension, mortgage interest and post-retirement medical fund each have a monthly cap. Only the amount up to the cap is deducted.
Forgetting to add a taxable benefit such as free housing makes PAYE too low, and the employer then owes the difference plus penalties.
NHIF, the old NSSF limits and old bands still appear in old notes and videos. Always use the rates in force for the exam sitting.
Use monthly bands with monthly pay and annual bands with annual pay. Never mix the two in one computation.
An employee has taxable pay of KES 30,000 for the month. Work out PAYE.
10% x 24,000 = 2,400; 25% x 6,000 = 1,500. Tax = KES 3,900 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
3,900 - 2,400 personal relief = PAYE of KES 1,500 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
A worker pays health insurance premiums of KES 40,000 a month. How much insurance relief can they claim each month?
15% x 40,000 = KES 6,000 a month (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
The cap is KES 60,000 a year, which is KES 5,000 a month. So the relief is KES 5,000, not 6,000 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Gross pay KES 100,000; the employee also pays KES 10,000 a month into a registered pension scheme. Work out PAYE and net pay.
NSSF 540 + 5,460 = 6,000; SHIF 2,750; Housing Levy 1,500; pension 10,000 (under the 30,000 cap). Taxable pay = 100,000 - 20,250 = KES 79,750 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
2,400 + 2,083.25 + 30% x 47,417 (14,225.10) = 18,708.35. Less relief 2,400 = 16,308.35, so PAYE is KES 16,308 (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Kenyan videos from 2025-2026. Older PAYE videos may show old rates (NHIF, old NSSF limits, no SHIF or Housing Levy), so always check figures against the KRA page.

children.topic: ▶ PAYE returns with SHIF and AHL
children.note: Lio Tech shows an employer filing the 2026 PAYE return, including SHIF and the Housing Levy.
KRA's own short guide to filing an individual tax return using your P9.
Official pages first, then background reading.
KRA's official PAYE page with the current bands, reliefs, deductions, deadlines and penalties.
The official calculator page that explains the NSSF tiers and lets you test any salary.

maps.title: CA26 · 3. Corporation tax and capital allowances

nodeData.note: How a Kenyan company works out the tax on its profit. You start from the accounting profit, adjust it to taxable profit, take off investment allowances on assets, and pay 30% in instalments and a final balance.

children.note: Corporation tax is income tax charged on a company's profit. It is the company version of the income tax you met for individuals in topic 2.
A company is a separate legal person, so it pays its own income tax on its yearly profit, apart from its owners.

manas.q: What is corporation tax?

children.note: Limited companies registered in Kenya, and foreign companies earning profit here through a branch. Sole traders and partners pay individual income tax instead.
A resident company pays 30% of its taxable profit. The Act writes it as Sh 6 in every Sh 20. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the corporation tax rate for a resident company in Kenya?

children.note: A foreign company's Kenyan branch (permanent establishment) pays a higher rate on its Kenyan profit. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Corporation tax is a big source of government revenue, linking back to topic 1 on public finance. For a business, it is often its largest single tax bill.
The rules are in the Income Tax Act (Cap 470). Note: the KRA copy of the Act read on 7 Nov 2026 says some 2026 amendments were still being applied, so confirm the latest text.

children.topic: From accounting profit to taxable profit
children.note: Accounting profit follows IFRS; taxable profit follows tax law. You adjust one into the other in a short statement.
Accounting profit + disallowed expenses − non-taxable income − investment allowances = taxable profit.

manas.q: What is the format for adjusting accounting profit to taxable profit?

children.note: Costs spent wholly and only to earn the business income, like salaries, rent and stock. They stay deducted.

manas.q: What is an allowable expense?

children.note: Depreciation is the business's own estimate, so tax law ignores it. Add it back and claim investment allowances instead.

manas.q: Why is depreciation added back in a tax computation?

children.note: Traffic fines, KRA penalties and other fines for breaking the law are not allowed. Add them back.

manas.q: Are fines and penalties allowable for tax?

children.note: Owners' or directors' personal costs paid by the company, like school fees or a home holiday, are not business costs. Add them back.
Buying an asset (a matatu, a building) is not an expense. Add back any capital cost charged in profit and claim the allowance.
A vague provision such as 'general bad debts' is not allowed. Only specific debts shown to be bad can be deducted.
Corporation tax charged in the accounts is not a cost of earning profit, so add it back if it was deducted.
After the add-backs, subtract the investment allowances worked out on qualifying assets. This replaces depreciation.

manas.q: What replaces depreciation in a Kenyan tax computation?

children.note: Tax law's own version of depreciation, set out in the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act. Each class of asset has a fixed rate.
A deduction for the cost of business assets, spread over the years the law sets. Since 2023 the law calls them investment allowance or deduction.

manas.q: What is an investment allowance?

children.note: Older books and past papers say wear and tear allowance or capital deductions. The idea is the same; learn the current rates.
Some assets get 50% in the first year of use and then 25% of the remainder yearly. Others get a flat straight-line rate (25% or 10%) on cost. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

Buildings and machinery used for manufacture, hospital buildings and equipment, hotel buildings, ships and aircraft. 50% in year one, then the residual at 25% a year in equal parts. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: Which assets get 50% investment allowance in the first year?

children.note: Motor vehicles, heavy earth-moving equipment, computers and software, photocopiers and filming equipment: 25% of cost each year for 4 years. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the investment allowance rate for motor vehicles and computers?

children.note: Commercial buildings, industrial buildings, educational buildings (including hostels) and docks get 10% of cost a year. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What rate applies to commercial buildings?

children.note: Furniture and fittings, telecom equipment and other machinery not listed elsewhere get 10% a year. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What rate applies to furniture and fittings?

children.note: Para 1A gives 100% for big investments outside Nairobi and Mombasa (thresholds in the Act) or in a Special Economic Zone. Rarely needed at this level. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Claim from when the asset is first used in the business. Use cost, not market value. Never mix in the accounting depreciation.
When adjusted figures give a tax loss, no tax is due that year.
Allowable costs plus investment allowances are bigger than taxable income, so taxable profit is below zero.

manas.q: What is a tax loss?

children.note: The loss is carried forward and set against taxable profits of later years, which lowers future tax. Check the Act for current conditions.
Keep a loss memo year by year so the amount used is clear to KRA.
Companies pay most of the year's tax during the year, then settle the balance and file the return after year end.
A company whose tax for the year is more than KES 40,000 must pay in instalments. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When must a company pay instalment tax?

children.note: 25% each by the 20th day of the 4th, 6th, 9th and 12th months of the accounting year. Dec year-end: 20 Apr, 20 Jun, 20 Sep, 20 Dec. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When are the four instalment tax payments due?

children.note: Base instalments on this year's estimated tax, or on 110% of last year's tax. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the prior-year basis for instalment tax?

children.note: Agricultural companies pay 75% by the 20th day of the 9th month and 25% by the 12th month. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Any tax left after instalments is due by the last day of the 4th month after year end. Dec year-end: 30 April. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When is the balance of corporation tax due?

children.topic: IT2C return by end of 6th month
children.note: File the company return (IT2C) on iTax by the end of the 6th month after year end. Dec year-end: 30 June. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When is the IT2C return due?

children.note: Three examples with real KES numbers. Every figure has been rechecked.
Year to 31 Dec. Accounting profit KES 4,200,000. Start here and adjust to tax payable. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Depreciation 1,350,000 + traffic fines 80,000 + director's private trip 120,000 = add-backs KES 1,550,000.
New matatus 6,000,000 × 25% = 1,500,000; computers 400,000 × 25% = 100,000; furniture 200,000 × 10% = 20,000. Total KES 1,620,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

4,130,000 × 30% = tax KES 1,239,000. Instalments paid 1,000,000, so balance KES 239,000 due by 30 April. Journal: Dr Tax expense / Cr Tax payable 1,239,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Two assets bought and used from day one of Year 1.
25% equal parts: 1,000,000 in each of Years 1, 2 and 3. Tax written-down value: 3,000,000, then 2,000,000, then 1,000,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Machinery for manufacture KES 10,000,000. Year 1: 50% = 5,000,000. Residual left: 5,000,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Residual 5,000,000 × 25% = 1,250,000 each year. After Year 3 the residual left is 2,500,000; total claimed 7,500,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Afya Pharmacy Ltd, Dec year-end. Last year's tax KES 1,600,000; this year's actual tax turns out KES 2,000,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
110% × 1,600,000 = 1,760,000 for the year, so each instalment is 1,760,000 ÷ 4 = KES 440,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
440,000 each on 20 April, 20 June, 20 September and 20 December. Total paid 1,760,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
2,000,000 − 1,760,000 = KES 240,000, payable by 30 April next year. File IT2C by 30 June. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Where students lose easy marks.
Leaving depreciation in the profit and also claiming allowances gives a double deduction. Always add it back first.
A matatu is a motor vehicle (25%), not other machinery (10%). Read what the asset is used for. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
For 50% assets, Year 2 is 25% of the residual (cost less the first 50%), not 25% of cost. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Instalments are due on the 20th; the balance by the last day of month 4; the return by the end of month 6. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Companies pay a flat 30%; the PAYE bands from topic 2 do not apply. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Older questions use wear and tear rates. Answer with today's Second Schedule rates unless told otherwise.
Try each one first, then open the steps.
Profit 1,000,000; depreciation 200,000; KRA penalty 50,000; investment allowances 300,000. Find the tax.
1,000,000 + 200,000 + 50,000 − 300,000 = taxable profit 950,000. Tax = 950,000 × 30% = KES 285,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
A hotel building cost KES 20,000,000 and opened in Year 1. Find the allowance for Years 1 and 2. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Year 1: 50% × 20,000,000 = 10,000,000. Year 2: residual 10,000,000 × 25% = 2,500,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
Last year's tax was KES 800,000. Using the prior-year basis, how much is each instalment?
110% × 800,000 = 880,000. Each of the four instalments = 880,000 ÷ 4 = KES 220,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)
A commercial office block cost KES 30,000,000. Find the yearly allowance.
Commercial building at 10% straight line: 30,000,000 × 10% = KES 3,000,000 a year for 10 years. (check the current KRA rate; checked 7 Nov 2026)

maps.title: CA26 · 4. VAT, excise duty and customs

nodeData.note: These are taxes on spending, not on income. Businesses collect them from customers and pass them to KRA. This topic shows how VAT works in Kenya, what excise duty is, and how tax is worked out on imported goods.

children.note: Start here: why spending taxes exist and who really pays them.
An indirect tax is charged on goods and services when people buy them. The seller collects it and pays it to the government, so the customer pays it without dealing with KRA.

manas.q: What is an indirect tax?

children.topic: The final customer carries the cost
children.note: Each business in the chain gets back the VAT it paid on its own purchases. Only the last buyer, the consumer, ends up bearing the tax.

children.topic: The business acts as tax collector
children.note: A VAT-registered duka or company adds VAT to its prices, keeps records, files returns and pays the money over. The VAT is not the business's income.
Income tax, PAYE and corporation tax are charged on what people and companies earn. VAT, excise and customs are charged on what is bought, made or imported.

VAT: the VAT Act 2013. Excise: the Excise Duty Act 2015. Customs: the East African Community Customs Management Act 2004, shared by EAC countries. Procedures and penalties: the Tax Procedures Act 2015.

manas.q: Which laws govern VAT, excise duty and customs in Kenya?

children.note: Spending taxes bring in steady money because people buy things every day. Excise is also used to discourage harmful goods such as alcohol and tobacco (link to Topic 1, public finance).
The core ideas: rates, output VAT, input VAT and what you pay KRA.
VAT is a tax on the value a business adds at each stage of making and selling something. Each business pays only on the part it added.

manas.q: What is value added tax (VAT)?

children.note: Most goods and services in Kenya carry VAT at 16% of the price before VAT. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the standard VAT rate in Kenya?

children.note: Zero-rated supplies (listed in the Second Schedule of the VAT Act) are taxable, but at 0%. The seller charges no VAT yet can still claim back the VAT on its purchases. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is a zero-rated supply?

children.topic: Exempt supplies: no VAT at all
children.note: Exempt supplies (First Schedule) are outside VAT. The seller charges no VAT and cannot claim back VAT on its purchases, so that VAT becomes a cost. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is an exempt supply and what happens to its input VAT?

children.topic: Output VAT: VAT on your sales
children.note: The VAT you charge customers on your taxable sales. You owe it to KRA.

manas.q: What is output VAT?

children.topic: Input VAT: VAT on your purchases
children.note: The VAT you paid suppliers on purchases used for your taxable business. You can deduct it from output VAT.

manas.q: What is input VAT?

children.note: Output VAT minus input VAT is what you pay KRA. If input is bigger, the extra is carried forward, or refunded in some cases.

manas.q: How is VAT payable worked out?

children.topic: Pulling VAT out of a price: 16/116
children.note: If a price already includes VAT at 16%, the VAT inside it is price × 16/116. Example: KES 11,600 × 16/116 = KES 1,600 VAT; price before VAT KES 10,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How do you find the VAT inside a VAT-inclusive price?

children.note: Who must register, how invoices work, and when and how to file and pay.
Who has to join the VAT system and who does not.
You must register if your taxable supplies are KES 5 million or more in a year. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the VAT registration threshold in Kenya?

children.note: A business below KES 5 million may ask to register, subject to KRA's conditions. It can then claim input VAT. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
A business that makes only exempt supplies does not need to register for VAT. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
A business may deregister if its taxable turnover falls below KES 5 million a year. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Non-resident suppliers selling through a digital marketplace must register for Kenyan VAT whatever their turnover. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

Turnover tax (1.5% of gross sales) is for residents with turnover above KES 1m and up to KES 25m. A TOT payer whose vatable supplies reach KES 5m must also register for VAT. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
The paperwork that proves the VAT.

VAT-registered persons must be on eTIMS. Tax invoices are serially numbered and generated from eTIMS; without one the buyer has weak support for an input claim. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: Where must a Kenyan VAT tax invoice be generated?

children.note: If a sale is reduced or goods are returned, issue a credit note within 6 months of the original invoice. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

children.topic: Tell KRA of changes in 21 days
children.note: Changes such as a new address or business details must be notified to KRA within 21 days. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Keep tax records in KES, in an official language, for 5 years from the end of the period they relate to (Tax Procedures Act s23). (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Deadlines and special rules.

children.topic: Tax point: when VAT becomes due
children.note: VAT is due at the earliest of: delivery or performance, a consultant's certificate, the invoice, or payment.

manas.q: What is the tax point for VAT?

children.note: File the VAT return on iTax and pay on or before the 20th of the following month. October VAT is due by 20 November. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When are the Kenyan VAT return and payment due?

children.note: Make a payment slip on iTax, then pay at the bank or by M-PESA Paybill 572572 using the payment registration number as the account. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Input VAT can be claimed only within 6 months after the end of the period in which the supply was made. Later claims are lost. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How long do you have to claim input VAT in Kenya?

children.note: Extra input VAT is carried forward. A refund is possible only if it comes from zero-rated supplies, withholding VAT, or approved aid-funded supplies. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

Appointed withholding agents keep back 2% of the taxable value from the supplier and remit it to KRA by the 20th of the next month. The supplier treats it as a credit. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is withholding VAT?

children.note: If you buy a service from abroad, you charge yourself the VAT and pay it. You can claim it back as input VAT if the service is for your taxable business. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is reverse VAT?

children.note: KRA lists nil filers, non-filers and missing traders. Buyers cannot claim input VAT on invoices from traders on this list. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Two more taxes, often met together when goods are made or imported.
A tax on selected goods and services.
A tax on certain goods and services made in or imported into Kenya, listed in the First Schedule of the Excise Duty Act 2015. Examples include drinks, tobacco and packaged water.

manas.q: What is excise duty?

children.note: Some products are taxed per unit (per litre, per kilo) and some as a % of value. Check the First Schedule for the current amount; this map gives no product rates.
Makers and importers of excisable goods apply for an excise licence on iTax (Registration, other registration, Excise licence).
Many excisable goods must carry KRA excise stamps under the EGMS system, with a fee per stamp. Stamps help KRA spot fake or untaxed goods.
Excise returns are filed on iTax by the 20th of the following month. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Taxes collected at the border.
A tax on goods brought into the country (import duty). Duties and taxes on imports are paid before KRA releases the goods, unless exempt.

manas.q: What is customs (import) duty?

children.note: Kenya applies the EAC Customs Management Act 2004. Its Fifth Schedule gives exemptions, for example for returning residents' personal goods.
EAC members charge the same import duty bands on goods from outside the EAC. The rate depends on the goods' tariff code. Look up the current band; none is given here.

manas.q: What is the EAC Common External Tariff?

children.note: The value duty is charged on: usually the cost of the goods plus insurance and freight to Kenya (CIF), converted to KES.

manas.q: What is customs value?

children.note: First import duty on customs value. Then excise (if any) on value plus duty. Excise is part of the VAT base. Then VAT on value plus duty plus excise.

manas.q: In what order are import taxes calculated?

children.note: Use a licensed clearing agent. Typical documents: Import Declaration Form (IDF), customs entry, invoices, and a Certificate of Conformity for regulated goods. Declare on KRA's customs portal.
Imports may also carry other levies such as the IDF fee and Railway Development Levy. Their rates change, so check KRA before using them.
Real numbers in KES. Every answer is checked.
Buy for 10,000 + VAT 1,600. Sell for 12,000 + VAT 1,920. Pay KRA 1,920 − 1,600 = KES 320, the VAT on the 2,000 value you added. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
A Nairobi hardware shop, VAT registered, all sales standard-rated. October sales KES 2,500,000 and purchases KES 1,800,000, both before VAT.
2,500,000 × 16% = KES 400,000. Customers are billed KES 2,900,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
1,800,000 × 16% = KES 288,000, backed by valid eTIMS invoices. Suppliers are owed KES 2,088,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
400,000 − 288,000 = KES 112,000 VAT payable. File and pay on iTax by 20 November. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Dr Trade receivables 2,900,000 / Cr Sales 2,500,000 / Cr VAT control 400,000. Sales are recorded without VAT.
Dr Purchases 1,800,000 / Dr VAT control 288,000 / Cr Trade payables 2,088,000.
Dr VAT control 112,000 / Cr Bank 112,000.
Credits 400,000. Debits 288,000 + 112,000 = 400,000. Balance nil. A credit balance at month end shows VAT still owed to KRA.

manas.q: What does a credit balance on the VAT control account mean?

children.note: Three traders each buy inputs of KES 1,000,000 + VAT 160,000 and sell for KES 1,500,000 before any VAT.
Output 240,000 − input 160,000 = pays KRA 80,000. Cost stays 1,000,000; profit 500,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Output VAT nil. Input 160,000 claimed back (carried forward or refunded). Cost 1,000,000; profit 500,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
No output VAT and no input claim. The 160,000 becomes a cost: 1,160,000. Profit 1,500,000 − 1,160,000 = 340,000. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Zero-rating is better for the seller: input VAT comes back. Exemption hides VAT inside costs and prices, cutting profit by KES 160,000 here.
A Mombasa trader imports goods: CIF USD 20,000 at an illustrative KES 130 per USD. Duty and excise rates below are illustrative rates, not the real ones. Other levies are ignored.
Illustrative rate, not the real one: 25%. 2,600,000 × 25% = KES 650,000.
Illustrative rate, not the real one: 10% of value plus duty. (2,600,000 + 650,000) × 10% = KES 325,000.
VAT-registered importer claims the 572,000 as input VAT, so inventory cost is 3,575,000. Dr Inventory 3,575,000 / Dr VAT control 572,000 / Cr Payables & bank 4,147,000.

Late filing: 5% of tax or KES 10,000, the higher. On VAT of 400,000 that is 20,000. Paying 112,000 one month late: 5% (5,600) + 1% interest (1,120) = KES 6,720. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Where candidates and new bookkeepers lose marks or money.
Both charge no VAT on sales, but only zero-rated lets you claim input VAT. Always say which one it is.
If the price already includes VAT, use 16/116, not 16%. 16% of 11,600 is 1,856, which is wrong; the VAT is 1,600.

children.topic: Showing VAT as income or expense
children.note: For a registered business, VAT collected is owed to KRA and VAT paid is reclaimed. Neither goes to profit, except unclaimable input VAT.
Input VAT older than 6 months after the supply period cannot be claimed. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Input VAT on their invoices is blocked. Check suppliers before buying. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Import VAT is on customs value plus duty plus excise, not on the invoice price alone.
An agent that fails to withhold VAT faces a penalty of 10% of the tax involved. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Try each, then open the steps.
October taxable sales KES 800,000 before VAT. Purchases KES 580,000 including VAT. Find VAT payable.
A withholding agent receives an invoice of KES 232,000 including VAT. How much is withheld and paid to the supplier?
2% × 200,000 = KES 4,000, remitted to KRA by the 20th of next month. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
232,000 − 4,000 = KES 228,000. The supplier counts the 4,000 as a credit against its VAT.
Customs value KES 1,000,000. Duty at an illustrative rate, not the real one, of 10%. No excise. Find import VAT.
Wanjiru's salon has taxable supplies of KES 4.2 million a year. Must she register for VAT?

4.2 million is below KES 5 million, so she need not register. She may register voluntarily, subject to KRA conditions, or use turnover tax if eligible. (check the current KRA rate; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Short videos found on YouTube today.
Startup Garage Africa: a Kenyan overview of VAT and who must register.
Counttuts: the difference between VAT on sales and VAT on purchases.
The Chief Finance Officer: why zero-rated and exempt supplies differ.
KRATV: KRA's own short walk-through of filing a VAT return.
Edspira: what an excise tax is and why governments use it.
KRATV: a long KRA session on how small businesses import and clear goods.
Trusted pages for checking the rules.
KRA's official VAT page: rates, registration, returns, withholding VAT.
KRA's page on excise duty, licences and stamps.
KRA's steps and documents for importing goods.
Background on how VAT works around the world.

maps.title: CA26 · 5. Tax procedures: returns, penalties, appeals

nodeData.note: How the tax system actually runs in Kenya: registering, keeping records, filing returns, paying on time, what happens when you are late, and how to argue with KRA. The main law is the Tax Procedures Act 2015 (TPA). It applies to the taxes you met in topics 2 to 4: PAYE, corporation tax, VAT and excise.

children.topic: What tax procedures are and why
children.note: The rules for HOW tax is collected, not how much. Topics 2-4 told you how to compute the tax; this topic tells you when to file, when to pay and what happens if you get it wrong.
The Tax Procedures Act 2015 (TPA) sets common rules for filing, paying, penalties, objections and refunds across income tax, VAT and excise. It is on Kenya Law.

manas.q: What does the Tax Procedures Act 2015 do?

children.topic: Who runs it: KRA and the Commissioner
children.note: Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) collects the tax. The Commissioner (KRA) makes assessments and decides objections and refund claims.
Most money lost to KRA by small firms is not the tax itself but penalties and interest for filing or paying late. Good procedures save real cash.
PAYE (topic 2), corporation tax (topic 3), VAT and excise (topic 4) each have their own return. This topic covers the deadlines and penalties for all of them.
Before you can file, you need a KRA PIN and you must keep proper records.
Your tax number on iTax. Every person and business dealing with KRA needs one. Misusing PIN rules is an offence: KES 2,000 per offence. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the penalty for a KRA PIN offence?

children.note: Add each tax you owe to your PIN: VAT when taxable supplies reach KES 5 million a year; an excise licence on iTax for excisable goods; turnover tax for small firms.
A VAT-registered business must tell KRA of changes (address, business details) within 21 days. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

TPA s23: keep records in an official language, in Kenya shillings, for 5 years from the end of the reporting period. Keep them longer if an amended assessment or case is still open. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How long must records be kept under TPA s23?

children.note: Sales and purchase invoices, eTIMS invoices, bank statements, payroll, and the books. A duka owner needs daily sales and purchase records even under turnover tax.
In Kenya you work out your own tax, file the return on iTax and pay it. KRA checks later. This is self-assessment.
The taxpayer computes and declares the tax due; KRA can review and change it later by an assessment.

manas.q: What is self-assessment?

children.note: VAT return and payment are due on or before the 20th of the following month, through iTax. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: When is the VAT return and payment due?

children.note: Excise returns are filed on iTax by the 20th of the following month. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
TOT return and payment by the 20th of the month after the tax period, via iTax or the M-Service App. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Withholding VAT agents remit what they withheld by the 20th of the following month. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
PAYE, income tax and rental income returns each have their own due date. Look them up on iTax before relying on a date from memory.
Generate a payment slip on iTax, then pay at the bank or by M-Pesa Paybill 572572 using the payment registration number as the account.
If you are registered for a tax and had no activity, you still file a nil return. Non-filers can land on the VAT Special Table, and buyers then cannot claim input VAT from them.

children.topic: Assessments: when KRA changes your tax
children.note: An assessment is KRA's official decision on how much tax you owe.
The return you file is treated as an assessment of your own tax.
TPA s29: if you do not file a return, KRA can estimate the tax itself and issue a default assessment.

manas.q: What is a default assessment (TPA s29)?

children.note: KRA can correct your self-assessment if it finds errors, for example missing sales.
An amended assessment must be made within 5 years. For fraud or wilful neglect there is no time limit. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the time limit for an amended assessment?

children.note: Records are kept 5 years (s23) because KRA can reopen a return for 5 years (s31(4)). Throw papers away early and you cannot defend yourself.
Being late costs you twice: a penalty for the late return and another for late payment, plus interest every month.
A fixed percentage of the tax due OR a minimum amount, whichever is HIGHER. The minimum is the floor. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How is a late filing penalty worked out?

children.note: 5% of the tax due or KES 10,000, whichever is higher. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the late filing penalty for VAT?

children.note: 25% of the tax due or KES 10,000, whichever is higher. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the late filing penalty for PAYE?

children.note: Companies and partnerships: 5% or KES 20,000. Individuals: 5% or KES 2,000. Whichever is higher. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: Late income tax return penalty: company vs individual?

children.note: KES 1,000 per month late, per the KRA turnover tax page. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
5% of the tax paid late. This is on top of any late filing penalty. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the late payment penalty under s83A?

children.note: 1% per month or part of a month on the unpaid tax. Two months and one day late counts as 3 months. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the late payment interest rate (s38)?

children.note: If you deliberately under-declare tax, the shortfall penalty is 75% of the shortfall. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
KES 1,000 per day, capped at KES 50,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Failing to deduct withholding VAT or withholding rental tax: 10% of the tax involved. Late payment of withholding taxes: 5%. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
You can apply to KRA for more time to pay or to pay in instalments. Ask before the due date.
An amnesty once waived penalties and interest if principal tax was paid by 31 Dec 2025. It has expired. Do not plan on it.
Real KES numbers. Check each one with a calculator.
VAT due KES 60,000. 5% = KES 3,000. The floor is KES 10,000, which is higher, so the penalty is KES 10,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
VAT due KES 400,000. 5% = KES 20,000, which is higher than KES 10,000, so the penalty is KES 20,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Tax KES 200,000 paid 3 months late. Penalty 5% = KES 10,000. Interest 1% x 3 months = KES 6,000. Extra cost KES 16,000; total paid KES 216,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
PAYE due KES 30,000. 25% = KES 7,500, below the KES 10,000 floor, so the penalty is KES 10,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
PAYE due KES 120,000. 25% = KES 30,000, above KES 10,000, so the penalty is KES 30,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Dr Tax penalties and interest (expense) KES 16,000 / Cr KRA payable KES 16,000. Penalties are a cost of being late, not part of the tax itself.
If you disagree with an assessment, follow the steps in order and never miss a deadline.
Object in writing within 30 days of the assessment notice. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: How long do you have to object to an assessment?

children.note: It states the grounds, the undisputed tax is paid, and supporting documents are attached. Miss one and the clock may not even start.

manas.q: What makes an objection valid under s51?

children.note: KRA must decide within 60 days of a valid objection. If it does not, the objection is treated as allowed. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What happens if the Commissioner does not decide an objection in 60 days?

children.note: Appeal to the Tax Appeals Tribunal within 30 days of the objection decision (s51, s52). Undisputed tax must be paid or arranged. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
A party unhappy with the Tribunal can appeal to the High Court within 30 days. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
The last step under the TPA is the Court of Appeal, again within 30 days. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

children.topic: ADR: talk it out in 120 days
children.note: Alternative Dispute Resolution is voluntary mediation with a facilitator, not arbitration. It should finish in 120 days (s55). (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is KRA ADR and how long does it take?

children.note: Not for matters against the Constitution or law, pure technical points of law, cases needing a court ruling for the public, issues already decided by a court, or where a party is unwilling.
Object 30, KRA decides 60, Tribunal 30, High Court 30, Court of Appeal 30. ADR 120.

manas.q: List the dispute steps and their time limits.

children.note: If you paid too much tax, KRA can set it against other tax you owe (offset) or pay it back (refund).
An overpayment is usually used to clear other tax debts before any cash comes back.
Income tax: within 5 years. Other taxes: within 12 months. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

manas.q: Time limits to claim an overpayment under s47?

children.note: The Commissioner should decide a refund claim within 120 days. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Excess input VAT is normally carried forward. A cash refund is possible only where it comes from zero-rated supplies, withholding, or approved aid-funded supplies.
Mistakes candidates make again and again.
Always compare the % with the minimum and take the HIGHER figure. 5% of KES 60,000 is not the answer; KES 10,000 is.
Late filing and late payment are separate penalties. Late return AND late payment means both apply, plus interest.
Interest is 1% per month or PART of a month. 2 months and 3 days = 3 months.
The PAYE late return penalty is much higher than VAT. Do not copy 5% across.
An objection that does not pay the undisputed tax is not valid, so the 60-day clock may not run.
The s37E amnesty ended with 31 Dec 2025. Do not give it as a current relief.
Try each one before opening the answer.
A trader files the VAT return late and pays KES 80,000 two months late. Total cost?
5% = KES 4,000; floor KES 10,000 is higher, so KES 10,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Penalty 5% = KES 4,000. Interest 1% x 2 = KES 1,600. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
Income tax due KES 50,000, return late. Penalty for a company vs an individual?
5% = KES 2,500; floor KES 20,000 is higher, so KES 20,000. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
5% = KES 2,500; floor KES 2,000 is lower, so KES 2,500. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)
A valid objection is lodged and KRA has not replied after 60 days. What happens?
The objection is treated as allowed (s51). The taxpayer wins by default. (check the current KRA rule; checked 8 Nov 2026)

KRA on how an objection is reviewed.
